4.s:
Robert Lee Bell Sr. was born on 5 November 1935, the fourth child of John Henry Bell, a house painter, and Margaret Beatrice Eaken. His family was moving between Birmingham and Atlanta in the very year he was born, and the records never agreed about which city it had been: the Social Security file says Birmingham, his own obituary says Atlanta, and the 1940 census — which found him at four years old and gave the household’s 1935 address as Atlanta — says Georgia. He may not have been certain himself.

His father walked out about 1942, when he was six, and never came back. The family went north to Wheaton, Illinois, where in January 1944 his eldest brother Thomas was killed in a car crash at sixteen; the death notice in the Birmingham papers lists “Bobby, 8” among the brothers left.

He enlisted in the United States Air Force on 4 February 1957, at twenty-one, and served nine years and ten days, to 14 February 1966, as an Airman Third Class. The service note on his veteran’s record names two wars — Korea and Vietnam — and the marker later cut for him credits him with service in both branches, as A3 in the Air Force and as a staff sergeant in the Army. Not one word of any of it appears in the family’s own papers; it was recoverable only because he was commemorated in a national cemetery.

He married Willie Joyce Stephens at Fort Payne in August 1960, three and a half years into his enlistment. Their first son was born at Birmingham in 1961 — the Birmingham News printed the birth, giving the parents as “Mr. and Mrs. Robert Lee Bell (Willie Joyce Stephens)” and the second at Fort Worth, Texas, in 1964 — Carswell Air Force Base is at Fort Worth, which is why an Alabama family was in Texas at all. So the first six years of that marriage were service years, lived at postings, with a husband twice overseas. It ended about 1972–73, and he married again afterwards. In January 1983 his mother’s obituary placed him at Mobile, Alabama, named among her four surviving children.

The later years were not quiet ones. On 20 November 1989 police in Blount County, Tennessee, searched a pair of massage businesses called Sue Lynn’s Health Studio and the 129 Health Studio, a mobile home and a dumpster, and he was charged with running them as brothels. In March 1990 he was convicted on five counts of promoting prostitution, for offences between 1987 and 1989, and sentenced to five consecutive two-year terms — ten years — and a $3,000 fine. The appeals court, affirming every part of it in August 1991, described an operation reaching at least seven establishments across several states, from Sevierville and Chattanooga to Fort Lauderdale, Florida; it noted an earlier guilty plea to possessing cocaine, that he had declined to give the probation officers an employment history, and it upheld the consecutive terms on the finding that he had made crime a major source of his livelihood. The Tennessee prison record for Robert Bell, born 5 November 1935 — six foot two, 170 pounds, blue eyes, grey hair — shows the sentence running out on 29 April 1999. It is the likeliest reason he ended his life in Chattanooga.

He died at Chattanooga on 14 February 2001, aged sixty-five — thirty-five years to the day after his discharge. Four photographs survive from his last years: beside a Tennessee lake in winter, deep-sea fishing in a straw hat, a plain portrait in a blue polo shirt, and one taken in a spring yard about 2000 or 2001, where he stands with his son, his daughter-in-law and his two grandsons. His name is cut on a white marble marker in the memorial section at Chattanooga National Cemetery, Section MA, site 36, beneath a cross and the words IN MEMORY OF.

5.s:
Willie Joyce Stephens was born on 19 March 1942, the daughter of Jess Steve Willard Stephens, a mechanic who went by “Willard” and “J. W.,” and Grace Estelle Truett of Coffeeville in Clarke County. She was a native of York, her father’s Sumter County town. Her name is in a Birmingham high-school graduating-class list printed on 27 May 1960, and three months later, on 26 August, aged eighteen, she married Robert Lee Bell at Fort Payne, in DeKalb County; the clerk wrote her father down as “J. W. Stephens.” Her first son was born eleven months later, in 1961, and a second followed in 1964 at Fort Worth. Her husband left the family about 1972 or 1973.

On 24 May 1980 she married again, to John Duncan Lammon, in the same town where she had married the first time. It was a home wedding, not a church one — a hired brass arch dressed with pink and blue flowers set up in somebody’s living room, white tapers in candelabra on either side, the bride in a full-length ivory gown with long sheer sleeves and the groom in a pale blue three-piece suit. She was thirty-eight.

By the end she was living at Jackson, in Clarke County, where she kept her own clothing shop. She died on Tuesday 27 July 1982, aged forty. The Birmingham News carried the notice the next day: her husband survived her, and so did her mother and stepfather, Charles L. and Grace Roberts of Birmingham, and two sons and a daughter. The funeral was at Latham Funeral Chapel that same day. She was taken south-west to Clarke County — the country her mother’s Truett people came from — and buried at Mount Gilead Cemetery, which is the Lammon family’s ground, not the Truetts’. Her second husband lies there, and so does the Lammon generation before him. Her stone calls her simply JOYCE STEPHENS LAMMON, and under the dates it carries Micah 6:8: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good: and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.” In the lower corner, in smaller letters, someone had cut two more words: AN ANGEL.

She graduated from Phillips High School in Birmingham in 1960, having transferred in from Ramsay in her third term. Her senior entry in the Phillips yearbook lists her as a Senior Y-Teen and its treasurer, a Student Representative Council member, a Red Cross representative and a Marshal — and prints her photograph, the earliest likeness of her the family has. She was married three months after that yearbook went to press.

For years she could not be found at all, because she did not die a Bell. Three photographs of her survive, all from her last two years: her wedding day; a restaurant above the water with her husband’s arm around her shoulders; and one of her alone in a panelled room hung with framed stamp collections. They are the only known pictures of her.

6.s:
Richard Clark Tuttle, known all his life as Dick, was born in 1929 in Terre Haute, Indiana, the second son of Gifford Herman Tuttle and Helen May Knott, into a family that had been in and around Terre Haute since the 1850s. The earliest photograph of him shows him at about nine, in a sweater and short trousers, standing beside his older brother Robert on a patch of spring grass. When he was ten the household also held his grandmother Martha — a woman he grew up under the same roof with, and whom his own daughter would later say she knew nothing at all about.

About 1944 or 1945, when he was fifteen, his father moved the family north to Evanston, Illinois — the moment this branch left Indiana after nearly a century. He graduated from Evanston Township High School in the class of 1947; the family still has his own copy of the yearbook, The Evanstonian of ’47, with his name printed in the corner. He took classes at Northwestern.

He enlisted in the United States Army and was certified at Fort Lee, Virginia, on 3 August 1951 as a quartermaster supply-records specialist. He served in occupied Germany: a photograph kept in the family shows him in uniform beside the sign for the Headquarters, Heilbronn Sub Post — the only evidence of where he was actually stationed.

At the end of 1952 he was a soldier in Germany, and the Terre Haute paper that announced his grandparents' golden wedding noted that he was sending his congratulations from there. His father's death notice in December 1974 named him simply as Richard C., one of two sons.

His senior portrait appears on the class pages of the 1947 Evanstonian, the Evanston Township High School yearbook — the printed pages inside the copy of the book the family still has.

The Terre Haute paper announced his birth at the end of July 1929 — on the 29th or 30th — as a son, Richard Clark, born to G. H. and Helen Tuttle of 2266 Warren Street.

Back in Evanston he met Judith Frost, who had come up from Marion, Indiana, to take a degree at Northwestern; they were introduced, the family says, through a friend. They married in the middle fifties and in 1959, expecting their first child, bought a house on Dartmouth Avenue in Deerfield, Illinois. He worked for a Chicago label printer until the owner of the firm killed himself with carbon monoxide, and in 1971 he moved the family to Cincinnati to take a job with H. S. Crocker Co., another label company. He lived out his life there and died in Cincinnati in 2015, two years after Judith.

7.s:
Judith Katharine Frost was born on 5 July 1934 at Parkersburg, West Virginia, the only child of Alan Chalmers Frost, who managed dime stores, and Velma Gladys Roush, a Mason County girl who had run away from home at sixteen. A studio photograph of about 1936 survives of her at two and a half, grinning in a knitted sweater-dress, ankle socks and white lace-up shoes.

Her father’s work moved them. By 1940 the family was renting on Stocking Road in Mansfield, Ohio, for thirty dollars a month; by 1950 they were at Marion, Indiana, where he ran the S. S. Kresge store seventy hours a week. In March 1947, when she was twelve, her mother took her to Akron to stay with her aunt Florence, and the two of them went on to Mason, West Virginia, to the bedside of her grandmother Bertha, who lay ill at home; another aunt came up from Georgia to join them. The Marion paper printed it as a social note.

She graduated from Marion High School and went on to Earlham College and to Northwestern, and it was at Evanston that she met Richard Clark Tuttle. They took out a licence in Cook County on 26 June 1957 and were married at three o’clock on Saturday 29 June in St. Luke’s Chapel, Evanston. A photograph of her at a college formal in the early 1950s — a dark floor-length gown, a young man beside her in a dark suit with a white boutonnière — belongs to the few years before that.

They bought a house on Dartmouth Avenue in Deerfield, Illinois in 1959, and moved to Cincinnati in 1971 when Richard took a job with the label printer H. S. Crocker. There were four children. She taught at the Indian Hill Schools — “a positive early influence for hundreds of small children,” her obituary said — and she was a portrait painter and a maker of very fine dollhouse miniatures. To her grandchildren she was Mimi.

Her photograph is in the 1952 Cactus, the Marion High School yearbook, in the fourth row of the class pages, and the entry beside it lists her: Latin Club, Booster Club, Y-Teens, Student Council, and co-chairman of the Mother-Daughter Christmas Tea.

She died at Cincinnati on 31 October 2013, after fifty-six years of marriage. Her funeral was held on 5 November at St. Barnabas Episcopal Church on Montgomery Road.

8.s:
John Henry Bell was born on 4 August 1901 in Barbour County, Alabama — a date his family still remembered in 2009, and one he wrote down himself on a draft card in 1942. He was the eldest son of Thomas Jefferson Bell and Alice May Bradley, farmers near Louisville, and he appears in their household in 1910 and 1920 simply as “Henry.”

By 1925 he had left for Birmingham, and a Barbour County court recorded him there — “Henry Bell, Birmingham” — when his grandfather’s estate was divided seven ways among Tom’s children. Two years later, on Friday the thirteenth of May 1927, he married Margaret Beatrice Eaken. Both Birmingham papers thought a couple marrying on such a date was worth a humorous column. Their first son arrived six months later, and he named the boy Thomas J., for his own father.

He drove a truck for a dry cleaner, then painted houses — in Birmingham, and in Atlanta through the middle thirties. There were six children. The second, a daughter named Marion, was born and lost in 1932 and buried at Forest Hill in Birmingham — his wife’s ground, and the one family burying place he would not be laid in either. In June 1940 he was convicted in Jefferson County of desertion and non-support, and served four months of a twelve-month sentence; the prison ledger records him at 163 pounds, physical condition good, teeth bad.

He was released on 17 October 1940 by order of Judge Emmett Perry, and about a year later he left for good. On 23 February 1942 he registered for the draft in Cincinnati — five foot nine, 160 pounds, blue eyes, brown hair, a knot on his left leg near the hip — and gave, as the person who would always know his address, his mother in Dothan. It is the last document he is known to have signed.

After that he vanishes. His family moved north to Wheaton, Illinois, where his sixteen-year-old son was killed in a car crash in January 1944; the certificate names the father simply as “Henry Bell.” By the time his mother died in December 1956 her obituary listed six surviving children, and he was not among them. He lies in neither family cemetery — not at Forest Hill with his wife and his baby daughter, and not at Bethlehem with his parents. The likeliest trace of him is a Henry Bell, fifty-one, white, born in Alabama and recorded as “separated,” lodging in a home for the homeless outside Cincinnati in April 1950 — the only man of that description in the entire county.

9.s:
Margaret Beatrice Eaken was born on 10 July 1908 at Cuba, in Sumter County, Alabama — her mother's home ground, the small town on the Mississippi line where her father would be buried fourteen years later. She was the eldest child of Andrew Jackson Eaken and Maggie Dillon Swain, and she appears aged one in the 1910 census of Mobile, where her father had found work and her young uncle Langford Swain was lodging with them.

She was eighteen when she married John Henry Bell on Friday the thirteenth of May 1927; both Birmingham papers thought a couple marrying on such a date worth a humorous paragraph. Their first son was born that November. There were six children; a daughter, Marion, died in infancy in 1932 and was buried at Forest Hill. In 1940 her husband was convicted in Jefferson County of desertion and non-support and served four months, and about 1942 he left for good.

By January 1944 she had taken the family north to Wheaton, Illinois, where her mother and stepfather were living, and there her eldest son Thomas Jackson — sixteen, and named for her brother — was killed in a car crash. She remarried in 1948, to Claude B. Smith, and the 1950 census finds her at Lineville, Clay County, Alabama, with her four surviving Bell children in the household.

Her later years were spent in Georgia. In July 1962, when her stepfather died, she was living at Fitzgerald in south Georgia and the notice called her “Mrs. Beatrice E. Smith”; her three brothers were then at Providence, Rhode Island, in Germany with the Army, and at Birmingham. Later she was at Clarkston outside Atlanta, where she retired as a saleswoman at Rich's department store and belonged to Vestavia Alliance Church. A cousin who had known her all her life remembered that she “always had a larger-than-life personality”; her grandson remembered “such a refined lady.” She died on Sunday 16 January 1983, aged seventy-four, and was brought back to Birmingham to lie at Forest Hill, in Section 19, near the infant daughter she had buried half a century before. Her flat granite marker reads MARGARET E. SMITH, JULY 10, 1908 — JAN. 16, 1983, GONE TO REST. Obituaries ran in both cities, naming her husband, her four children, her mother and her two brothers; neither version mentioned John Henry Bell.

Her grave is marked under her second married name: a flat granite stone carved with praying hands and a flower, 'MARGARET E. SMITH, JULY 10 1908 - JAN 16 1983, GONE TO REST'. A snapshot survives of her out in the cold in a dark coat, sitting on a wooden trestle in a bare winter yard with an iron fence behind her.

She worked for Rich's, the Atlanta department store, and belonged to the Vestavia Alliance Church in Birmingham; she died on Sunday 16 January 1983 at Clarkston, Georgia, and was buried at Forest Hill in Birmingham.

For a long time the family believed she died in 1985. 1985 was the year her own mother died, and the two had quietly become confused.

10.s:
Jess Steve Willard Stephens was born on 29 April 1917 at York, in Sumter County, Alabama, the son of John Willis Stephens and Mary Price Williams. His parents had christened him for Jess Willard, the heavyweight champion of the world, who had been heavyweight champion of the world for thirteen months when he was born. The name stuck twice over: he signed himself “Willard” and “J. W.” by turns, which is one reason he was so hard to find — his father went by “J. W.” too. In 1920 the family was living at Election Precinct 6, York, in the same small Sumter County precinct where the Swains — the family of the man his daughter would one day marry into — had lived twenty years before.

On 8 April 1939, aged twenty-two, he married Grace Estelle Truett at Fort Payne, in DeKalb County, at the other end of the state; she was twenty, and the clerk wrote his parents down as “J. W. Stephens and Mary Price.” Their daughter Willie Joyce was born on 19 March 1942. The marriage did not last — Grace married again in 1947 — and he married again himself; his second wife was named Jessie.

The York he was born into was small and plain. Its 1924 insurance map gives the population as 1,651 and notes, in the blunt shorthand of the trade, 'Water Facilities: None. Fire Dept: None. Public lights electric; streets not paved.'

He worked as a mechanic. In April 1947, when his father died, he was in the Army and stationed at Washington, D.C.; by 1957 he was living at Birmingham. He died on 18 March 1971 at Charleston, South Carolina, aged fifty-three, and his obituary ran two days later. He is buried at Magnolia Cemetery in Charleston under a low granite stone he shares with Jessie, who followed him in 1990. The cutter put four words under his name that no document had ever bothered to record: BORN YORK, ALA.

11.s:
Grace Estelle Truett was born on 14 January 1917 in Clarke County, Alabama, the daughter of Thomas William Truette and Sennie Lawrence. In 1920 she was a toddler in her father's household at Coffeeville, listed as “Gracie E.” with a younger sister, Gladys. Her father died before she was thirteen; her mother was a widow for four years and then married again in the next county, and a third sister, Jewel Rae, is named in the family's Social Security records.

On 8 April 1939, aged twenty, Grace married Willard Stephens at Fort Payne in DeKalb County, two hundred and fifty miles north-east of the Clarke County villages her family had lived in for four generations. Their daughter Willie Joyce was born on 19 March 1942. The marriage did not last. In 1947 she married Eugene Raiford Rivers Jr. at Montgomery, and later Charles Leroy Roberts; Social Security records carry her under a fourth name, “Grace Tru Morgan,” so there was probably one more marriage still.

She outlived her daughter, who died at forty in 1982. Grace herself died on Monday 9 November 1992 at Irondale, in Jefferson County, aged seventy-five. The Birmingham papers carried her death notice on the Wednesday morning, the same morning the family drove west for the graveside service at eleven o'clock. It named the two sisters who survived her: Gladys, who had never left Clarke County and was living at Jackson, and Jewell, four hundred miles away at Lawton, Oklahoma.

She lies at Tuscaloosa Memorial Park under a bronze companion marker cut with roses and the words TOGETHER FOREVER. Her plate reads only GRACE T. — the T for the Truett name she had been born with seventy-five years earlier and had not used in half a century. Charles L. Roberts, who died in 1999, lies beside her under the other plate.

12.s:
Gifford Herman Tuttle was born on 7 October 1903, the first child of Dennis Clark Tuttle and Leona Marie Alexander, who had married on New Year's Eve nine months and six days earlier. His name was almost certainly a tribute: his father Dennis had been orphaned of his own father before his first birthday and was raised by a stepfather, Gifford H. Spear. A name that looked arbitrary for four generations turns out to be a small monument to the man who stepped in.

He grew up in Terre Haute, where the family lived through every census from 1910 to 1940 — his father a freight-car repairman on the Pennsylvania Railroad, his widowed grandmother Mary under the same roof. On 2 April 1923, at nineteen, he married Helen May Knott in Rush County, Indiana. They had two sons, Robert Dale and Richard Clark.

On Saturday 8 October 1910, the day after his seventh birthday, his small friends gave him a surprise party at his home in Terre Haute. There were games and contests with prizes, ice cream and cake, and thirteen children: Grace McKee, George Hoffman, Raymond Lier, Opal Smith, Mary Hoffman, Kenneth Tucker, Margaret Dooley, Ron Dooley, Frank Hoffman, Edward McKee, Francis McKee, A. Tucker, and the honoree. The birthday cake was a gift from his grandmother. Six years on, in February 1916, he turns up again in the society column as one of twenty-one children at Gretchen Cunningham's birthday party at Twelfth and Mulberry streets, where the house and the ices were decorated in pink and white.

The earliest printed appearance of his name yet found is a line of small-town social news: in August 1914, aged ten, "Mr. and Mrs. Dennis Tuttle and children, Gifford and Dorothy, and Mrs. Mary Alexander, of Terre Haute" went out to West Terre Haute for the weekend.

About 1944 or 1945 he moved the household out of Terre Haute to Evanston, Illinois — the moment this branch of the family left Indiana, where Tuttles and Fuerstenbergers had lived since the 1850s. By 1970 he and Helen were at Highland Park, Illinois. He died suddenly on 18 December 1974 at Highland Park, Illinois, aged seventy-one, and his body rested at St. Luke's Episcopal Church at Lee and Hinman Streets in Evanston, where a requiem mass was sung on the Friday evening of 20 December. The interment was private and the family asked that flowers be omitted. His father, Dennis, then ninety, outlived him by eight months. The day is known only because somebody wrote it by hand on the deaths page of the family Bible; the Social Security index records nothing finer than the month. A photograph survives of him with Helen in the early 1970s, the two of them hand in hand and wearing flowers, most likely at their fiftieth anniversary.

13.s:
Helen May Knott was born on 12 June 1905 in Indiana, the younger daughter of Joseph McGee Knott, a heater in a Terre Haute steel mill, and Martha Ellen (Lamb) Ford Knott. Her sister Mildred was seven years older; a half-brother, Percy Ford, was a grown man by the time Helen could walk. The 1910 census of Terre Haute Ward 4 catches all three of them under one roof — Helen four, Mildred eleven, Percy twenty-four.

Three photographs survive of her childhood in Terre Haute about 1911 to 1913: one on the lawn beside her big sister Mildred, which their mother sent as a postcard inscribed “My too sweet dauters, Mildred and Helen”; and two of Helen with her friend Grace, both girls in wide straw hats. The friend was almost certainly Grace Estella Schomer, born six months after Helen in December 1905, the daughter of the man who ran Terre Haute’s dancing school — a child performer the local paper once called “the miniature Pavlowa.” She lived to be ninety-seven.

On 2 April 1923 Helen married Gifford Herman Tuttle in Rush County; the marriage application names both her parents, and her son Robert Dale’s obituary named them again more than eighty years later. Two sons followed, Robert Dale in 1925 and Richard Clark — Alec’s grandfather — in 1929. They raised them in a rented house in Terre Haute through the Depression, with Helen’s widowed mother living under the same roof; the 1940 census has Martha Knott in the household with the two boys. Her father had died in January 1932 — the Cedar Rapids paper that printed his death notice named his two daughters, “Mrs. E. C. Cooper of this city and Mrs. Helen Tuttle of Terre Haute” — and he lay in Highland Lawn Cemetery across the city, under a flat granite marker cut simply “Joseph Knott 1851 1932”; her mother joined him in the same grave in 1945, under a matching stone.

The Chicago Tribune of Tuesday 26 April 1977 carried her under her own maiden name - "Helen Knott Tuttle of Wilmette" - naming her two sons, her seven grandchildren and her sister Mildred Cooper of Cedar Rapids, and setting the visitation and a requiem eucharist for that evening in the Lady Chapel of St. Luke's Episcopal Church, Evanston, the church the family had belonged to for thirty years. The notice ends with the two words that explain why no grave has ever been found for her: "Interment private." Terre Haute had not forgotten her. On the same morning the Terre Haute Tribune ran her among its DEATHS under the heading MRS. HELEN TUTTLE, saying word had been received by a sister-in-law still living in the city of the death of "Mrs. Helen Tuttle, 71, Wilmet, Ill., formerly of Terre Haute, who died Sunday evening at Evanston, Ill." Sunday was the 24th; the evening is a detail no other record gives, and the age of 71 is the strongest evidence yet that she was born in 1905 and not 1904. When her second son was born in the last days of July 1929 the family were living at 2266 Warren Street, Terre Haute, and the paper announced him in a single line: "to G. H. and Helen Tuttle, 2266 Warren street, a son, Richard Clark."

About 1944 or 1945 the family moved north to Evanston, Illinois. A hand-tinted studio portrait shows Helen in her late thirties, dark hair set in rolled waves; another photograph catches her with Gifford in the early 1970s, near their fiftieth anniversary. Gifford died in 1974, and Helen lived on as a widow in Wilmette. She died on 24 April 1977 at Evanston Hospital, aged seventy-one. Her death notice in the Wilmette Life named her two sons — Robert D. of Evanston and Richard C. of Cincinnati — her sister Mildred Cooper of Cedar Rapids, and seven grandchildren. Mildred followed her six months later. Where Helen was buried is not known: she is not in the Knott plot at Highland Lawn, and no memorial has been made for her anywhere.

14.s:
Alan Chalmers Frost was born on 10 February 1903 at Paterson, New Jersey, the third child of Harry B. Frost, an English-born silk manufacturer, and Katharine Chalmers of Orange. His middle name was his mother’s maiden name. The earliest picture of him is a studio photograph of about 1903 or 1904: an infant in a long white gown and bonnet, propped on a stool between his sister Katherine, six or seven, and his brother Harry, three or four.

He was two years old in the Paterson household of the 1905 state census, which kept a live-in servant. By 1910 the family had moved out to Wyckoff, in Franklin Township, Bergen County, and in 1915 he was twelve and set down as a “scholar” — the transcriber read his handwritten name as “Ellen C.”, which is why he is hard to find there.

By the time his father died in December 1930 he was living at Wilmington, Delaware, and he was still there the following January, when the Wyckoff column noticed that “Alan Frost, of Wilmington, Del., spent Sunday and Monday with his mother, Mrs. Harry B. Frost, of Wyckoff avenue.” She died three weeks later.

Some time in the early 1930s he married Velma Gladys Roush of Mason County, West Virginia; no record of the marriage has been found. Their daughter Judith was born at Parkersburg in July 1934. By 1940 he was managing a five-and-ten at Mansfield, Ohio, and by 1950 the family was at Marion, Indiana. When he registered for the draft on 16 February 1942 he was at 1506 West Fourth Street, Marion, working for the S. S. Kresge Co. — five foot ten, a hundred and forty-five pounds, light complexion, brown hair, blue eyes — and the person who would always know his address was Velma Gladys Frost. He spent his whole working life in that chain, running the Marion store for many years at seventy hours a week, until Jupiter took over the location about 1962 and the Frosts moved to Flint, Michigan.

Velma died at Flint on 3 October 1964, and the cremation certificate gives his address as 316 West Dartmouth. He outlived her by eighteen years and died in May 1982, aged seventy-nine, at Clyde, a village in Wayne County, New York. What took him to the Finger Lakes has never been explained in this family, but his elder brother Harry had married a Clyde girl, Esther Baird, in the village church there in December 1933 and lies in its Maple Grove cemetery — which is very likely the answer.

15.s:
Velma Gladys Roush was born on 21 June 1907 in Mason County, West Virginia, the daughter of John G. Roush and Bertha E. Nease. The assessor's birth register for Graham District wrote the date down that year, with her mother as the informant.

She was fifteen months old on the evening of Saturday 12 September 1908, when her father tried to fill a coal-miner's lamp from an oil can that had been standing by a hot cook stove, and the house at Broad Run went up. Her eldest sister, who had been ironing beside the table, died within hours; a second sister died five days later; the house and everything in it burned, including the family's clothes. Velma was the infant asleep in the room, and a six-year-old sister carried her out through the smoke to their grandparents' house, unseen and unaided. Her father died of his burns on 21 October. She can never have remembered any of it, and within six weeks the two people best able to tell her were dead.

Her widowed mother kept the four surviving girls together. In 1910 the household at Wagner, Mason County, was Bertha at its head with Iva, Florence, Velma and the baby Claudia; in 1920 Velma was still in the county, about thirteen. She ran away from home at sixteen. She was five feet tall, and somebody wrote in her school yearbook, “She's small but oh my!”

On 6 September 1931 she married Alfred Hesterberg at Greenup, Kentucky, signing as Velma Roush and giving her parents as John Roush and Bertha Nease. He divorced her at Akron in October 1933, when she was living at Charleston, West Virginia. Her daughter was born at Parkersburg in July 1934. By 1940 she was at Mansfield, Ohio, and by 1950 at Marion, Indiana, where her husband Alan C. Frost managed the S. S. Kresge store and worked seventy hours a week; about 1962 the family moved to Flint, Michigan, when another chain took the Kresge location over. She belonged to the Episcopal church at Flint.

In Marion the family lived at 914 South D Street. Her husband managed the S. S. Kresge dollar store on the square, and she went with him to the staff parties: a Valentine dinner for the employees at the Marion Hotel in February 1947, and in May 1949 a dinner for both Marion stores' staff to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the Kresge chain. On a Monday morning in May 1953 she cut one of the ribbons at the opening of a new Marion store, standing in for the town's retail trade beside the mayor's wife and the wives of the president and vice-president of the Chamber of Commerce. At Christmas 1953 she and her husband put up a neighbourhood tree with the Drummonds at the corner of Ninth and D Streets, and the neighbours held a party round it; the Marion Chronicle printed a photograph of it lit up at night. In August 1955 she gave a lawn shower for a bride-elect at her own house, her daughter helping as assistant hostess, with an umbrella and a miniature bride and bridegroom over the gift table. She went away when she could: a few days with relatives at Cleveland in 1951, a whole month in Florida in the spring of 1954. Her health was failing well before the end. She was admitted to a Marion hospital twice within nine days in November 1959.

She is in the public record before she was two. In the Mason County court of May 1909 her mother "Bertha Roush qualified as guardian for Iva Roush, Florence Roush, Velm Roush and Della Roush, infant children of John G. Roush, deceased, and gave bond in the penalty of $500, with Moses Roush as surety" — the four fatherless girls, their mother, and their grandfather standing behind the bond, printed in the Point Pleasant Register.

She had arthritis, and the treatment of the day was aspirin in high doses, which is hard on the stomach. She died on 3 October 1964 at Hurley Hospital in Flint, aged fifty-seven, of a perforated duodenum, and was cremated at White Chapel three days later. Her paid death notice named her two surviving sisters, Mrs. Joseph Walk of Akron and Mrs. William Kirton of Boynton Beach. Two photographs of her survive: a studio portrait, and a colour snapshot of her in her fifties, laughing in a red-and-black plaid coat with the autumn leaves down behind her.

16.s:
Thomas Jefferson Bell — “Tom J.” to the stonecutter, “Tom Bell” to the probate clerk — farmed near Louisville in Barbour County, Alabama. He was one of the eleven children of John T. Bell and Sallie Cox, and he married Alice May Bradley on 13 August 1895, when she was eighteen. They had nine children. Seven were still living when the 1920 census found the whole household together at Louisville — Thomas J. 44, Alice 42, Henry 18, Ray 16, William 12, Ethel 10 and Juanita 2 — and two were already buried in the churchyard at Bethlehem Baptist, the congregation his people had belonged to since it was organised in 1824.

He died on 30 August 1921, at about forty-three, and was laid beside those two children. The Clayton Record called him a son of Mr. and Mrs. John Bell Sr., pioneer citizens, and said he was buried at Bethlehem “where two of his children are buried.” The granite his family set over him afterwards gives different dates — SEPT. 18, 1874 and AUG. 27, 1920, each a year adrift of the newspaper — and the two have never been reconciled.

He left no estate. The county’s probate minutes for the year after his death record no administration in his name, and the clerk’s index to seventy years of administrators’ records contains no Thomas J. Bell at all. There was simply nothing to divide — and his own father had died six years earlier worth fifty thousand dollars in lands, cotton, insurance and money.

So when his children finally received something, it came through that estate instead. In April 1925 a Barbour County court divided one deceased heir’s share seven ways among Tom’s children, naming each of them — Ellie, Ray, Ruth, William, Ethel, little Juanita, and “Henry Bell, Birmingham.” That decree is the court’s own answer to the question of who his children were, and it is the document that finally settled this family’s longest-standing puzzle.

The church he and Alice lie beside, Bethlehem Baptist on the Clayton–Louisville road, had been gathered by thirteen people in April 1824, six years before the Bells came into the county.

The index to his Alabama death record gives his age at death as 45 years, 11 months and 18 days. Set against the Clayton Record's date of 30 August 1921, that puts his birth at about 12 September 1875 -- which agrees with the 1920 census's 'Thomas J, 44' and with the month, though not the day or the year, cut on his headstone.

Alice outlived him by thirty-five years, married again, and was brought home to lie beside him. Their names are cut side by side on one block of grey granite at Bethlehem, under the single word BELL.

17.s:
Alice May Bradley was born on 8 October 1876 in Barbour County, Alabama, the daughter of Henry Bradley and Elvira Loveless. She lost both parents young. Her father and mother lie together at Clayton City Cemetery, under two draped marble stones inside one iron rail, and the cemetery record reads their worn figures as 27 February 1887 for Henry Bradley, when Alice was ten, and 14 June 1891 for Elvira. That October a county court appointed a guardian for Alice, then fourteen, and her younger sister Katie, twelve, recording that the minors had no father living. The petitioner was a great-aunt, L. M. Bell, and among the seven signers of the four-thousand-dollar bond were two Bradley relations and John T. Bell — the man who would be her father-in-law four years later. Two years after that, a Eufaula paper printed the probate court’s own settlement of an earlier guardianship and listed her by name among “the following named minor children of Henry Bradley, deceased.”

She married Thomas Jefferson Bell on 13 August 1895, at eighteen, and had nine children. Her sister Katie married Tom’s younger brother George, so the two orphaned Bradley girls went into the same farming family at Louisville. Widowed in 1921, Alice married Mack K. Norton — and there is a quiet symmetry in it, because Mack’s first wife had been Katie, who died in 1924. Two Bradley sisters each married a Bell, each was widowed, and the same man married them in turn.

By 1935 she was living with Mack at 118 East North Street in Dothan, and it was that address her eldest son wrote on his draft card in 1942, when the form asked who would always know where he was. The 1940 census records her, on the supplementary line, as married more than once, eighteen at her first marriage, nine children born. Mack died in 1954; his obituary called her children his step-sons and step-daughters and named them as Bells, which is how this family was finally proved from the outside.

Her sister Katie married George Bell, a brother of Alice's own husband: two Bradley sisters married two sons of John T. Bell.

She outlived her first husband by thirty-five years and died at Montgomery on 29 December 1956, aged eighty. They brought her home to Bethlehem, in Barbour County, and buried her beside Tom under the name Bell — not Norton. Her dates are cut on the right-hand half of his stone: ALICE, OCT. 8, 1876, DEC. 29, 1956.

18.s:
Andrew Jackson Eaken was born on 1 May 1881 in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, one of the youngest children of Joseph William “Joel W.” Eakins and Sarah Hudson Payne; he is the newborn “Andrew J.” in his father's household in the census of 1880. His people had come to Mississippi out of New Hanover County, North Carolina, and when he was asked in 1910 where his parents had been born he answered North Carolina for both.

About 1907 he married Maggie Dillon Swain, of York and Cuba in Sumter County, Alabama — the next county across the state line. The 1910 census finds the two of them at Kosters, in Mobile, with their one-year-old daughter Beatrice and Maggie's young brother Langford Swain lodging in the house; that lodger is the thread that, a century later, opened the entire Swain side of this family. In 1917 he registered for the draft at Princeton, in Jackson County at the far north-east corner of Alabama, and in 1920 the census caught him under yet another spelling, “Eakans.” He was a man who crossed the state repeatedly.

He died on 20 March 1922, aged forty. He was not buried at Birmingham, as the family's own compilation long had it, but at Clay Memorial Cemetery in Cuba, Sumter County — his wife's home ground, among her people. He left Maggie a widow at thirty-five. Their children included Alec's great-grandmother Margaret Beatrice; Andrew Jackson “Jack” Eaken, who became a colonel; Joseph William “Jo Will” Eaken, who rose to be a vice-president of American Airlines; and Melvin Swain Eaken.

The surname moved under him. “Our name was originally spelled Eakins,” his granddaughter wrote in 2009. “My father's grandfather stopped dotting the ‘i’ and it became an ‘e’. My father dropped the ‘s’, as did his brothers.” Andrew Jackson was the Eakens in the middle of that sentence.

19.s:
Maggie Dillon Swain was born on 27 September 1886 in Sumter County, Alabama, a daughter of Joseph L. Swain and the woman the records call Dillon Simmons. Her middle name was her mother's given name, and it puzzled the family for three generations. In the 1900 census she is at Election Precinct 6, York, with her brothers and sisters — Leila, Patton, Maggie, Kirkland, Pinky and Langford.

She married Andrew Jackson Eaken about 1907. Their daughter Margaret Beatrice was born in 1908, and in 1910 the three of them were at Mobile with her brother Langford boarding in the house. Andrew died on 20 March 1922, and she took him home to Cuba to bury him, twenty miles from where she had been born. She was thirty-five.

On 6 November 1925 she married Thomas J. Bloebaum at Birmingham, and the marriage took her north — to Milton, in DuPage County, Illinois, by 1930, and to Wheaton in the same county in 1940 and 1950. That is the “Chicago area” her great-grandson remembered without being able to name it. The Bell family came north to join her, and in January 1944 her great-grandson Thomas Jackson Bell was killed in a car crash at sixteen; she had been going to give him a car for his birthday, and he took the keys a few days early.

Illinois held her for thirty-five years, but she kept coming home. In May 1951 the Sumter County paper reported that “Mrs. Bloebaum, of Wheaton, Ill., has returned home after a visit with her mother, Mrs. Dillon Swain” and her sisters, Mrs. Geo. McElroy and Mrs. M. C. Cobb. Her mother died within the next two years, and on 6 February 1953 Maggie and her two sisters were granted letters testamentary on the will in the Sumter County probate court, signing the notice to creditors together — Maggie S. Bloebaum, Pinkie S. McElroy, Merle S. Cobb. Her second husband died at Wheaton in July 1962 and was brought down to Clay Memorial at Cuba for burial.

She came back to Birmingham in the end, to the house her great-grandson still pictures, with a set of rosewood twin beds with beautiful inlay that later passed out of the family. She died there in March 1985 at ninety-eight, outliving her own daughter by two years. The Birmingham Post-Herald of 13 March 1985 called her Margaret Swain Eaker Bloebaum, listed her sons Col. Andrew J. and Joseph W. Eaker and her sisters Mrs. G. R. McElroy of Chattanooga and Mrs. Cliffton Cobb of Meridian, and sent her home for burial at Clay Memorial Cemetery in Cuba — where her first husband had lain since 1922 and her second since 1962. Her two surviving sisters are the Pinkie and Merle who had signed the probate notice with her thirty-two years before.

She died on Sunday 10 March 1985 at Birmingham, aged 98, after fifteen years back in Alabama, and was buried beside her second husband in Clay Memorial Cemetery at Cuba.

She is the “Ms Blevon” of family memory: Bloebaum, softened by sixty years, and written down as “Blevaughn” by a Social Security clerk who heard it from a grandson.

20.s:
John Willis Stephens was born on 12 March 1876 in Sumter County, Alabama, the son of Caswell Massey Stephens and his first wife, the widow recorded on the chart as Ava Marilla Shelton. His mother died when he was fourteen and his father remarried the following year.

On 4 July 1906 he married Mary Price Williams in Sumter County; she was nineteen, and had been born across the state line at State Line, in Greene County, Mississippi. They had four children — Lois Mildred, born 1908, who married Thomas Turnipseed; Rufus D.; Jess Steve Willard, born at York in 1917; and Clara Mae, born 1922, who married Edgar Herndon. In 1920 the family was at Election Precinct 6, York.

Livingston as he knew it was mapped in April 1910: the court house and county jail on Marshall Street, the Everitt Hotel on Spring, the public school, the M.E. church, the public library, and two livery stables still doing business in the middle of town.

Like his son he went by “J. W.,” which is precisely why marriage clerks in 1939 and again in 1960 both wrote down “J. W. Stephens” meaning two different men of this family; it took the 1920 Sumter County census to sort the generations out. He farmed and kept a dairy, and the county paper called him a life-long resident of Sumter County and a Baptist of fifty years’ standing. He was living at Livingston, the county seat, when his father died in February 1935 — the obituary calls him simply “J. W. of Livingston,” and the Livingston paper offered its sympathy to him by name “in the loss of his father.” On the last Sunday of July 1939 he and his wife gave the Stephens-Williams reunion at their Livingston house, and the company that day ran from his brother at Halsell to her Williams brothers coming in from Pascagoula, Baton Rouge and Jackson. He died at home on the night of Sunday 13 April 1947, aged seventy-one, after a long illness. The funeral was held in the house at half past ten on the Tuesday, Rev. Audrey Granade assisted by Rev. Henry Niles, and he was buried in Myrtlewood Cemetery. He lies in Myrtlewood Cemetery at Livingston under a double stone with his wife: his half is headed FATHER, hers MOTHER, with a stone urn between them and the family name cut across the base.

21.s:
Mary Price Williams was born on 18 March 1887 at State Line, in Greene County, Mississippi — a railroad village that sits flat on the Alabama border — the daughter of Francis R. Williams and Mary J. Lewis. In 1900 the family was a few miles west, in Beat 3 of Clarke County, Mississippi, where the census lists her at thirteen with her brothers and sister Jesse F., Etta S. and Knox A.

On 4 July 1906, at nineteen, she crossed back over the line to marry J. W. Stephens in Sumter County, Alabama, and she lived the rest of her life on the Alabama side. Her children included Lois Mildred, born in 1908, who married a Turnipseed; Jess Steve Willard, born at York on 29 April 1917; and Clara Mae, born in 1922, who married a Herndon. She appears in the Alabama birth registers as a mother and in her son’s Social Security file as the parent who gave him his name. She made her home at Livingston for many years and was a faithful member of the Livingston Baptist Church. On Sunday 30 July 1939 she and her husband gave the Stephens-Williams reunion at their house, and her own people came a long way for it — her sister Mrs. L. L. Craig from Gulfport, and her brothers H. H. Williams from Pascagoula, K. A. Williams from Baton Rouge and J. F. Williams from Jackson.

She was widowed in April 1947 and outlived her husband by ten years. She died at her home on the Sunday morning of 20 October 1957, aged seventy, after a long illness; the funeral was at the Livingston Baptist Church at three the next afternoon, Rev. Jackson Robertson officiating, and she was buried beside her husband at Myrtlewood Cemetery, under the half of their double stone headed MOTHER. Her paper printed her out in full, as the chart has her: Mrs. Mary Price Williams Stephens.

22.s:
Thomas William Truette was born in September 1893 in Clarke County, Alabama, the son of William Curtis Truett and Amanda Webb. The census taker found him on 19 June 1900 at Clarksville, six years old and entered in the family's own pet name, “Tamie” — fifth of six children in a farmhouse full of them: Tela, thirteen; Jane, twelve; Bigy, ten; Lillie, eight; himself; and Bessie, who was one.

He grew up around Clarksville and Coffeeville, the strip of Clarke County where his people had farmed since before the Civil War — his great-grandfather had enlisted at Coffeeville in 1862 and his grandfather is buried at New Prospect. About 1916 he married Sennie Lawrence, a Coffeeville girl six years younger. The 1920 census finds them at Coffeeville with two small daughters, “Gracie E.” and “Gladis G.”; Grace Estelle, born in January 1917, was Alec's great-grandmother. A third daughter, Jewel Rae, is named in the family's later Social Security records.

He died before 1930 — the census of that year finds Sennie without him, and in 1934 she married again as a widow. He was somewhere under thirty-seven. No death record has been found for him, no estate, and no grave: he is not among the eight Truetts buried at New Prospect with his father, no memorial for him has been registered anywhere, and his own county newspaper, which is digitised right through the years in which he must have died, printed no notice of it. Of the four generations of Truetts in Clarke County he is the only one whose burial place is unknown.

ph.w: COUNTY MAP AT THE RIGHT TIME, and it carries every Truett place by name. New Prospect (where William Curtis Truett farmed), Chilton (where he grew up), Clarksville (where the 1900 census found him), Coffeeville (where John Wesley Truett enlisted in 1862, 'his own village') and Harris Cr. all appear within a few miles of one another in the north-centre of the county.

23.s:
Sennie E. Lawrence was born at Coffeeville, Clarke County, Alabama, on 5 January 1899 — the date her gravestone gives; the 1900 census said January 1897 and the 1910 census 1898, which is the ordinary drift of a child's age reported by a parent. She was the fourth of seven children of “Calm” Lawrence, a farmer, and his wife Eliza. When the enumerator called at the house in 1900 her baby brother Alfonso was entered as “0 days” old: the man came on the day the child was born.

Her father was gone by 1910 — the census that year lists her mother Eliza as head of the house with six children — and the family name wanders through the records as Lawrence, Larance and Laurence, and her own given name as Sennie, Senie, Cenis and Zennie.

About 1916 she married Thomas William Truette. Their daughters Grace Estelle and Gladys appear with them at Coffeeville in 1920; a third, Jewel Rae, is named in later records. Thomas died before 1930 and she was a widow at about thirty. On 24 June 1934 she married again, at Chatom in Washington County — the index garbles the groom's given name, but his stone names him: Sol L. James Sr., born 18 April 1891. He died in 1953 and she was widowed a second time.

She died on 13 September 1975, aged seventy-six, and lies beside him at Ulcanush Cemetery, Coffeeville, under a double granite marker with the name JAMES on the base and a cross and spray of flowers cut on each stone. Her own slab reads SENNIE E., JAN. 5, 1899, SEPT. 13, 1975. The graveyard runs out into open field behind a chain-link fence, with a grain silo on the skyline. Her parents lie in the same ground, about forty yards off, under two slabs of rough concrete.

24.s:
Dennis Clark Tuttle was born on 25 January 1884 at Peoria, Illinois, where his parents Richard B. Tuttle and Emma S. Fuerstenberger were living for reasons nobody has yet explained — they had married at Terre Haute two years before, and they were back there within the year. On 17 December 1884, before Dennis was a year old, his father died of consumption. He was named for his father's elder brother Dennis, and for his grandfather Clark Strong Tuttle, the miller of Otter Creek — so the “Clark” he carried had come down from a Connecticut bride of 1788 and would go on to his own grandson.

His mother married twice more, and the man who raised him was her third husband, Gifford H. Spear. Dennis repaid that in the plainest way a man of his time could: he gave his own first son the name Gifford.

On New Year's Eve 1902 he married Leona Marie Alexander of Clinton, Indiana; Gifford was born nine months and six days later, and a daughter, Dorothy, followed. Leona's widowed mother Mary lived in their house through the censuses of 1910, 1920 and 1930 — forty years under their roof.

He spent forty-three years as a freight-car repairman for the Pennsylvania Railroad and retired onto its Roll of Honor. His Social Security card was issued on 22 April 1937, and he kept it in his wallet, which survives with the rest of what he carried: a Kerman Grotto courtesy card — he was the Grotto's Prophet — an accident policy from the Terre Haute Tribune-Star dated 7 May 1952, and the card from an Indiana unemployment claim that paid him twenty dollars a week in his sixties. In April 1942 he registered for the “Old Man's Draft” with Vigo County Board 1. In 1934 the probate of an in-law's estate found him at 2626 Fenwood Avenue, Terre Haute, taking $1,813 as his late mother's one-fifth share.

By the early 1950s Dennis and Leona were living at 2438 North Eleventh Street in Terre Haute. On New Year's Eve 1952 they marked fifty years of marriage, and the Terre Haute Tribune printed their photograph two days before: a stiff-collared old railroader beside his wife, under the heading FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY. They issued no invitations - the paper simply told the city that the Tuttles would be at home on New Year's Day to their friends, and that all were invited. Their son Gifford came down from Evanston with his wife, their daughter Dorothy Stephens was living at home, and their two grandsons sent word, one from Rochester, New York, the other from an army post in Germany. He outlived his son Gifford, who died in December 1974, by eight months.

Terre Haute's Daily Tribune carried the wedding twice in the week it happened. On 27 December 1902 it told readers that "The marriage of Miss Leona Alexander and Mr. Dennis Tuttle will take place Wednesday evening at the home of the bride's mother on North Sixth street" — Wednesday being New Year's Eve — and added that "Mr. Tuttle is an employe of the Van shops." A second notice the next day called him "a well known employe of the Van shops." The Van shops were the Vandalia Railroad's Terre Haute works, which the Pennsylvania Railroad absorbed in 1917; so the forty-three years he eventually gave the Pennsylvania begin in these two paragraphs, in a railroad town, four days before he married.

He and Leona were married sixty-seven years. She died in 1970; he died on 22 August 1975, and the two of them lie at Highland Lawn Cemetery in Terre Haute, in the same ground as the Bavarian grandfather he never knew.

25.s:
Leona Marie Alexander was born on 16 February 1883 at Clinton, in Vermillion County, Indiana, the only child William L. Alexander and Mary Elizabeth Fletcher ever had. Her father died while she was small — somewhere between her birth and 1900 — and by the summer of 1900 she was seventeen and living with her widowed mother at 314 Mulberry Street in Terre Haute, in a house her mother owned outright and paid for by keeping house for other people. The census-taker wrote her name down as “Leon.”

On New Year's Eve 1902 she married Dennis Clark Tuttle, a young railroad man. Their son Gifford arrived nine months and six days later — which is how the date of the wedding was finally pinned down against a family tradition that had it a year later. A daughter, Dorothy, followed. Her mother moved in with them and stayed: Mary appears in their household in 1910, in 1920 and again in 1930, and died there in 1934.

She was a member of St. Stephen's Episcopal Church in Terre Haute — the earliest sign of a family that had been Congregational for six generations turning Episcopalian, and the change may well have come in with her. She was a life member of the Daughters of Mokanna, Kerman Caldron No. 19, the women's side of her husband's Grotto; her 1964 membership card is among the family papers.

On New Year's Eve 1952 she and Dennis had been married fifty years, and the Terre Haute Tribune printed their photograph - Leona in a dark lace-shouldered dress, smiling, her glasses catching the flash - above a caption inviting the whole city to call on them on New Year's Day. Her daughter Dorothy Stephens was living at home with them that winter; her son Gifford came from Evanston.

Her wedding was announced in the Terre Haute Daily Tribune on 27 and 28 December 1902. The ceremony was to be "Wednesday evening at the home of the bride's mother on North Sixth street" — so the family tradition of a New Year's Eve wedding is confirmed by the newspapers of the week, and the house it happened in was her mother's.

She died at three o'clock on the afternoon of Sunday 13 September 1970 at St. Anthony Hospital, aged eighty-seven, from the house at 501 North Seventh Street she and Dennis had lived in. Her notice records a husband of sixty-seven years, a daughter in Terre Haute, a son at Highland Park, Illinois, two grandsons and seven great-grandchildren. The funeral was at St. Stephen's, the Rev. Harold Taylor officiating; she was buried at Highland Lawn, where Dennis joined her five years later.

26.s:
Joseph McGee Knott was born on 5 March 1851 at Lowell, in Washington County, Ohio, on the Muskingum, the son of Benjamin and Margaret Nott. The 1851 is what his death certificate says, what his Cedar Rapids death notice said, and what is cut on his stone; the 1900 census is the dissenter, giving March 1855. The family spelled the name both ways for a century; he died a Knott and was indexed a Nott, which is why it took this project four counties and two states to find his death.

He grew up on his father’s farm in Adams Township. The census of 1860 found the household on page one, dwelling six, with the post office given as Lowell: Benjamin forty-three, Margaret forty-three, P. J. fifteen, William F. thirteen, and “Jos M” eleven. A brother, John A. Nott, had been born in 1846 and died in 1851, the year Joseph was born, and lies in the Mason cemetery near the village; in the summer of 1859 diphtheria went through Adams Township and filled the mortality schedule with five-year-olds, among them a Thomas H. Nott, aged five. Joseph, then eight, came through it.

By about 1868 he was at work in a steel mill, and he stayed at it: his death certificate records “Heater — Steel Mill,” fifty-seven years in the trade, last worked in 1925. The work took him to Terre Haute, Indiana, about 1881 — the city paper that reported his death said he had been a resident there for fifty years — and he appears in four consecutive censuses of it. About 1897 he married Martha Ellen (Lamb) Ford, a widow with a young son, Percy; their daughters were Mildred and Helen. He is named as their father on Helen’s 1923 marriage application. The family lived at 3500 Wabash Avenue.

He was not only a mill hand. By the summer of 1915 Joseph Knott of 623 North Ninth Street was one of the City of Terre Haute's four park superintendents, in charge of Steeg Park; on 1 October 1915, with the formal close of the park season, he and the other three superintendents and nine labourers were dropped from the city payroll. Two days later he was in the witness chair. The city council was taking evidence in the great Terre Haute election-fraud inquiry into Mayor Donn M. Gossom, and "Joseph Knott, of 623 North Ninth street, until recently superintendent of Steeg park, was next called." He testified that the mayor had asked him to wake him on the morning of the election to go down and organise the board, that Gossom then left the precinct in Knott's charge and drove off saying "he had a lot off 'hunkies' he wanted to run in" — to be picked up "around the Malleable works or stamping mill" — and that Gossom told him that night, "I finished up across the river this evening." In November 1914 he and his wife announced their elder daughter's engagement, and in July 1916 their first grandson was born in their house and the Tribune put him on page one as the first war baby born in Terre Haute.

On 1 September 1931, at eighty, he left Terre Haute for Cedar Rapids, Iowa, to live with his elder daughter Mildred — Mrs. E. C. Cooper, of 2505 First Avenue. He had been there four and a half months when he died, in her house at 10:40 in the morning on Friday 15 January 1932, of arteriosclerosis, with a cerebral haemorrhage on the 7th and bronchopneumonia on the 14th among the causes; a doctor had attended him since 24 October. The informant who gave the particulars — a Mrs. Nott of Cedar Rapids — signed with a mark, and left the line for his mother’s maiden name dashed out. He left a wife, two daughters and four grandchildren. There was no service in Iowa: the family set off for Terre Haute the next day, and on 18 January the Ryan funeral home buried him at Highland Lawn, Terre Haute, Section 14, Lot 386. His flat granite marker reads simply Joseph Knott 1851 1932. Thirteen years later his widow was laid in the same grave, of the same cause, by the same undertaker.

27.s:
Martha Ellen Lamb was born on 27 August 1865 at Richmond, in Wayne County, Indiana — the date her 1945 death certificate gives, and the year cut on her gravestone, though the 1880 census suggests a birth closer to 1862 or 1863. She was the second of the four children of Erwin R. Lamb and his first wife Melissa J. Bailey, and she was ten years old when her mother died at Newport, after a few days’ illness, on the evening of 29 November 1875.

Her father married again in May 1879, to Mary Elizabeth (Jackson) Hall, a Civil War widow with five children of her own, and the census of 1880 found the blended household on Main Street in Vermillion, Indiana: Erwin forty, his new wife, “Mattie E.” seventeen, her brother Frank fifteen, her sister Bell thirteen, and a nine-year-old stepsister, Effie Hall. It is the last record that shows Martha at home. Her father eventually left Indiana altogether and died at Jonesboro, Arkansas, in 1919.

She married twice. Her first husband was George Ford, and their son was Percy. About 1897, at Terre Haute, she married Joseph McGee Knott, a steel-mill heater fourteen years her senior, and had two daughters — Mildred and Helen. One small document in her own hand survives: the back of a real-photo postcard of the two girls, pencilled “My too sweet dauters, Mildred and Helen” and signed “Mama.” The spelling is phonetic, and it is the only specimen of her writing anyone has found.

A single line of Terre Haute social news from 1890 very probably puts her father in her house: "Erwin Lamb, of Plainfield, Ind., is visiting his daughter, Mrs. Mattie Ford, and son, Frank Lamb, on north Third street." Mattie was what the family called her, Ford was her first husband's name, and Frank was her brother — both of them are the children aged 17 and 15 in Erwin Lamb's 1880 household. She announced her elder daughter Mildred's engagement with her husband in November 1914, and in July 1916 her first grandchild was born in her house.

Joseph died in January 1932 at Cedar Rapids, in their daughter Mildred’s house; Martha was there — the Iowa paper’s notice says he was survived “besides his wife” by two daughters — and the family travelled home to Terre Haute together for the funeral. Widowed, Martha moved in with her daughter Helen and son-in-law Gifford Tuttle, and the 1940 census still has her in that household — so Alec’s grandfather, Richard Clark Tuttle, then ten, grew up under the same roof as his grandmother. She died on 18 January 1945 at Terre Haute of a cerebral haemorrhage, aged seventy-nine, and two days later the Ryan funeral home buried her in Highland Lawn Cemetery, Section 14, Lot 386 — the same grave as Joseph, under a flat granite marker matching his: Martha E. Knott 1865 1945.

28.s:
Harry B. Frost was born at Macclesfield in Cheshire, the English silk town, about March 1860, the second son of George Frost and Frances W. Bell. He was four years old when the family crossed: he “came to America in 1864 and settled with his parents in Paterson” — the silk-weaving capital of America, built on English hands. He went through the Paterson public schools, finishing at the J. Waters school.

He began work with his father in the throwing business — the twisting of raw silk into yarn — while still a boy. In June 1880 the census found him at 309 Straight Street, aged twenty, “works in silk mill”, with his father (fifty-eight, silk manufacturer, with “rheumatism” written against his name in the health column), his mother, a sister and three brothers. That same year his father took him and his brother Frank into partnership, and George Frost & Sons built the Albion Mill, a hundred feet of frontage on Madison Street. An industrial history of Paterson published in 1882 credits the firm with being the first in the city to bring in the celebrated Atwood machinery.

On 10 June 1896, aged thirty-six, giving his trade as silk manufacturer and his home as Paterson, he married at Detroit, Michigan. The bride was Kathaline Chalmers, thirty, a schoolteacher living in Detroit but born at Orange, New Jersey. Why a Paterson man married a New Jersey woman in Michigan has never been explained. A pastor named John Reed performed the ceremony, with Mary N. Reed and Edith May Reid as witnesses.

Three children followed: Katherine King, born in September 1898; Harry Bell, born in Pennsylvania in July 1900; and Alan Chalmers, born at Paterson in February 1903. The household kept a live-in servant in every census that catches it. About 1908 he moved the family out of the city to Wyckoff Avenue, in Wyckoff, Bergen County, and lived there the last twenty-two years of his life. He was in silk for fifty years — George Frost & Sons, then the Frost & Van Riper Co., with mills at Paterson and at Scranton and Pittston in Pennsylvania, and at the end the Special Rayon Throwing Company. He was a Mason of Joppa Lodge and a life member of Mecca Temple of the Mystic Shrine.

The mill he was taken into partnership in can be seen on paper: Paterson's 1887 fire-insurance survey draws it as a brick block on the north side of Madison Street, Nos. 34 to 52, lettered GEO. FROST & SONS — SILK THROWING, with three hundred hands, a 350-horsepower engine and an artesian well.

He was ill through the second half of 1930 and died at home on the evening of Thursday 18 December, in his seventy-first year. The funeral was held at the house on the Saturday afternoon at half past two, taken by the rector of St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, Paterson, and the minister of the Wyckoff Reformed Church, and he was buried at Cedar Lawn in Paterson, where his father and his brother Frank already lay. “He was of a kindly and generous disposition,” the Wyckoff paper said, “and was always happiest when he had a group of friends around him.” His widow Katharine outlived him by thirteen months.

29.s:
Katharine Chalmers was born in January 1866 at Orange, in Essex County, New Jersey — her obituary says East Orange — the daughter of Mathew Chalmers and Ellen King, both of them Scots. She became a schoolteacher, and by 1896 she was living in Detroit; it was there, on 10 June that year, that she married Harry B. Frost of Paterson, an English-born silk manufacturer six years her senior.

She named her children from both sides of the house. Katherine King Frost, born in September 1898, carried her own mother’s maiden name; Harry Bell Frost, born in Pennsylvania in July 1900, carried his father’s mother’s; and Alan Chalmers Frost, born at Paterson in February 1903, carried hers. About 1908 the family left the city for Wyckoff Avenue, in Bergen County, and she lived there for the rest of her life — twenty-five years, the papers said.

She was a figure in both towns. She was second vice-president of the Paterson Woman’s Club in 1930, and until her death a member of its board of directors and chairman of its reception committee; she was a past president of the Wyckoff Woman’s Club; she was an active member of the Wyckoff Reformed Church, and for many years before that of the Baptist church at East Orange.

Harry died at the house on 18 December 1930, and she was a widow for thirteen months. In January 1932 her youngest son came up from Wilmington for a weekend; three weeks after that she went into the Paterson General Hospital with a short illness and died there at a quarter to eleven on the night of Sunday 31 January. The service was held the following Wednesday afternoon at the house on Wyckoff Avenue, taken by the curate of St. Paul’s, Paterson, and the Paterson Woman’s Club postponed its regular meeting and went to the funeral in a body. She left a daughter and two sons, and two sisters at East Orange — Mrs. Margaret Jordan and Miss Sarah Chalmers.

30.s:
John G. Roush was born in the autumn of 1876, the third son of Moses B. Roush and Sarah Duckworth. The 1900 census puts his birth in September 1876 in West Virginia; a Meigs County, Ohio birth register records a son John born to Moses Roush and Sarah Duckworth on 20 September 1877, and the family was certainly in Sutton Township, Ohio when the census taker called in 1880 and wrote him down as two years old. He was three when his mother died, and his father took the four children across the river into Mason County.

On 22 February 1897 he took out a licence at the Mason County courthouse to marry Bertha Ellen Nease. He gave his age as twenty and hers as eighteen; the party who swore the information was her own father, L. J. Nease. They were married two days later at the Evangelical Lutheran parsonage at New Haven by the Rev. D. W. Files. In June 1900 the young family were at Hartford village in Graham District, five lines down the same census page from his father Moses.

He was not only a miner. He had been in the insurance business at Mason, and moved his family to Broad Run about September 1907 to work in Claude Ryan's mine below Hartford. A year later, at about seven on the evening of Saturday 12 September 1908, his wife had been baking and a gallon oil can stood near the hot stove. He set a miner's lamp on the table where a daughter was ironing, and in trying to fill the lamp from the can touched off an explosion that threw burning oil in every direction. The girl was enveloped in flames and died within a few hours; a second daughter died five days later at New Haven; the house burned with everything in it. His fellow workmen gave up a day's wages for the family and the mine operator gave fifteen dollars.

Two weeks after his death the Weekly Register added that he left "a wife and two children" — a miscount: three daughters survived him and a fourth was born after his death.

He left four small daughters. In May 1909 his widow Bertha qualified in the Mason County court as guardian of "Iva Roush, Florence Roush, Velm Roush and Della Roush, infant children of John G. Roush, deceased," on a $500 bond with Moses Roush as surety.

He was badly burned, especially about the legs, and the newspaper doubted he would live. He died on 21 October 1908 in Graham District - “effects of burns,” certified by Dr. D. A. Sayre - a married coal miner of thirty-two. Two weeks later the Weekly Register noted it in a paragraph: “John D. Roush, who was injured several weeks ago at Broad Run, near Hartford, by the explosion of a lamp, died last week from injuries received at that time.” He lies at Broad Run Cemetery under a low granite marker that says only FATHER, and the years 1876 - 1908.

31.s:
Bertha Ellen Nease was born on 12 January 1878 in Mason County, West Virginia, the eldest child of Lewis J. Nease, a farmer, and Martha Jane Love, who had married the April before. Her father reported the birth himself.

On 22 February 1897, at eighteen, she took out a marriage licence with John G. Roush at the Mason County courthouse - her father stood as the informant who gave the clerk her age and birthplace - and two days later they were married at the Evangelical Lutheran parsonage at New Haven. In 1897 she was marrying back into her own grandmother's family: her father's mother had been born a Roush.

By 1900 the couple were at Hartford village with two small daughters, living a few doors from John's father. In 1907 they moved to Broad Run so that John could go into the mine. On the evening of 12 September 1908 Bertha had been baking when the oil can by the stove took fire; she fought the flames and was burned about the hands and arms. Her eldest daughter died that night, a second five days later, and her husband on 21 October. The house, the furniture and the family's clothes were all gone, and she was carrying another child.

She did not go back to either set of grandparents. In April 1910 she was the head of her own household at Wagner, Mason County - a widow of thirty-three with Iva Mae, Florence, Velma and the baby Claudia under her roof. On 2 March 1914 she married William L. Knopp at Mason City, he thirty-two and she thirty-four, by the Rev. C. H. Cox of the Church of the United Brethren in Christ. In March 1947, when she was ill at Mason, two of her daughters travelled down from Akron and Indiana to see her.

The county paper printed the licence among the week's news: "Marriage licenses issued yesterday: Andrew C. Grimm and Desta D. Clark, John Roush and Bertha E. Nease."

Widowed with four daughters under ten, she went to the Mason County court in May 1909 and qualified as their guardian on a $500 bond, her father-in-law Moses Roush standing surety.

Bertha Ellen Knopp died on 5 April 1950 at St. Joseph's Hospital, Parkersburg, aged seventy-one, her usual residence still Mason, West Virginia. Her daughter Iva gave the information for the certificate, which names her parents as Lewis Nease and Martha Jane Love. She was buried at Broad Run on 7 April, under a stone cut MOTHER / BERTHA E. ROUSH KNOPP / 1878 - 1950: she carried both her husbands' names to the grave.

John T. Bell was born on 10 June 1841 and died on 6 November 1915 near Louisville, in Barbour County, Alabama — his death recorded not in a newspaper but in the petition his sons filed two days later, which says he died “at his house in Barbour Co. on or about the 6th day of November 1915.” He married Sarah Ann “Sallie” Cox in March 1861, weeks before the war, and they raised eleven children of whom eight outlived him.

His obituary ran in the Montgomery Advertiser at the end of that November and again, unchanged, in the hometown Clayton Record a few days later. It gives his birthday to the day, names all eight surviving children and two brothers, W. W. and C. A. Bell — and then says the sentence the rest of this family history hangs from: “His parents moved to Alabama from Darlington, S. C., about 1830, and settled in the neighborhood where he lived at his death.” He was born in Alabama eleven years after that move. The journey was his father and mother’s, not his, and Darlington District is where everything above them has to be looked for.

He farmed, and he prospered, on a place six miles south of Clayton that was known on the map simply as Bell’s. In April 1888 he and Sallie sold a right of way across their land to the Eufaula & East Alabama Railway. When Sallie died in 1910 the county paper called him John T. Bell, Sr. — five years before the will, and a useful sign that the two Johns were already being told apart in print. By 1910 he was sixty-nine and living in his son Ben T.’s household, in his son Tom’s own precinct. When he died his executors told the court that the estate consisted “chiefly of lands, cotton, insurance and money, all of said real and personal estate being estimated to be worth about fifty thousand dollars” — something like a million and a half in modern money, to be divided among ten children and grandchildren’s lines.

His will names those children in his own voice, and the first of them carried his name: John T. Bell Jr., who became an undertaker at Clayton and who, nine years after his father’s death, paid for the burial of his uncle William. For a long time this file could not tell the two Johns apart, and the confusion sat on the chart as a warning that would not go away. It was the record that settled it, not the argument: the 1925 clerk wrote the word Junior, and the 1929 bond that closed the son’s own estate wrote it again.

Among his children was Tom — Thomas Jefferson Bell — and that is the step in Alec’s own line. Tom died six years after his father, leaving nothing at all to administer.

The county town he traded in was mapped for the insurance companies in February 1910, five years before he died. Three cotton warehouses stood on the Public Square — J. C. Thomas's, the Alliance's and the Farmers Union's — with the court hall and fire department, the Fryer Hotel, the post office and a town water works and electric light plant beside the Central of Georgia tracks.

He was a Freemason for thirty-two years, raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason in Royal White Hart Lodge No. 10 on 16 March 1883. The lodge met and passed resolutions of respect a fortnight after his death, regretting that the distance he lived from town and his last illness had kept him from its meetings. Letters testamentary on his will were granted on 19 November 1915 by Thomas D. Grubbs, judge of probate, to four of his sons - John T. Bell Jr., Mack Bell, Will A. Bell and Ben F. Bell - who advertised for claims against the estate in the Clayton Record that winter.

He lies at Bethlehem Baptist churchyard inside a low wrought-iron rail, under a marble shaft whose pediment is carved with the square and compasses of the Freemasons. Sallie’s stone stands a few feet from his across the same plot.

33.s:
Sarah Ann Cox — Sallie — was born on 24 August 1841 and married John T. Bell on 7 March 1861 in Barbour County, Alabama. He was twenty, she was nineteen; the war began the following month.

They had eleven children, of whom eight outlived their father and were named in his will — six sons and two daughters. One of the sons was Thomas Jefferson Bell. A daughter married in 1886 was named Sallie for her. The 1880 census of Louisville is the one record that states it plainly: Thomas J. Bell, aged about four, with his parents named on the same lines, Sarah and John T.

In April 1888 she signed her name beside her husband’s on a deed selling a right of way to the Eufaula & East Alabama Railway, giving up her dower in about forty-six acres of it. She signed it Sarah A Bell. A wife joined her husband’s deed in order to release dower, and that formality is the reason her name is on the paper at all.

Her photograph survives, and it is the oldest likeness of anyone on the Bell side: an oval vignette portrait of an old woman with white hair swept up, a lace jabot at the throat of a dark dress, on an embossed cream mount that somebody in the family has labelled in blue ink “Mrs. John T. Bell. Mother of Sallie Bell Stallings.”

She died on the morning of Friday 11 March 1910, five years before John, at the home that was known on the map simply as Bell’s, six miles south of Clayton, after what the county paper called a long and lingering illness. It called her “one of the most estimable and widely known women in the county … a lady who has raised a large family and maintained the high respect and goodwill of all who knew her,” and recorded that she was survived by her husband, many children, grandchildren and some great-grandchildren. The funeral was preached at Bethlehem church by her former pastor, the Rev. W. R. Bickerstaff of Florala, and she was buried in the adjoining cemetery. By the time John’s will was probated no widow was named anywhere in it. Her headstone stands beside his inside the Bells’ iron-railed plot at Bethlehem Baptist churchyard, a white marble tablet under a carved egg-and-dart band, and it does not give her a surname at all: SALLIE A., WIFE OF J. T. BELL.
