36.s:
Joseph William Eakins — “Joel W.” on most of the paper and “William J.” on some of it — was born in December 1838 or 1839 in New Hanover County, North Carolina, a son of John Eakins Sr. and Nancy Costin. He is the “Jos., 12” enumerated in his father's house on the Moores Creek land in 1850, one of nine children there.

By the end of the 1850s the family's reach had extended to Lauderdale County, Mississippi, where an uncle, William Eakins, had already settled, and where four orphaned Eakens boys born in North Carolina were being raised in the household of William Payne. On 13 May 1861, a month after the war began, Joel married Payne's daughter Sarah Hudson Payne. The marriage happened inside a house that had already fused the two families for a decade.

Two of his North Carolina kin went the other way that same May: his brother John J. B. Eakins and his cousin Owen J. enlisted at Lower Black River in the Moore's Creek Rifle Guards, Company E of the 18th North Carolina, and both were dead within two years — John at Sharpsburg, Owen at Chancellorsville.

He and Sarah farmed in Lauderdale County and had ten or more children. The 1880 census lists Mary A., Ada J., Jno. N., Minnie, Cassie E., Orgun, Joel P., Nancy and the newborn Andrew J.; a son Sam follows by 1900. Two of those names, Orgun and Joel, are Sarah's own younger brothers' names, carried over from the Payne household she had grown up in. In 1900 the enumerator wrote him down as “William J Eakins, born December 1838, North Carolina, married 1861.”

He died in 1902 in Mississippi. His other lasting mark on the family was a piece of handwriting: he stopped dotting the “i” in Eakins, and his descendants have been Eakens, and then Eaken, ever since.

37.s:
Sarah Hudson Payne was born in Mississippi in 1842 — in May 1842, according to the 1900 census, which asked. She first appears aged eight, in the 1850 census of Lauderdale County, in a crowded house: William Payne, fifty-nine, born in Virginia; Mary, thirty, born in North Carolina; four boys born in North Carolina carrying the Eakens name, aged ten to sixteen, who were orphans being raised there; and four younger children born in Mississippi, of whom Sarah was the eldest. Two of the little ones were called Origon and Joel.

Whether William Payne was her father or her stepfather is the one thing about her childhood the records have not settled. What is certain is the household — and what came of it. On 13 May 1861 she married Joseph William “Joel W.” Eakins, of the very family whose orphaned boys had grown up under that roof.

They farmed in Lauderdale County for forty years. She bore ten or more children: Mary A., Ada J., John N., Minnie, Cassie, Nancy, a Sam, and two she named Orgun and Joel after the brothers she had been raised with. Her youngest, Andrew Jackson Eaken, born in 1880 or 1881, is the one through whom the line runs down to Alec.

Her stone survives, leaning in a fenced Mississippi burying ground, and it gives her life to the day: SARAH H. EAKINS, born May 2, 1842, died May 1, 1908, aged 65 years 11 months and 29 days — one day short of her sixty-sixth birthday. Her middle name, Hudson, has never been explained, and no record yet found says who her mother was.

Joseph Lee Swain was born on 23 December 1861, the eldest child of Joseph Tolbert Swain and Nancy E. Jane, who had married in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, the year before. He was four or five when his parents crossed the state line into Sumter County, Alabama in the first months after the war, and he grew up at Cuba; the 1880 census finds him there, nineteen, at the head of a row of eight younger brothers and sisters.

He married twice. On 10 February 1884 the Sumter County register has him marrying a Eugenia Simmons, with J. M. Patton the minister — and the couple would name a son for him. He had an earlier wife named Leila Eugenia whose stone, in the churchyard at Salem Baptist across the line in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, gives 1861–1885 and calls her “wife of J. L. Swain”: she died before the end of 1885. On 23 December 1885, his own twenty-fourth birthday, he married the woman the register enters as Rebecca A. D. Simmons and everyone else called Dillon. The minister that day was D. C. Langford, and they named a son for him too: Joseph Langford Swain.

They farmed at York and Cuba. The 1900 census of Election Precinct 6 lists the children at home as Leila, Patton, Maggie, Kirkland, Pinky and Langford, and gives his years married as sixteen — counting, it seems, from the first wedding rather than the second. He stood for public office: at a meeting of the voters of the third commissioners district at Livingston on 28 August 1911 the vote went fifty-seven to twenty-seven in his favour, and in September he announced himself from Cuba as a candidate for county commissioner, “subject to the action of the Democratic party.” The Livingston paper thought he would make a good commissioner.

The family burying ground at Salem Baptist holds a hard chapter of their life. Its roster records five of their children there: Marvin, dead at two in 1892; Fletcher, dead at two in 1905; and then Patton, dead at nineteen in January 1916, Lucille Kirkland, dead at eighteen in January 1917, and Myrtle, dead at sixteen the following month. Three grown children in thirteen months.

Cuba was drawn out building by building on 4 May 1928 by L. L. Parker for the state rating bureau — the Walker-Shaw planing mill and saw mill at one end, a grist mill and feed store, G. W. McElroy's blacksmith and carpenter shop, the Cuba Mercantile Co., the Southern Railway depot with its covered platform, a Methodist church and two Holiness churches.

He lived out his life on the land three miles west of York, near the old McConnell Station — a six-room house on twenty acres, with running water and a telephone. He died there at a quarter to one on the afternoon of Thursday 21 November 1940, aged seventy-nine, after a long illness, and the funeral was held in the house the next afternoon. The county paper listed his widow, “Mrs. Dillon Simmons Swain,” four daughters — Leila Collier of Meridian, Maggie Bloebaum of Wheaton, Illinois, Pinkie McElroy of Fort Knox and Merle Cobb of Geiger — one son, Langford of Cuba, a brother and two sisters. He was buried at Salem Baptist. His stone gives his name as JOE L. SWAIN and, under the dates, one word: PAPA.

39.s:
Dillon Simmons was born on 1 December 1863 in Sumter County, Alabama, a daughter of Ben and Adeline Simmons of Cuba. She appears in her father's household in 1880, aged sixteen, written down by the enumerator as “Dellon” and stated to be his daughter.

She married Joseph L. Swain of the same small village on 23 December 1885, the county register entering her as Rebecca A. D. Simmons. He had been married before: an earlier wife, Leila Eugenia, had died by the end of that year. The Swains farmed at York and Cuba, three miles out near the old McConnell Station, in a six-room house on twenty acres. The 1900 census lists her simply as “Dillon Swain, 36,” with six children at home: Leila, Patton, Maggie, Kirkland, Pinky and Langford.

Five of her children lie in the churchyard at Salem Baptist, across the state line in Lauderdale County, Mississippi: two who died as infants, and Patton, Lucille Kirkland and Myrtle, who died grown within thirteen months of one another in 1916 and 1917.

Her daughter Maggie Dillon Swain carried her name forward, and it travelled two more generations as a middle name nobody could explain. The documents give it back in her own lifetime. Her husband's obituary of November 1940 calls her, in print, “his wife, Mrs. Dillon Simmons Swain.” In May 1951 the county paper reported her Wheaton daughter coming down to visit “her mother, Mrs. Dillon Swain.” And her son Joseph Langford Swain's death certificate, issued at New Orleans in 1946, names his mother as Dillon Simmons.

She outlived her husband by twelve years and died on 1 November 1952, aged eighty-eight. She left a will: on 6 February 1953 Judge Wilbur E. Dearman of the Sumter County probate court granted letters testamentary on it to three of her daughters — Maggie S. Bloebaum, Pinkie S. McElroy and Merle S. Cobb — and they published the notice to creditors through that February and March. She lies beside her husband at Salem Baptist under a matching stone: DILLON S. SWAIN, DEC. 1, 1863 – NOV. 1, 1952, and beneath the dates, answering his PAPA, the single word MAMA.

She died in the first days of November 1952; her four daughters thanked their neighbours in the Sumter County Journal a fortnight later, calling her 'our precious mother'.

One question about her is still open. The register records Joseph L. Swain marrying a Eugenia Simmons in February 1884 and this woman in December 1885, and the two brides have long been supposed sisters — but no document yet seen says so, and none puts “Rebecca A. D.” and “Dillon” on the same woman either. The research keeps them apart.

Swain's wife and Joseph Langford Swain's mother; the birth year 1863 matches the 1870 and 1880 census ages; and the stone is cut to match her husband's. There is no second Dillon Swain.

40.s:
Caswell Massey Stephens was born on 8 January 1852 in Sumter County, Alabama, the son of Henry H. Stephens and Sarah Ann Jones. He was named, at the very least, for a neighbour: in 1850 a twenty-four-year-old North Carolina man called Caswell Massey farmed the dwelling that stood between the Stephens house and the Joneses’. Whether he was kin to either family nobody has yet established. His mother died before he was three, and his father married her sister Elizabeth in October 1854. By 1860 the family had moved to Newton County, Mississippi, where the census catches him at eight.

On the last day of 1869, not yet eighteen, he stood in the Sumter County probate court before Judge J. A. Abrahams, said he was over fourteen, and chose his own father as his guardian — he and his brothers Calvin and John were the “minor heirs of Daniel Jones deceased,” their mother’s father, and his bond was set at $800. There was enough property in it that his father was filing annual settlements two years later.

In October 1871, aged nineteen, he married a widow thirteen years his senior. The register enters her as “Mrs. A. M. James,” and the officiant was H. H. Stephens, Minister — his own father. Her gravestone never gives her a first name either: it calls her A. M., wife of C. M. Stephens. Their children included Martha Alice, born 14 April 1874, who married John William Knight, and John Willis, born 12 March 1876; a son Rufus L. belongs to one marriage or the other. She died on 8 January 1891 — his thirty-ninth birthday — and on 19 April that year he married again, near Cuba. The county paper gave the whole of it in eleven words: “Married — Near Cuba, on the 19th, Mr C M Stephens and Mrs I Dearman.” The bride was Isabella, a Britt by birth and a Dearman by her first marriage, and she was about forty-five.

A family photograph posted online by a Stephens descendant as him shows a bearded old man in wire spectacles and a dark coat, sitting on a huge heap of split firewood with a small fair-haired child in a white dress leaning against his knee; the poster names her Clara Mae Stephens.

The index to his Alabama death record of 1935 calls him a farmer, a widower, aged 83, dead at Halsell in Choctaw County and buried at Siloam -- and names his father as Henry Stephens.

At twenty-three he very probably took the registration oath in Precinct No. 5 of Sumter County on 19 June 1875, entry 67, signing “C M Stephens” in his own hand and giving his occupation, like almost every man on the page, as farmer.

He farmed on into old age at Halsell, in Choctaw County, just over the Sumter line. In May 1928 his son Rufus died intestate at Livingston leaving about a thousand dollars; the probate papers record the only heir as “The Father Caswell M Stephens of Livingston Ala., age 76 years,” and he declined to administer it. He died at eight o’clock on the morning of Sunday 10 February 1935 — the county paper of the 14th already reports him buried, though his stone was later cut with the 17th —, at the home of his daughter Mrs. Alice Knight, after a short illness. The Sumter County Journal ran the notice on its front page. Funeral services were at eleven on the Monday at Siloam Church, Revs. Ezell and Dearman officiating, and he was buried in the church cemetery at Siloam, where his first wife had lain for forty-four years. He left two sons, J. W. of Livingston and H. R. of Halsell, one daughter, two brothers — Bob Stephens of Kewanee and Bill Stephens of Cuba — and thirteen grandchildren and fifteen great-grandchildren.

41.s:
The woman the family remembers as Ava Marilla Shelton was born on 21 November 1839, and nothing she left behind gives her a first name. Her gravestone calls her A. M.; the marriage register calls her Mrs. A. M. James; the initials are all there is.

She came to Caswell Massey Stephens as a widow. On 2 October 1871 — the alphabetical copy of the same register types the 5th — the Sumter County register entered “C. M. Stephens · A. M. James · Married by H. H. Stephens, Minister” — the groom’s own father officiating. That is family memory rather than record, but it fits the register exactly.

With Caswell she had Martha Alice, born 14 April 1874, and John Willis, born 12 March 1876, and probably others. She died on 8 January 1891, her husband’s thirty-ninth birthday, aged fifty-one. He remarried near Cuba on 19 April that year, which fixes her death before that date from a second direction. She lies at Siloam Cemetery in Sumter County under a marble headstone carved with a dove above a spray of flowers: In memory of A. M., wife of C. M. Stephens, born Nov. 21, 1839, died Jan. 8, 1891, and below it four lines of verse now almost weathered away. Her husband’s flat granite marker lies in the grass beside her.

42.s:
Francis R. Williams lived on the Mississippi side of the Alabama line, in the strip of pine country where Greene and Clarke Counties meet. He married Mary J. Lewis, and their daughter Mary Price Williams was born at State Line, in Greene County, on 18 March 1887 — a railroad village that takes its name from sitting flat on the Alabama border.

The one record that shows him keeping house is the 1900 census of Beat 3, Clarke County, Mississippi, where he appears as Francis R. Williams with his wife Mary J. and four children: Mary Price, Jesse F., Etta S. and Knox A. Six years later his daughter crossed the line into Sumter County, Alabama, to marry J. W. Stephens. Nothing else of his life has been found, and nothing at all of his parents; he carries the commonest surname in the American record, in a county whose nineteenth-century histories were never written.

44.s:
William Curtis Truett was born on 25 July 1867, the son of John Wesley Truett and Emily Caroline Ward. He grew up at Chilton in Clarke County, Alabama, and the 1880 census catches the whole family on one page: his father, a Confederate veteran who could not write his own name; his mother; his brothers and sister; and his grandmother Alcey, widow of the Reverend William Hampton Truett, living in the house at sixty-seven. Three generations under one roof.

On 17 June 1886, not yet nineteen, he married Amanda Webb in Clarke County. The 1900 census finds them at Clarksville with fourteen years of marriage behind them and six children in the house — Tela, Jane, Bigy, Lillie, Tamie and the baby Bessie — and it records both parents as able to read and write, which neither his father nor his grandmother could do. Thomas William, the “Tamie” of that schedule, was Alec's great-grandfather.

Amanda is gone from the record after 1900, and he married again, to Zella Shewmake, born 1 June 1878. He farmed at New Prospect, a settlement whose little Baptist church had been constituted about 1860 by an Elder C. J. Miles, who for his trouble was paid “one dollar per day while in active service.” When the county's thirty-four Baptist churches were apportioned in 1892, New Prospect was asked for sixteen dollars — near the smallest sum in the county.

All the places of his life sit within a few miles of each other on the 1928 county map — Chilton, where he grew up; Clarksville, where the census found him in 1900; and New Prospect, where he farmed, with Harris Creek running between them.

He died at New Prospect on 21 December 1925, aged fifty-eight, and is buried in the church graveyard. His stone is a low double marker of pale granite, TRUETT across the top, his own name on the right and Zella's on the left; she outlived him by thirty-five years and the marker was almost certainly cut when she joined him in 1960. Amanda, the mother of his eldest son, is not on it, and is not buried there. His own county paper printed nothing when he died, though the issues for the weeks after are all there to read.

45.s:
Amanda Webb was born in July 1868 in Alabama and married William Curtis Truett in Clarke County on 17 June 1886, when she was not quite eighteen and he not quite nineteen.

The 1900 census is the one full look anyone gets at her. On 19 June 1900 the enumerator James A. Coate Jr. called at dwelling 118 at Clarksville and wrote her down as Amanda, wife, born July 1868, aged thirty-one, fourteen years married, mother of six children and six living — and all six were in the house with her: Tela, thirteen; Jane, twelve; Bigy, ten; Lillie, eight; Tamie, six; and Bessie, one. Tamie is Thomas William, born that September of 1893, and Alec descends from him. Both she and her husband are marked as able to read and write, which neither his father nor his grandmother could do. Two dwellings down the same page lived a Tom P. Webb, born September 1862, a farmer — the right surname at the right door, though nothing yet says he was her brother.

After that she is gone from the record. Her husband married again, to Zella Shewmake, and it is Zella's name, not hers, on the other half of his gravestone at New Prospect. No grave has been found for Amanda anywhere.

The Webbs were old Clarke County people: a William Webb came into the county about 1812 and died at his home there in February 1853 at about seventy-eight, the Webb mill on the Tallahatta was built about 1836, and Webbs were among the families forted up at McGrew's Fort during the Indian troubles of 1810. Whether Amanda belonged to them has not been shown.

46.s:
Sennie Lawrence's father was born in Alabama in September 1860, to a father from North Carolina and a mother from South Carolina. The census taker of 1900 wrote his given name in a hand the indexers have read as “Calm”; what it was meant to be has never been settled.

He married Eliza about 1888 — the 1900 schedule says they had been married twelve years — and they farmed at Coffeeville in Clarke County. The same schedule lists five children in the house: Tomas N., 11; Sallie E., 9; Mary E., 6; Senie E., 3; and Alfonso, entered as nought days old. The enumerator had called at the house on the day the baby was born. Two more children followed, Lucy about 1905 among them.

He was not an old Clarke County man. The county's 1882 history names hundreds of its families across 780 pages and has no Lawrences among them at all — the first of his people must have come in from somewhere nearby, Washington or Choctaw or Marengo, and the family is indexed LARANCE as readily as Lawrence.

The index to the Alabama death record of C. J. Lawrence, 1929, gives his age as 72, his birthplace as Monroe County, Alabama, and his death as near Jackson in Clarke County. He was a widower. The clerk entered his burial place as Coffeeville and the cemetery as a church ground whose name the indexer could not read.

By 1910 he was gone from the household: Eliza is enumerated as head of the house with six children and no husband. He is very probably buried at Ulcanush Cemetery in Coffeeville, in the same ground as his daughter Sennie and his son Alphonso — under one of two home-made markers that stand side by side there, slabs of rough concrete with the lettering scratched into them with a nail while they were still wet. His gives only initials, C J Lawrence. The other gives no name at all, only Mrs Lawrence, and a birth year that is his wife's to the year. The dates cut beside his initials do not agree with the census, and the question of exactly whose stone it is has not been closed.

47.s:
Eliza was born in Alabama about 1863 or 1864 and married, about 1888, a Clarke County farmer named Lawrence — the 1900 census taker wrote his given name in a hand the indexers have read as “Calm.” They farmed at Coffeeville, and in 1900 she was thirty-six with five children in the house: Tomas N., Sallie E., Mary E., Senie E., and a baby, Alfonso, whom the enumerator recorded as nought days old. Two more followed, Lucy about 1905 among them; seven children in all.

By 1910 her husband had gone, and the census lists her as head of the household — “Elizon A. Larance,” with six children under her roof and no man in it. She kept them together for at least another decade.

She died in 1927, in her early sixties. At Ulcanush Cemetery in Coffeeville — the graveyard where her son Alphonso and her daughter Sennie were buried — stands a marker that is very probably hers: a slab of rough concrete, the lettering scratched in by hand while it was still wet, reading Mrs Lawrence · Born 1864 · Died 1927. The 1864 is the year the 1900 census gives her. The stone does not give her name. What is written on it, for a hundred years, is the word Mrs.

48.s:
Richard B. Tuttle was born on 24 March 1858, the fourth child of Clark Strong Tuttle and his second wife Nancy A. Harbert, at Tuttle's Mills in Otter Creek Township, Vigo County, Indiana. He first appears in the record aged two, in the 1860 census of Otter Creek, in a prosperous miller's house with three hired hands and a servant living in — and with an older brother named Dennis, aged four, whose name he would give his own son.

He followed his father's trade and was recorded as a miller. By the time he was grown the mill had gone: his father sold the 117-acre mill tract in July 1870, dissolved the firm a fortnight later, and was out of the township altogether by the autumn.

On 12 October 1881, at twenty-three, he married Emma S. Fuerstenberger, the daughter of a Bavarian shoemaker in Terre Haute. Some time in the next two years the young couple went to Peoria, Illinois, where their son Dennis Clark Tuttle was born on 25 January 1884; nobody has yet found out why they were there.

Terre Haute as he knew it survives in a bird's-eye view drawn in 1880, four years before he died: the grid of streets running back from the Wabash, the bridges, the mills along the river and the Normal School on its square.

They were back in Terre Haute before the year was out, and on the morning of Wednesday 17 December 1884 he died of consumption. He was twenty-six. The Daily Wabash Express carried the notice the next day under ANNOUNCEMENTS — DIED, and it says where he died: the funeral was at ten o'clock that morning from the house of his father-in-law Frank Fuerstenberger on South Third Street. No gravestone for him is known.

49.s:
Emma S. Fuerstenberger was born in July 1863 in Terre Haute, Indiana, the fifth of the eight children of Francis Fuerstenberger, a Bavarian shoemaker, and his Pennsylvania-born wife Sophia. She grew up in the one house her father occupied for forty years, 521 South Third Street, and was still at home, aged seventeen, when the census-taker came in 1880 and wrote the family name down as “Fuerstebuger.”

On 12 October 1881, at eighteen, she married Richard B. Tuttle, a young miller. Their son Dennis Clark Tuttle was born at Peoria, Illinois, on 25 January 1884, and in December of that year Richard died of consumption in her father's house. She was twenty-one, with a baby.

She married twice more — Hamilton B. Martin on 24 May 1891, and on 20 December 1894, at Charleston in Coles County, Illinois, Gifford H. Spear, the record indexing her as “Emma Furstenberger Tuttle.” Spear is the man who finished raising her son, and Dennis repaid him by naming his own firstborn Gifford.

In September 1916 she and Gifford Spear were living at 512 North Eighth Street in Terre Haute and had just come home from a month's holiday in California.

She died on 9 April 1926 as Emma S. Spear. The family Bible records the death under that name, with “Tuttle” pencilled faintly above it — somebody wanting the record to remember which husband she belonged to. Eight years later her son stood in her place when a Fuerstenberger estate was divided five ways among her brothers' and sisters' lines.

William L. Alexander lived at Clinton, in Vermillion County, Indiana, on the Wabash upriver from Terre Haute. He married Mary Elizabeth Fletcher there on 16 June 1881; she was twenty-two and had been working as a live-in domestic in another family's house the year before. Their only child, Leona Marie, was born at Clinton on 16 February 1883.

After that he disappears. By the census of June 1900 Mary was recorded as a widow at the head of her own household in Terre Haute, so he died somewhere between 1884 and 1900 — most of that window falling before Indiana began issuing death certificates in 1899, which is probably why no record of his death has been found. He is named as the father of the bride, “Wm. Alexander” of Clinton, in the Vigo County marriage register that recorded his daughter's wedding in 1902, nineteen years after she was born and years after he was dead.

His own parents are not known. A candidate couple was found in the Vermillion County marriage register — a William Alexander who married Mary Ellen Lucas in 1850 — and tested against both of their censuses; the household has no son William, and the candidate was withdrawn.

51.s:
Mary Elizabeth Fletcher was born on 21 September 1858 in Indiana, the daughter of John Fletcher and Sarah Wallace. Where the family was through her childhood nobody has managed to find; no John-and-Sarah Fletcher household containing a Mary of the right age appears in the Indiana census indexes for 1860 or 1870.

She surfaces in 1880 at Clinton, in Vermillion County, aged twenty-three, single, and enumerated alone in another family's house as a “houseworker” — a live-in domestic servant. A year later, on 16 June 1881, she married William L. Alexander of the same small town, and in February 1883 their daughter Leona was born. She bore one child and one only.

She was a widow by 1900, and she had not gone under. The census of that June finds her at 314 Mulberry Street in Terre Haute, forty years old, head of her own household, working as a housekeeper and owning the house — with her seventeen-year-old daughter beside her. Two years later Leona married Dennis Tuttle, and Mary moved in with them. She is in their household in 1910, in 1920 and again in 1930: thirty-four years under her daughter's roof.

In December 1902 she was living on North Sixth Street in Terre Haute, and it was in her house that her only child was married: the Daily Tribune said the ceremony would be "at the home of the bride's mother on North Sixth street." Twelve years later she was still travelling with the family — "Mr. and Mrs. Dennis Tuttle and children, Gifford and Dorothy, and Mrs. Mary Alexander, of Terre Haute" went out to West Terre Haute for the weekend in August 1914, and again in September.

She died on 16 April 1934 at East Ellen, Vigo County, aged seventy-five. The family Bible records the death simply as “Mary Elizabeth Alexander (1934).” Her death certificate is the one document that names her parents, and it is the only door this family has into the Fletcher and Wallace lines.

56.s:
George Frost was born in England about 1820, at Macclesfield in Cheshire, where his family were “engaged largely in the silk manufacture.” He entered the trade himself in 1838, while still in his early boyhood, and his department from the first was throwing — the twisting of raw silk into yarn.

He married Frances W. Bell, also English. Their children included Mary, Frank (born at Macclesfield in April 1858), Harry B. (about March 1860), Morris (about 1863, still in England) and Charles, who was born in New Jersey about 1866; Harry’s obituary says the family came to America in 1864 and settled in Paterson. An industrial history of the city published in 1882 says he “commenced business in this country about 1870 with but four hands.”

By June 1880 he was at 309 Straight Street, Paterson, fifty-eight years old and set down as a silk manufacturer, with rheumatism noted against his name in the health column; two of his sons were working in the mill. That year he took Frank and Harry B. into partnership, and George Frost & Sons built the Albion Mill, with a frontage of a hundred feet on Madison Street and, the 1882 history remarked, “an air of taste too rarely seen in factory buildings.” They threw yarn exclusively on commission, and were the first house in Paterson to install the celebrated Atwood machinery. By the middle eighties the firm was advertising from 36 to 52 Madison Street as makers of “Organzine, Tram, Floss, etc. On Commission,” and in September 1885 a fire in Straight Street singed the back of a new mill they were putting up.

In February 1887, when the Paterson silk dyers struck and the whole trade seized up, George Frost & Sons told their four hundred hands that the Albion Mills would not reopen until the strike was settled. The paragraph went out on the wire from the New-York Tribune and was reprinted as far away as Topeka, Grand Island and Victoria, British Columbia. It is the one day his name travelled.

The Albion Mill can still be looked at. Paterson's fire-insurance surveyors drew it in 1887, a long brick block on the north side of Madison Street running from No. 34 to No. 52, lettered along the pavement GEO. FROST & SONS — SILK THROWING. The surveyors wrote the work down floor by floor: reeling on the first, spinning on the first and second, winding and doubling on the third, winding on the fourth, and a carpenter's repair shop in the basement. One engine of 350 horsepower drove the whole of it, there was an artesian well sunk in the yard, and against the block the surveyor noted “300 hands.” The same sheet puts the mill among its competitors — Wm. Strange & Co. and Doherty & Wadsworth across the street, Jno. Dunlop's silk twist mill and Naef Bros. & Co. round the corner, Benj. Eastwood making silk machinery a block away.

He died four months later, at Paterson, on 27 June 1887, aged sixty-seven, and lies in Cedar Lawn Cemetery. The burial entered there is almost certainly his, and it remembers him in the terms he would have chosen: “senior member of the firm, George Frost & Sons, silk manufacturers; native of Macclesfield, England.” He is named as Harry B. Frost’s father twice over: on his son’s 1896 Detroit marriage record, where the clerk wrote “father Geo Frost, mother Frances W Bell”, and again thirty-four years later, when Harry died and the Paterson paper called him “the second son of George and Frances W. Frost.”

57.s:
Frances W. Bell was born in England, and came, like her husband, out of the Cheshire silk country; the 1880 census of Paterson sets down her own birthplace, and both her parents’, as England. She married George Frost, a Macclesfield throwster, and bore the children who carried the firm on — Mary, Frank, Harry B., Morris, and Charles, the youngest and the first of them born in America.

In June 1880 the census found her at 309 Straight Street, Paterson, keeping house for a household of seven: her husband, a daughter at home, three sons, the two eldest boys already working in the family’s silk mill. Her surname is a coincidence that has to be said plainly — this Bell family has no connection whatever to the Alabama Bells elsewhere in this history — but the name did carry forward: her grandson, born in Pennsylvania in 1900, was christened Harry Bell Frost.

She is named twice in print. Once on her son Harry’s 1896 Detroit marriage record, where the clerk wrote the groom’s mother as “Frances W. Bell”; and once more thirty-four years later, when Harry died at Wyckoff and the Paterson paper, still knowing whose child he was, called him “the second son of George and Frances W. Frost.”

She outlived George by a dozen years. A Cedar Lawn burial that is very probably hers records “Frances W Frost … widow of George,” who died at Paterson on 5 January 1899, her last address 189 Tyler Street.

60.s:
Moses B. Roush was born on 30 January 1842 in Meigs County, Ohio, in the riverside settlement the Roushes and the Neases had founded together, and which was called the Nease Settlement. He was a son of Benjamin “Bennie” Roush and Sophia Altman, and he appears in their Sutton Township household aged seven in 1850 and eighteen in 1860.

He went to the war late. He entered service on 23 July 1864, aged twenty-two, as a private in Company A - and afterwards Company B - of the 28th Ohio Volunteer Infantry, Ohio's “2nd German Regiment,” raised at Camp Dennison from German-speaking volunteers and by 1864 taking whatever recruits the state had left. He served the last twelve months of the war, from the Atlanta summer through to three months after Appomattox, and was discharged on 6 July 1865.

On 1 September 1870 he married Sarah Duckworth, the daughter of a Lancashire collier, at Orange Township in Meigs County; her brother Adam married in the same township eight days later. They had Sarah Ann in 1871, Charles Benjamin in 1874, John G. in 1877 and Richard in 1880. In March 1880 Moses applied for an invalid pension on his war service; eleven months later, on 4 March 1881, Sarah died, leaving him four children under ten. He married Lydia E. in Mason County in August 1883 and took the family across the Ohio into Graham District, where he lived about twenty years and had five more children. In June 1900 he and his son John were enumerated on the same page at Hartford village, five lines apart.

Lydia died in 1906. In 1908 he buried his son John and two granddaughters. He married a third time, to Margaret A. Zerkle, in 1911. From 1920 the government paid his invalid pension at an increased rate, and raised it again in 1923.

In January 1887 his name went into the Point Pleasant paper in a notice headed "ATTENTION! — The boys who wore the blue": the pensioners of the county were being called before the United States Board of Examining Surgeons, which sat every Wednesday at Dr. Hoy's office, and the Register printed him in the list as "Moses Roush, Co. A. 28th Ohio Vols." He had to be re-examined before the quarter closed on 31 March or lose his place on the pay roll. The notice ran three weeks running.

In May 1883 the Grand Army of the Republic mustered in Washington Post No. 13 at New Haven, Mason County, with fourteen charter members; its Officer of the Guard was a Moses Roush — very probably this one. He stood surety on his widowed daughter-in-law's $500 guardianship bond in May 1909, and he was still doing road work with a team for the county in his sixties — 'Moses B Roush, team and labor' appears in the Graham District road accounts printed in 1907 and 1910.

He died at six in the evening on 23 August 1925 at New Haven, aged eighty-three years six months and twenty-three days, of general arteriosclerosis with senility, after Dr. R. S. Bryant had attended him for three days. The informant was his son Charles B. Roush - and it is that certificate, naming “Bennie” Roush of Graham Station and Sophia Aultman of Portsmouth, Ohio, that gave this family its grandparents. He was buried at Broad Run, under a barrel-topped stone of the same pattern as his parents', reading FATHER & MOTHER / MOSES B. ROUSH / BORN JAN. 30, 1842. His widow filed her pension claim eight days after he died, and the money that paid for the end of his life had been granted for a war that ended sixty years before.

61.s:
Sarah Mary Duckworth was born in June 1851 in Pennsylvania, the fourth child and the first American child of James Duckworth, a Lancashire collier, and his wife Ann Collins. Her three elder brothers and sisters had been born in England and her two younger brothers in Pennsylvania and Ohio, so she is the one who dates the family's crossing: they were still in England when Adam was born in March 1847, and in Pennsylvania by the time she arrived.

By 1860 the Duckworths had moved on to the Ohio Valley coalfield, and the census taker at Syracuse, Meigs County, wrote the family name down as “Deckworth” and Sarah's age as nine. She was still at home in the summer of 1870, aged nineteen, and on 1 September that year she married Moses B. Roush at Orange Township in the same county - a Union veteran nine years her senior. Her brother Adam married eight days later in the same township. It was a busy fortnight for the family.

They had four children: Sarah Ann in 1871, Charles Benjamin in 1874, John G. in 1877 and Richard, born at Syracuse in 1880. She named the youngest for her own brother. The June 1880 census finds the little household in Sutton Township - and her widowed mother Ann keeping house five doors away.

Sarah died on 4 March 1881, aged twenty-nine, leaving four children under ten; her youngest was a baby. Her mother was living at the end of the row when it happened. She is buried at Broad Run Cemetery in Mason County - the same ground her husband, her son John and her grandchildren would come to - and her stone gives June 1851 to 4 March 1881.

62.s:
Lewis J. Nease was born on 20 November 1854 in Mason County, then still Virginia - by the family's own reckoning the second child of George Nease and Nancy Roush, who had married six years before. He is in the household in 1860, aged six, where the census taker spelled the surname “Neoce.”

On 12 April 1877, aged twenty-two, he married Martha J. Love, seventeen, who had been born across the river in Athens County, Ohio. He gave the clerk the information himself; the clerk wrote his surname “Nean” three times, and the index later made it “Man.” Their eldest, Bertha, was born the following January, and Lewis reported the birth as a farmer of Mason County. At least nine more children followed over the next twenty years, down to births registered in 1891 and 1895.

Twenty years after his own wedding he stood at the same counter for his daughter's. On 22 February 1897 the Mason County clerk wrote that “the name of the party giving the foregoing information is L. J. Nease of Mason County” - and his looping capital L is the thing that finally settled, in 2026, which man this was, after two research threads had closed the slot with two different people. In 1900 he gave his marriage as twenty-three years old, with Martha born in Ohio; the enumerator wrote his household one page from his daughter Bertha's.

By the end he was a labourer. He died on 17 February 1917 in the Waggener District of Mason County, of heart trouble, aged sixty-two years two months and twenty-eight days - an age that works back to 20 November 1854 to the day. He lies at Broad Run under a small obelisk carved with a gate or lattice, and the inscription, in the form he used all his life, is L. J. NEASE, 1854 - 1917. His own parents were left out of the register: both columns carry ditto marks running down from “not given.”

63.s:
Martha Jane Love was born on 30 January 1860 in Athens County, Ohio. Her mother was Leah McDonald; her father's name is not recorded anywhere, and when she died the registrar wrote “unknown” in that column in his own hand.

On 12 April 1877, aged seventeen, she married Lewis J. Nease of Mason County, West Virginia, who was twenty-two. She was from across the river in Ohio and he from the Virginia side; the licence catches the whole river-crossing habit of this family in one line. Their first child, Bertha, was born nine months later, in January 1878, and at least nine more followed; children of Lewis and Martha were still being registered in Mason County in 1891 and 1895.

The 1900 census shows the couple married twenty-three years, with Martha put down as born in Ohio, living one page away from their married daughter Bertha. She was widowed in February 1917 and stayed on in Mason County a widow for the last twenty-four years of her life.

She died at Mason on 12 August 1941, aged eighty-one years six months and thirteen days - an age that checks back to 30 January 1860 exactly - and was buried at Broad Run two days later, in the same ground as her husband, her daughter and her Roush in-laws. Her stone reads MARTHA J. NEASE, 1860 - 1941. Her maiden name, LOVE, survived on two later certificates: her daughter Bertha's in 1950, which names her as Martha Jane Love, and a grandson's in 1942, where the clerk heard it as “Lue.”

72.s:
John Eakins was born about 1795 in New Hanover County, North Carolina, the eldest son of Joseph Eakins and the woman who was probably Elizabeth Pigford. He was about ten when his father died in the first months of 1805, leaving a widow, a houseful of small children and four hundred acres on Moores Creek, and an estate the county court had to superintend for the next fourteen years.

That estate paid for his upbringing. In February 1816 it was charged $3.83 for schooling Joseph and William Eakins and $10.50 for boarding them; his sisters Sarah and Deborah were put into calico and cambric and a pair of shoes. Part of the money came from hiring out the three people the estate held in slavery — Simon, Rachel and Cesar — who were still in the administrator Edward Pigford's hands in 1817.

At the February term of 1819, aged twenty-four, he took over from Timothy Pigford as guardian of his own younger brothers and sisters, and on 22 March that year he rendered his first account to the court and signed it “John Eakins, Guard'n.” One of the securities named in that return was Stephen Coston.

He married Nancy Costin — of that same Coston family — probably about 1828 or 1829. The 1850 census finds him in the first dwelling enumerated in the county, a farmer with $800 in real estate, aged fifty-five, with Nancy, forty-three, and nine children at home: Margaret, Ella, John, Andrew, Joseph, Susan, Presilla, Cornelia and Sarah. His younger brother Joseph was in the next house; the two brothers' tracts adjoined on the east side of Moores Creek, where their father had bought in 1790.

The war took two of the family. In May 1861 his son John J. B. Eakins and his nephew Owen J. enlisted at Lower Black River in Company E of the 18th North Carolina — the Moore's Creek Rifle Guards, a company named for the water the Eakinses had farmed since before the Constitution was ratified. John J. B. was killed at Sharpsburg; Owen at Chancellorsville. On 29 January 1863, in New Hanover County, John Eakins Sr. swore before a justice of the peace that he was the father of the dead soldier and claimed the $100.23 owed on his account. Daniel McAlister, who had known the boy for twenty-five years, witnessed it. The government paid in November 1864.

He was still living after 1880. No stone for him has been found in the Eakins family burying ground on the creek.

73.s:
Nancy Costin was born in 1807 in North Carolina and married John Eakins Sr. of New Hanover County, probably about 1828 or 1829 — not in 1819, as a family record has it, because in 1819 she was twelve.

She bore at least nine children between about 1830 and 1848: Margaret, Ella, John J. B., Andrew, Joseph William, Susan, Presilla, Cornelia and Sarah. The household sat in the first dwelling the 1850 enumerator came to in the county, on the Moores Creek land her husband's father had bought in 1790.

Two of her sons went into the 18th North Carolina in 1861 and one of them, John J. B., was killed at Sharpsburg in September 1862; she was alive to know it, and her husband swore the affidavit that claimed the dead boy's pay.

Her own people were Costins or Costons — one family spread across two counties, rooted on Stump Sound in Onslow and moving down into New Hanover in the 1790s. A Stephen Coston stood security on her husband's guardian bond in 1819, which is as close as the record has yet come to naming her father. She died in 1870, and like her husband she has no marked grave in the Eakins burying ground.

76.s:
Joseph Tolbert Swain was born on 24 May 1838 in Wilcox County, Alabama. By his early twenties he had moved west into Lauderdale County, Mississippi, where on 6 February 1860 he married Nancy E. Jane; their first child, Joseph Lee, was born there that December.

He went to the war as a private in Company C of the 2nd Mississippi Cavalry. A photograph of him survives, reproduced from a printed page — a man in a dark coat and a hard round hat, with a heavy beard down his chest and a direct, unsmiling stare.

Whatever happened to him between 1861 and 1865, he did not wait once it was over. His two eldest children were born in Mississippi, in 1861 and 1864; every child from 1866 onward was born in Alabama. He moved his wife and two small children across the state line into Sumter County in the first months after the surrender, when he was about twenty-seven, and settled at Cuba. The 1880 census finds the household there: J. T. Swain, 42, Nancy E. J., 42, and seven children at home, from Joseph L., nineteen, down to John M., six.

On 3 July 1875 he walked into the registrar's office at Cuba, in Precinct No. 18 of Sumter County, and took the registration oath ahead of that August's referendum on a new state constitution. The printed oath he swore made him promise that he would "never countenance or aid in the secession of this State from the United States" and that he "accept[ed] the civil and political equality of all men" — ten years after he had ridden with the 2nd Mississippi Cavalry. The registrar W. H. Lewis wrote his name for him and he made his mark: he could not write. The remarks column calls him a farmer near Cuba. Two lines below him on the same page, registering the same day, was B. A. Simmons, the miller and farmer whose daughters his son Joseph Lee would marry nine and ten years later.

Two more babies, Jesse and Hassiel, were born and died in 1876–79. Nine children in all are known, and four of them were still living in 1940: Joseph Lee, John M. Swain of York, Mattie Shamburger and Laura McDonald. Joseph Tolbert Swain died on 14 January 1904, aged sixty-five, in Sumter County; his son William T. followed him four months later, and in November 1905 his eldest son advertised a probate sale of a hundred and sixty acres at the post-office door at Cuba, for distribution among the heirs of the estate of “J. T. Swain, deceased.” He lies in Clay Memorial Cemetery at Cuba under a government-issue marble marker reading JOSEPH TOLBERT SWAIN, PVT CO C 2 MISS CAV, CONFEDERATE STATES ARMY. A visitor left a line on his memorial page in 2013: “Here rests one who so bravely fought for the land he could not save.”

77.s:
Nancy E. Jane was born in Mississippi — in 1838 by the census reckoning she gave all her life, and on 26 December 1837 by the date recorded from her grave. She married Joseph Tolbert Swain in Lauderdale County on 6 February 1860, when she was twenty-two, and their first child was born that December.

She bore at least nine children. The two eldest, Joseph Lee and Alice Jane, were born in Mississippi; from 1866, after the family crossed into Sumter County, Alabama, the rest were born there — Martha Ann, Laura, Minnie Lou, William T., John M., and two who did not live, Jesse in 1878 and Hassiel in 1879. The 1880 census finds her at Cuba with seven of them still at home.

Four of her children outlived her husband by decades: her eldest, Joseph Lee, and John M. Swain of York, Mattie Shamburger and Laura McDonald, all three of whom were still at York in 1940. She was widowed in January 1904 and lost her grown son William T. that May. She died on 2 June 1908, aged seventy, and lies beside her husband in Clay Memorial Cemetery at Cuba; the inscription recorded from her stone is simply “Wife of J. T. Swain.”

A Mississippi marriage index compiled from the county's filmed records lists J. T. Swain and Nancey E. J. Phillips, married in Lauderdale County on 6 February 1860; the register page itself has not yet been seen.

Her maiden name has never been documented by this family's research.

80.s:
Henry H. Stephens was born on 8 August 1822 in North Carolina, the son of Moore Stephens and Rebecca Moize of Orange County. He was a small child when the family left for Alabama — they were in Greene County by 1824 — and he grew up on the Alabama side of the Tombigbee country, moving on with his father into Sumter County.

On 4 June 1846, at twenty-three, he married Sarah Ann Jones, who had been born in North Carolina about 1833 and whose family lived a few doors from his own. The 1850 census caught the whole arrangement on one page. In the “Intercourse” division of Sumter County, enumerated on 7 June 1850, Henry was twenty-seven and farming at dwelling 1184 with Sarah, seventeen, and a son Calvin, aged one; a boarder, Redden Marshall, twenty-three and North Carolina-born, was in the house. Two dwellings along lived Daniel Jones, Sarah’s father; six houses away, at dwelling 1190, lived Henry’s own father Moore. A son, Caswell Massey Stephens, was born on 8 January 1852.

Sarah died young and is not recorded dying. On 21 October 1854 Henry married again, to Elizabeth Jones — almost certainly his first wife’s younger sister — before Jesse B. Thorne, Justice of the Peace. By 1860 the family had followed Moore Stephens west into Newton County, Mississippi, where the census lists Henry with Elizabeth, twenty-one, and the children Caroline, Caswell, James and William. By 1870 they were back at Cuba, in Township 17 of Sumter County — the third leg of one continuous migration, 1850 Sumter to 1860 Newton County to 1870 Sumter again.

His gravestone survives, cut with a Masonic square and compasses inside a carved wreath, and it reckons his life to the day: born 8 August 1822, died 20 October 1879, aged 57 years, 2 months and 12 days. The carver spelled the family name STEAVENS.

Four years before he died he very probably took the 1875 registration oath at Thornville, Precinct No. 3 of Sumter County, on 22 June 1875, entry 25, written in his own hand — “H. H. Stephens”, farmer. Two lines further down the same page a D. C. Stephens registered the same day, and immediately above him A. J. Shelton, “Farmer & Blk Smith.”

He was a Minister of the Gospel, and the Sumter County marriage registers have him performing weddings through the 1860s and seventies, including his own son Caswell’s in October 1871. On 31 December 1869 he stood in the Probate Court at a special term before Judge J. A. Abrahams and was appointed guardian of three of his own sons — Caswell M., Calvin D. and John M., each of them over fourteen and each described as “a minor heir of Daniel Jones deceased” — posting bonds of $800, $800 and $1,000. The property was real enough that he was filing annual settlements two years later. He died in October 1879 at Gaston, in Sumter County, aged fifty-seven.

81.s:
Sarah Ann Jones was born about 1833 in North Carolina, almost certainly the eldest daughter of Daniel Jones. Her younger brothers and sisters were all Alabama-born from about 1837, which puts the family’s move south in the middle thirties, with Sarah born just before it.

On 4 June 1846 she married Henry H. Stephens in Sumter County, Alabama. If her recorded age is right she was about thirteen; the census ages may be a year or two light, in which case she was fourteen or fifteen. Either way she was a very young bride, and she had her first child, Calvin, at about sixteen.

The 1850 census is the only record that describes her household directly: “Sarah Stephens, 17,” born North Carolina, in dwelling 1184 of the Intercourse division of Sumter County with her husband, their one-year-old son, and a boarder. Her father’s house stood two doors away and her husband’s father’s six houses off — the whole connection fitted into one short row. Caswell Massey Stephens was born to her on 8 January 1852, and a son John M. probably followed.

She died somewhere between then and October 1854, when Henry remarried; the new wife, Elizabeth Jones, was in all likelihood her own younger sister. Nothing records Sarah’s death, her age at it, or where she lies. What survives instead is an inheritance: in December 1869 her three sons were bonded in the Sumter County probate court as “minor heirs of Daniel Jones deceased” — a share that could only reach grandchildren through a parent already dead. That document is her epitaph.

88.s:
John Wesley Truett was born on 20 October 1833, the son of the Reverend William Hampton Truett and Alcey Wiggins.

On 2 November 1854, at twenty-one, he married Emily Caroline Ward in Henry County. She was seventeen, so her father had to sign: five days earlier W. H. Ward had written out his consent for the clerk to copy into the marriage book — “license should issue for the marriage of John Truett with my daughter Emily C.” The father-in-law wrote a firm, practised hand. The bridegroom could not write at all.

By the war the family had moved three hundred miles west to Clarke County. He enlisted on 15 October 1862 at Coffeeville, his own village, signing on “for the War” with Colonel Alexander McKinstry — Private, Company D, 32nd Alabama Infantry, under a Captain Cox. He was twenty-eight. Four weeks later he was in the Confederate post hospital at Dalton, Georgia, with chronic rheumatism, and he never really came back: sent on to Tullahoma in February 1863, drawing clothing at Dalton that April and signing the receipt with an X, furloughed for thirty days at the end of May. Every muster roll in his file says the same word, absent. The file stops in the summer of 1863 with no discharge, no capture and no parole, and fifty-seven years later his widow, asked on a state form when he had quit the service, left the line blank. The family did not know either.

He farmed at Chilton. The 1880 census takes the whole house in one page: John, 46; Emlie C.; the children, William Curtis among them; and his mother Alecey, the preacher's widow, at sixty-seven. In 1907 the state counted him among its surviving old soldiers at Coffeeville, aged seventy-three.

On 9 July 1909 he went in person before the county pension board. What he owned, sworn on the schedule: thirty-six acres at $150, a “Small Frame Box House one Room” at $25, and one cow and calf at $10. The other eleven categories — horses, hogs, guns, watches, furniture, tools — all say None. The board wrote to the State Auditor at Montgomery: “He has some head trouble, is unable to do but little work, has no income except what little work he can do himself, no one to look to for support.” He signed John his X mark Truett, as he had at Dalton forty-six years before.

Elizabeth Roberts on 27 December 1905. Another Truett lies in the same cemetery as his son under a Confederate government marker that reads G. W. Truett, Corporal, Company D, 32nd Alabama Infantry — his own company.

His own pension application, filled in for him at Grove Hill in July 1909, says he enlisted in October 1862 at Murfreesboro in Tennessee — not at Coffeeville — and that he was honourably discharged in May 1865; the compiled service record, which stops in the summer of 1863, says neither thing. Asked on the printed form what made him unable to make a living, the board wrote three words: catarrh of the head. He had no children he could look to for support, the form says, though six of them were living. Two neighbours swore to his service, Elijah Brown and J. H. Geiger senior, and both of them signed with a mark, as he did. The county board put him in Class 4 and the state board at Montgomery agreed; he drew pension number 27126 in Clarke County until he died.

He died on 17 April 1914, aged eighty, and lies at Oak Grove Cemetery, Chilton, under a rounded marble headstone with clasped hands carved at the top and the words GONE BUT NOT FORGOTTEN. Caroline outlived him by eight years and lies three hundred miles away in Florida. A studio photograph of the two of them survives, with their son George standing behind.

89.s:
Emily Caroline Ward was born on 25 December 1836 at Abbeville in Henry County, Alabama — a date she swore to herself, under oath, at seventy-nine. She was the second daughter of William H. Ward, a South Carolina-born farmer with four hundred dollars of land at Rowville. Her mother is uncertain: Syntha, the wife beside him in 1850, married him only in December 1844, eight years after Caroline was born, and was very probably her stepmother. In 1850 she was twelve, one of eight children in the house.

She married at seventeen. Because she was under twenty-one her father had to consent, and the clerk copied his words into the Henry County marriage book above the licence: “I give my free and unqualified consent that license should issue for the marriage of John Truett with my daughter Emily C.” The licence issued on 28 October 1854 and they married five days later. Neither bride nor groom could write.

They moved west to Clarke County. Children came — Sarah Ann in 1858, William Curtis in 1867, George in 1872, John Wesley in 1875, Elisha Dozier in 1877, Carrie in 1878 — and in 1880 she is “Emlie C.” at Chilton, keeping house for her husband, four children and her mother-in-law Alcey. When her father's Henry County estate was broken up in 1870 she was so far away that the administrators left her off the petition altogether; a neighbour, Abijah Wiggins, put her back in six weeks later, swearing that among the heirs of full age was “the wife of JOHN TRUETT.”

She was widowed on 17 April 1914 and applied for her Confederate widow's pension three months later. In April 1915, at Coffeeville, she swore she had been born at Abbeville on the 25th day of December 1836, and signed with her mark. Then, in 1917, at eighty, she left Alabama for good: her daughter Sarah and Sarah's husband William Green Geiger moved the household to Hardeetown in Levy County, Florida, and the old woman went with them. On 13 December 1920 she put her X on an Alabama pension form with the word ALABAMA struck out and “Florida” written in, giving her address as Hardeetown and her income as “NONE.”

A second likeness of her survives besides the family group: a head-and-shoulders portrait of a dark-haired woman with her hair parted in the middle, kept in a cousin's scrapbook and copied so many times that the face has gone to black and white patches. Her gravestone at Hardeetown gives her birth as Christmas Day 1829 -- seven years earlier than she herself swore to in 1915.

She died at Chiefland at six in the evening on 30 November 1922, of what the doctor called paralysis of the bowels after a fortnight, with old age contributing — eighty-five years old. The informant was simply “Son,” who gave her father's name as John Ward and answered the next three questions with a question mark. She is buried at Hardeetown Methodist Cemetery in plot S5, the only Truett in the ground, with her daughter Sarah on one side and Sarah's mother-in-law on the other: three old women in a row. Her stone reads CAROLINE W. TRUETT — the W for Ward, her maiden name cut into her own marker — and a birth year, 1829, that is seven years wrong and came from the son standing at the registrar's desk two days after she died.

96.s:
Clark Strong Tuttle was born on 27 April 1811 in Jefferson County, New York — the date is in the family Bible; the 1883 Tuttle genealogy says the 28th. His father, Colonel Gershom Tuttle, kept a farm and a famous tavern outside Watertown; his mother was Pamelia Strong Clark, and he carried both of her surnames, which is unusual enough that a United States land officer wrote him down in full in 1837 as Clark Strong Tuttle. He used the name himself.

In November 1817 a federal clerk at the Vincennes land office entered his father as “Gershom Tuttle, Jeff'n Co N.Y.”; three weeks later the same ledger calls him “Gershom Tuttle, Fort Harrison.” The family had crossed to Indiana, and Clark grew up on the Wabash. His father died in September 1823, when Clark was twelve, leaving an estate that proved insolvent and took nine years to close. In 1830, aged nineteen, he was counted not under any Tuttle roof — there was none in the county — but in the household of Henry Markle, his sister Amanda's husband.

He came of age in April 1832 and married Harriet M. Sweany two weeks later, on 11 May. Their children, in the Bible's hand, were Gersham, Aula, Hannah, Chester, Josephine, Frank and a second Aula; four of the first five died as infants or children and lie together under “C.S. & H. TUTTLE” stones at Otter Creek Union Cemetery. The second Aula was named for the sister who had died four years before she was born. Harriet died on 3 June 1851, aged thirty-seven; five weeks later, on 10 July, Clark married Nancy A. Harbert, and they had Edward, Emma, Dennis, Richard B., Harriet B. and Dollie A.

He was a miller, and a rich one. The 1850 census gives him $9,500 in real estate; in 1860 it is $14,000 in land and $9,215 in personal property, with three hired hands and a servant living in and every school-age child in the house at school. He took United States patents on four parcels in 1839 and 1841. He became a county commissioner in October 1858, and he was postmaster at Ellsworth — which was the post office at his own Tuttle's Mills. The 1874 county atlas prints the mill on its own plate: a four-storey frame mill under a smoking stack with box cars on the siding, captioned C. S. TUTTLE & CO., MILLERS & DEALERS IN GRAIN, FLOUR, MEAL &c., ELSWORTH, VIGO CO., IND., with his name, his son Frank's and a partner's beneath it. The same atlas letters the township plat “C. S. Tuttle · Mill · ELSWORTH STA.” The mill was the town.

Not everything went well. In October 1869 a postal detective charged his son Frank, who ran the office under him, with robbing the mail, and the Terre Haute paper reported that “Mr. Clark Tuttle, the father of young Frank, is terribly distressed at the result of this unfortunate affair.” The following summer he sold out: the 117-acre mill tract on 12 July 1870 for $6,000, the partnership of C. S. Tuttle & Co. dissolved on the 26th, and the home parcels gone by 24 October. By 1878 a correspondent could write that the mill “has been standing idle for four years.”

He was still alive and public-spirited in June 1876, when the Centennial Fourth of July committee listed him among its vice-presidents as “Clark Tuttle, Otter Creek.” He was dead by 5 May 1880, when the paper called his daughter “daughter of the late C. S. Tuttle.” No death notice survives — the Terre Haute dailies of those years are digitised nowhere. His widow Nancy was buried from Union Church in Otter Creek in April 1883. No stone marks either of them.

97.s:
Nancy A. Harbert — the Vigo County clerk wrote it Herbert — was born about 1826 or 1827 in Ohio. Nothing is known of her parents or of how she came to Indiana.

On 10 July 1851 she married Clark Strong Tuttle, the miller of Otter Creek Township, before Harvey W. Allen, justice of the peace. His first wife Harriet had died five weeks earlier, leaving him with young children and a mill to run; four of Harriet's children were already buried in the Otter Creek ground. Nancy had six children of her own by him — Edward, Emma, Dennis, Richard B., Harriet B. and Dollie A. — and the line of this family runs through her.

The census of 1860 shows the house she kept: her husband a miller worth $14,000 in land, three hired hands and a servant living in, and every school-age child at school. She was thirty-three and born in Ohio, and that single line is the first recorded fact of any kind about her.

She outlived her husband by several years. She died on 25 April 1883 and was buried the next day from Union Church in Otter Creek Township, the church attached to the cemetery where her stepchildren lie. The paper gave her no name of her own: Mrs. Clark S. Tuttle — the widow of the late Clark S. Tuttle, the miller. No stone survives for her.

98.s:
Francis Fuerstenberger — Frank, to Terre Haute — was born in Bavaria in 1826 or 1827. He is the immigrant on this line, and nothing of his German town, his crossing or his naturalisation has been found; his name is mangled in every index that touches it, which is why the family was invisible for so long. The censuses have him as Fersenburger and Fuerstebuger; the marriage clerks as Ferstenberger and Furstenberger.

On 26 February 1852, in Clark County, Illinois, he married Sophia, a young widow. Their first child was born at Marshall, in that county, the following November. About 1854 they came to Terre Haute, and from that year to the end of his life he lived in one house: 521 South Third Street. He was a shoemaker, and by 1870 he owned $2,000 of real estate; on the same census page, a few doors away, lived another Bavarian in the leather trade — the immigrant quarter of a river city in miniature.

Eight children were born to them. In October 1881 his daughter Emma married Richard B. Tuttle, a young miller; three years later, in December 1884, Richard died of consumption, and the funeral was held at ten in the morning from Frank's own house on South Third Street. The widow and the baby stayed.

Sophia died about 1890. Frank died in the autumn of 1894, aged sixty-eight; the Saturday Evening Mail gave him a paragraph on its front page as “an old and well known citizen” and noted the thing he was known for — forty years in one city and all of it in one house. He lies at Highland Lawn Cemetery, Section 3, Lot 162, under a shared obelisk with Sophia, the inscription recording his age to the day: sixty-eight years and twenty-four days.

The earliest time his name appears in a Terre Haute newspaper is as a man who had not collected his post. On 15 October 1864 the Terre Haute Star printed the post office's list of uncalled letters, and in the gentlemen's column, between Foulke and Fort, stands "Fuerstenberger F."

The Clark County, Illinois record book holds both halves of his marriage. A licence was granted to Francis Fiestenburgen and Sophia Flint, 'now both of this County', in February 1852, signed by J. Stockwell, Clerk; and the minister's certificate beneath it reads that on the 26th day of February 1852 he joined them in the state of matrimony 'according to the usual custom and laws of the State of Illinois'. It was returned, registered and filed on 1 March 1852.

On the Wednesday before 1 March 1890 he and Sophia kept their fortieth wedding anniversary at the South Third Street house, "very delightfully," afternoon and evening. She was dead within four months.

The censuses of 1870 and 1880 both find him in Terre Haute, and long after he was gone, a family lawsuit over an inheritance in 1934 still named the heirs of five of his eight children.

99.s:
Sophia was born in 1828 in Pennsylvania.

She was married before she met Francis Fuerstenberger. The Clark County, Illinois index records the bride of 26 February 1852 as Sophia Flint — so she had very probably been married before. That is almost certainly why a generation of searching under “Snyder” found nothing.

She and Francis had eight children between 1852 and 1870: John Fredrick, James W., Anna, Clara Rebecca, Emma, Daniel, George and Eliza. The family came to Terre Haute about 1854 and lived at 521 South Third Street, where Francis made shoes and where, in December 1884, her daughter Emma's young husband was buried out of the front room.

She married as SOPHIA FLINT. The Clark County, Illinois book names her that way twice on one page -- once in the licence granted to her and Francis Fiestenburgen, 'now both of this County', and again in the minister's certificate of 26 February 1852. Her being a widow Flint rather than a Snyder at the altar is why the Clark County free layer went on returning nothing for 'Snyder'.

She died on 15 June 1890 at 520 South Third Street, Terre Haute, aged sixty-two, of pleuro-pneumonia, and was buried at Highland Lawn — four months after she and Francis had kept their fortieth wedding anniversary in the same house.

She died on 14 June of pleuro-pneumonia, in that house, aged sixty-two years, three months and two days, and was interred the following day at Highland Lawn. The year is in dispute: the project's own records and Find a Grave's header say 1889, while the City of Terre Haute's old cemetery database, quoted on her memorial, says 1890 — and her husband's 1894 death notice, which said his wife had died “four years ago,” points the same way. She lies with Francis in Section 3, Lot 162, under a stone that records her age but not her birth.

⭐ 27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep. Benjamin has his own Find a Grave memorial, 43764784, which the notes did not carry (ROUSH-21 lists his stone with a dash where the memorial number should be). It links him to John 'Blackbird John' Roush (72226020) and Regina (72226047) as parents, and shows the same stone photograph already held as ROUSH-36b. [ROUSH-88]
120.s:
Benjamin Roush was born on 30 August 1816 at Graham Station, in Mason County, Virginia - the fifth child, by the family's own record, of John “Blackbird John” Roush and his wife Regina. He was the last of them born on the Virginia bank: his sister Hannah arrived in May 1820 in the Nease Settlement across the river in Meigs County, Ohio, so the family crossed in the years between.

On 23 May 1839 he married Sophia Altman at Orange Township, Meigs County. The justice of the peace who joined them did not get round to filing his return until the following July, when he certified two weddings at once in a single sentence. Sophia was not yet sixteen. Twelve children were born to them; nine of them are in the house in the 1860 census.

He farmed in Sutton Township. In 1850 he was thirty-four, Virginia-born, with seven children and an older woman, Mary Roush, thirty-six and also born in Virginia, living in the household. Four dwellings up the same page was John Roush, sixty-six, born in Virginia. In August 1849 that John Roush - a man who could not write and signed every deed with a mark - sold Benjamin sixty-nine acres and twenty poles in the north-east corner of Section 25, Town 3, Range 12 for five hundred dollars; on the same day, before the same justice and the same two witnesses, the rest of that same strip went to John Roush Junior. No deed says why.

By 1870 Benjamin and Sophia were at Syracuse, the salt and coal village on the river, in the same census year as the English Duckworth family whose daughter their son Moses would marry that September. By 1880 they had crossed back into West Virginia and were living in Waggener District, Mason County.

He died on 5 March 1897. Sophia outlived him by sixteen months. They lie together at Broad Run Cemetery under a barrel-topped stone on a rough-faced plinth: FATHER & MOTHER / BENJAMIN ROUSH / BORN AUG. 30, 1816 / DIED MAR. 5, 1897. To his own son, giving the names to a county clerk in 1925, he was “Bennie.”

Outstanding: ⚠ Because she was a minor, a parental consent naming her father was filed in Meigs County in May 1839 — but Meigs County has no licence, bond or consent series on film (vols 1–24 are returns only). It is a loose paper in the Probate Court, off-line [ROUSH-37].
121.s:
Sophia Altman was born on 1 June 1823 in Ohio. Her son's death certificate, written eighty-four years later, says she came from Portsmouth, in Scioto County, sixty miles down the same river.

She married Benjamin Roush at Orange Township, Meigs County, on 23 May 1839, at fifteen years and eleven months - nine days short of her sixteenth birthday. Ohio required a parent's consent for a bride that young, so a paper naming her father was filed at the Meigs County courthouse that May; it has never been found, and her parents remain unproven.

Twelve children were born to the marriage. Nine of them are in the Sutton Township household in 1860: Moses, Joseph, Sarah, Livina, Zillah, Hannah, Maria and the rest. Six are known by name and fate - Moses B., Sarah Elizabeth Kauff, Mary Lovina Findley, Maria Ann Goodnite, Serepta Ann, and Dillia McDaniel - and four of the daughters lived long enough for Ohio and West Virginia to register their deaths, each certificate naming Sophia as their mother, spelled Altman on some and Aultman on others.

The family farmed Sutton Township through the 1850s and 1860s, were at Syracuse in 1870, and by 1880 had crossed into Waggener District, Mason County, West Virginia. Sophia died back in Meigs County, Ohio, on 4 July 1898, sixteen months after Benjamin, on Independence Day. She was buried beside him at Broad Run, under a stone that calls her only SOPHIA, HIS WIFE - the granite does not give her maiden name at all.

A COLLIER. “James Duckworth, of full age, Bachelor, Collier, of Wood Head Hill” — m. Ann Collins 21 January 1839 at St Mary, Bury, Lancashire, after banns, by J. F. Amos, curate; both signed with an ✗ mark; his father entered as GEORGE DUCKWORTH, HATTER [ROUSH-34]. Emigrated c. Outstanding: ⭐ The Athens asylum admission and death registers, 1874–1880, would give his death and burial — and would close the story. There is no estate because a man sent to a state asylum leaves no will.
122.s:
James Duckworth was born in Lancashire about 1813 to 1818, the son of George Duckworth, a hatter of the Bury district. He went down the pit instead. On 21 January 1839, described in the register as “of full age, Bachelor, Collier, of Wood Head Hill,” he married Ann Collins of Freetown at the parish church of St Mary, Bury, after banns, by the curate J. F. Amos. Both of them signed with a mark; so did one of the witnesses, Richard Duckworth.

Three children were born to them in England - Mary about 1842, William about 1844, Adam in March 1847 - and a daughter later told an Ohio registrar that her parents came from Manchester, nine miles south of Bury and the name a Lancashire family abroad would naturally use. Then the family crossed the Atlantic, very probably in 1850 or 1851: they are not in the 1850 United States census, and Sarah was born in Pennsylvania in 1851. Ralph followed there about 1856, and by about 1859, when Richard was born, they had moved on to Ohio. It is the classic path of an English mining family - the Pennsylvania coalfield first, then the Ohio Valley pits.

In 1860 the census taker at Syracuse, Meigs County, put the name down as “Deckworth” and James at forty-seven, with Ann and six children in the house. In 1870 he was still the head of the household, aged fifty-six. Sarah married Moses Roush that September.

On 24 April 1874 the Meigs County probate court heard a case headed “In the Matter of the Insanity of James Duckworth.” James was present. On the sworn testimony of Wm Duckworth - almost certainly his own son William - and of Henry and August Bartels and David Thomas, the court found him insane, of less than two years' duration, with a legal settlement in Sutton Township, and entitled to admission to the Lunatic Asylum of the State of Ohio at Athens, which had opened only three months before. Dr. Isaac Irwin was ordered to file his medical certificate; in the meantime the court directed that the patient be held in the county jail “separate and apart from those who are charged with crime.”

He was dead by June 1880, when Ann was enumerated a widow. Where he died, and where he lies, is not known. A man sent to a state asylum leaves no will and no inventory, which is why there is no estate to find.

123.s:
Ann Collins was born in Lancashire after 21 January 1818 - that much is fixed, because she was still under twenty-one on that day in 1839, when she married. She was the daughter of Adam Collins of Freetown, in Bury, and it is only because she was a minor and her father's consent was required that his name was written into the register at all.

She married James Duckworth, a collier of Wood Head Hill, at St Mary's, Bury, on 21 January 1839. Neither of them could write; both made their mark. Three children came in England - Mary about 1842, William about 1844 and Adam in March 1847, named for her father. Then the family crossed to America, most likely in 1850 or 1851, and Sarah was born in Pennsylvania, Ralph about 1856, and Richard in Ohio about 1859.

In 1860 she was forty-three and keeping a house of eight at Syracuse, Meigs County, in the Ohio Valley coalfield. Her children married into the same English and Cornish mining families around them: Mary to John W. Treadwell, himself a Manchester man; William to Sarah Pascoe, a Cornish name; Sarah to Moses Roush, and Adam eight days after Sarah, in the same township, in September 1870.

By June 1880 James was gone. Ann, sixty-two and widowed, kept her own house in Sutton Township - and the census taker put her down five households from her daughter Sarah's family, where Sarah had four children under ten. Sarah died the following March, and her mother was right there when it happened. After that Ann disappears from the record; nothing has been found of her death or burial.

Her maiden name survived by a single thread. In 1924 her eldest daughter died in Ohio, and the certificate reads: “MOTHER: ANN COLLINS, England.”

127.s:
Leah McDonald was born in Ohio. One record names her, and it was written eighty-one years after the event it describes: when her daughter Martha Jane (Love) Nease died in Mason County, West Virginia, on 12 August 1941, the register gave her mother's maiden name as Leah McDonald, born Ohio, and her father as unknown.

Martha Jane was born in Athens County, Ohio, on 30 January 1860, so Leah was living in that county at the turn of that year. Five years later, on 4 October 1865, an Athens County marriage index records a Leah McDonald marrying Ranslier Graham, a widower who had married once before in 1851. If that is the same woman, she was a young widow remarrying - which would explain neatly why the family remembered her by her maiden name and not by either husband's. Ransler Graham himself died at Mason City, Mason County, West Virginia, on 12 February 1913, aged eighty-four, a farmer and a soldier: he had crossed the river into the county where Martha Jane lived out her life, and his death went into the same 1913 register book as her mother-in-law's, two pages apart.

None of that is proved. No period document names Leah beside Ransler Graham, and nothing has yet been found of her own birth, her first husband or her death.
