144.s:
Joseph Eakins arrives in the records of New Hanover County, North Carolina all at once, in 1790, aged about twenty-four and already able to pay. On 11 June that year James Fleming, a Wilmington merchant, conveyed to “Joseph Eakins of the same place, Gentleman,” for fifteen pounds currency, two tracts: a hundred acres beginning at a black oak below the old track path, and three hundred acres on the east side of Moores Creek. Nothing before that date has been found — no father, no brother, no uncle of the name anywhere in the county, and no Eakins household in the county at all in the 1790 census. He came from somewhere else, and where that was is still the oldest open question on this side of the family.

He worked that land for fifteen years. In December 1793 he sold a parcel to Jacob Moore, signing himself “planter” this time rather than gentleman. In 1796 he went to the state land office and took out a patent of his own — grant No. 482, two hundred and ten acres on the east side of the Widow Moore's Branch, beginning at a pine on the east side of the New Road in the meadow, witnessed by Samuel Ashe, Governor, Captain General and Commander in Chief, at Raleigh. The boundary calls run past “a pine, Parker's corner, now Eakins.”

He married, almost certainly, Elizabeth Pigford, and they had at least five children: John, born about 1795, William, Joseph, Sarah and Deborah.

He died in the first months of 1805, leaving children too young to act for themselves. At the March 1805 term the county court sent three men out to set aside his widow's year's provision, and they wrote down what they left in the yard to keep the household alive for twelve months: the corn in hand with the bacon, four cows and calves, one four-year-old steer, and the mark or right of hogs. On 11 April the rest went under the hammer — cattle, hogs, sheep, plantation tools, household furniture — and made $1,657.57. The inventory came in that June. Edward and Jacob Pigford were the administrators; Timothy Pigford took the children; Solomon Pigford stood security on the estate's notes. He also left three people he had held in slavery, Simon, Rachel and Cesar, whose hired-out labour went on paying the estate's bills for years afterwards, including the schooling of his sons.

The family never moved off that ground. His son Joseph bought the adjoining 138 acres in 1834, the deed running from “Joseph Eakins's own corner” along “Eakins's line”; and the Eakins Family Cemetery still stands on the Moores Creek land, in what is now Pender County. That son, born in 1797 and eight years old when his father died, lived to ninety-three; his is the oldest grave in it, and the newest is from 2019.

145.s:
Elizabeth Pigford was, in all probability, the wife of Joseph Eakins of Moores Creek and the mother of his children. No marriage record has been found, and the notes keep the word “probably” in her name.

What is certain is that when Joseph died in the first months of 1805 the Pigfords closed around his family. Edward and Jacob Pigford administered the estate and ran the April auction. Solomon Pigford stood security on its notes. Timothy Pigford was guardian of the minor children for fourteen years, until the eldest, John, was old enough to take over at the February term of 1819. Four Pigfords in one court file is not neighbourliness; it is kin. And a Pigford was still selling Eakins land to an Eakins in 1834.

She is the “Widow Eakins” to whom the county court allotted a year's provision in March 1805 — the corn and the bacon, four cows and calves, a four-year-old steer and the mark or right of hogs that would keep her children fed while the estate was settled — and very likely the “Elizabeth Eakens” who appears in the 1819 accounts holding a note for $220.76.

Her father was almost certainly William “Lost Billie” Pigford of Sill's Creek, whose 1801 will, as the family's 1967 historian transcribed it, leaves a shilling each to a list of children that includes “my daughter Elizabeth Aiken” — Aiken and Eakins being one name in New Hanover clerks' hands. But a second, independent transcription of the same will, posted on the county's own genealogy website, gives that clause without her in it. Until the original will book is read, that is exactly where she stands: a woman the records keep pointing at and never quite name.

160.s:
Moore Stephens was born about 1796 in North Carolina, one of at least ten children of a Stephens household in Orange County whose father’s name has not survived. On 3 September 1817 he took out a marriage bond in Orange County to marry Rebecca Moize. His brother Charles stood bondsman and Joseph A. Woods witnessed it; both men signed with a mark, so Moore could not write his own name.

Within a few years the whole family picked up and went to Alabama — they were in Greene County by 1824 — and Moore worked his way west again into Sumter County. On 12 October 1846 the Greene County Orphans’ Court divided the estate of Mary Thorn among ten heirs at law in equal shares, and he was one of them, due $107.50 and receipting $95. The nine others are his brothers and sisters: William, Lewis, Charles and James Stephens, Nancy Barnett, Mary Barnett, Lucinda Ball, Elizabeth Beavers and Esther Hitt. He bought nothing at the sale, because by then he no longer lived in the county; the clerk’s cost bill files him under “Heirs of Sumter Co., Ala.”

The 1850 census shows what his house actually held. At dwelling 1190 in Sumter County were Moore, fifty-four, Rebecca, fifty, and the children Benjamin W. 21, James M. 18, John F. 16, Mary A. R. 13, Charles L. 12, Easter C. 10 and William K. 6 — and two more, Rebecca J. and Richard Hitt, both ten, the orphans of his dead sister Esther, being raised alongside his own. He had named a daughter Easter for that sister. His son Henry farmed six houses up the road. The slave schedule for the same county that year records Moore Stephens holding one enslaved person, a Black girl of about seven, born around 1843, whom the schedule was designed not to name.

His marriage bond survives in the North Carolina archives: on 3 September 1817 he and Charles Stephens bound themselves to the Governor in five hundred pounds that there was no lawful cause to obstruct his marriage to Rebecca Moize. Both of them signed with a mark.

In 1853 and 1854 he stood surety three times in the county court alongside his neighbour Daniel Jones — twice on the administration of Thomas Fowler’s estate, for $1,200 and $2,800, and once on a $5,000 guardianship of Willis Thomas’s small children. By 1860 he had moved on again: the census of Newton County, Mississippi, lists “Moore Stevens, 66, born North Carolina,” with Rebeca 55 and five children still at home. Henry brought his family to the same county. When Moore died is not known. The Newton County courthouse burned in September 1876, “supposed to have been of incendiary origin,” and the probate records that would have dated his death burned with it.

161.s:
Rebecca Moize was born about 1800 to 1805 in North Carolina, into a Moize family that had held the same few square miles of Orange County for generations and would still be in Lebanon Township there in 1880. Her own parents have never been identified; the marriage bond that records her wedding does not name a father, because the bondsman carried the groom’s surname rather than hers.

On 3 September 1817, at about seventeen, she married Moore Stephens in Orange County. Within seven years the couple were in Greene County, Alabama, and by the 1840s in Sumter County. She bore a large family — the 1850 census of Sumter County lists seven of her children still at home, from Benjamin W. at twenty-one down to William K. at six — and when Moore’s sister Esther Hitt died she took in Esther’s two orphaned children as well, Rebecca J. and Richard, both ten years old and sitting in the household list between her own.

She was still beside her husband at the next census. In 1860 the enumerator of Newton County, Mississippi, wrote down “Rebeca Stevens, 55, born North Carolina” in Moore’s household — forty-three years and two states after an Orange County wedding at seventeen. She was alive after 1860; when and where she died is not recorded.

176.s:
William Hampton Truett was born in 1806 in Sumter District, South Carolina, and became a preacher. His was the generation that carried the family out of the Carolina low country and onto the Alabama frontier — Darlington and Sumter districts to Henry County in the south-eastern corner of Alabama, and from there west again.

He married Alcey Wiggins, a daughter of the Daniel Wiggins family who had made the same journey from Darlington. The family record of that marriage gives 10 October 1831 at Benton County, Alabama, and that cannot be right: Benton County was not created until 18 December 1832, out of Creek land ceded that March. Either the date is right and the place is not, or the county name was written back onto an older event by a later hand.

Their son John Wesley was born on 20 October 1833, and a daughter Winnie married a Joshua Johnson; their grandson, James Lafayette “Fate” Johnson, was born in Clarke County in 1861. The Truetts and the Wigginses went on marrying each other in Alabama for another hundred years.

He married Alcy Wiggins on 10 October 1831 in Henry County, Alabama; Wiley Peebles, justice of the peace, performed it and entered it as number 191 in the county book.

He died in 1870 in Henry County, Alabama. He is a hard man to find in print. Holcombe's register of Alabama Baptist ministers of 1803–1840 does not carry his name, and the 1882 history of Clarke County — where his widow and son ended up — names only two Truetts in seven hundred and eighty pages, neither of them a preacher. No grave has been found. Truitt, 1814–1864, lies in the same Oak Grove Cemetery at Chilton where his son John Wesley is buried, and the family trees make him William Hampton's brother; no record has yet been read that proves it.

177.s:
Alcey Wiggins was born about 1813, almost certainly in Darlington District, South Carolina. The 1820 census of Sumter District puts Daniel Wiggins there with two girls under ten in the house, and she fits one of them; Daniel and his wife Susannah Truitt had married at Darlington in 1800 and would end their lives in Henry County, Alabama.

She married William Hampton Truett, a preacher, about 1831 or 1832 — the family's record of the date and the family's record of the place cannot both be right, because the Alabama county it names did not yet exist. Their son John Wesley was born on 20 October 1833. A daughter, Winnie, married Joshua Johnson, and there was a daughter Martha who became Martha Powers.

Widowed in 1870, she went to live with her son. The 1880 census of Chilton in Clarke County finds her at about sixty-seven in John Wesley Truett's household — one enumerator's page holding three generations of the family at once: the old preacher's widow, her son the Confederate veteran who could not write, and her grandson William Curtis, Alec's great-great-grandfather. She died that same year.

She married at eighteen: Alcy Wiggins and William Hampton Truett, 10 October 1831, before Wiley Peebles, justice of the peace in Henry County.

The Truetts and the Wigginses kept marrying each other. Her own husband's brother married her sister; Truett×Wiggins marriages run on in the Alabama records into the twentieth century; and the man who swore the deposition that named her daughter-in-law among the heirs of the Ward estate at Abbeville in 1870 was an Abijah Wiggins — very probably her own brother.

178.s:
William H. Ward was born about 1806 in South Carolina and came west to the south-eastern corner of Alabama. The 1850 census of Henry County finds him at family 646 — “W. H. WARD, 44, m, Farmer, $400, S.C.” — with his wife Syntha, thirty-five and also South Carolina-born, and eight children, all of them born in Alabama. He was invisible to the indexers for a century and a half because the enumerator wrote the dwelling and family numbers one line low, onto his wife's line, so the machines made Syntha the head of the house and pushed him up into somebody else's household.

On 28 October 1854 he put his name to one of the better documents in this family's record. His daughter Emily Caroline was seventeen and wanted to marry John Truett, and Alabama required a parent's consent for a bride under twenty-one. The clerk copied his words straight into the marriage book: “I give my free and unqualified consent that license should issue for the marriage of John Truett with my daughter Emily C.” It is signed Wm. H. Ward in a firm, practised, unmistakably literate hand — which is worth noticing, because the bridegroom and the bride both signed their own papers with an X for the rest of their lives.

By 1860 he was at Rowville, Beat 5, aged fifty-three, with Cyntha and the younger children. Then he died, intestate, somewhere between 1860 and September 1869 — and probably in 1868 or 1869, because by 18 September 1869 his administrators, his son-in-law C. J. Hutto and his eldest son John E. Ward, were already in the Probate Court of Henry County applying for the widow's dower, with notice ordered to be published for thirty days in the Henry County Register.

He died on 6 February 1869 -- his son and his son-in-law swore to the date six weeks later when they asked the Probate Court for letters. He left about a thousand dollars of land and twenty-five hundred dollars of personal estate, most of it other men's promises: eleven notes, from twenty-four dollars to three hundred and thirty, several of them marked 'doubtfull'. The family's lawyers were Oates & Cowan of Abbeville, and the receipt for their hundred and five dollars is signed by W. C. Oates himself.

He took out a marriage licence in Henry County, Alabama on 11 October 1844 and was married on 18 December 1844 by Wm. R. Kelly, a justice of the peace, to Syntha Armstrong. It was at least his second marriage: several of the children in his house in 1850, Emily Caroline among them, were born years before it.

His land could not be divided, so it was sold. The petition of 28 September 1870 names every heir: the widow Cynthia; Ann Elizabeth Hutto; John E. Ward; Mary Nichols; Martha Driggers; William H. Ward, named for his father; and the minors George R., Eliza and Isaiah C. Ward, each “over fourteen and under twenty-one.” One name was left off — the daughter who had gone away west — and six weeks later a neighbour, Abijah Wiggins, put her back in under oath: among the heirs of full age, he swore, was “the wife of JOHN TRUETT.” His daughter said in 1920 that he had died in Clarke County; his widow was still at Rowville in 1880. Both are recorded, neither is proved.

179.s:
Syntha Ward — the clerks also wrote Cyntha, Cynthia and Cintha — was born in South Carolina about 1813, and both of her own parents were born in North Carolina. She married William H. They had at least ten children.

She is on the 1850 schedule of Henry County, Alabama as “Syntha, 35”, next to her husband and eight children, and on the 1860 schedule at Rowville Beat 5 as “Cyntha, 47”. Her youngest son was given the unusual name Caraway — or Conway; the records read it both ways — which is exactly the way a mother's maiden surname usually travels, and it is the best clue anyone has to hers.

Her husband died intestate before September 1869, and on the 18th of that month the court appointed a day to hear the application for her dower, with notice to be published in the Henry County Register and J. H. Simonton named guardian ad litem for the minor heirs. When the estate's land was sold the following year she is “Cynthia Ward, widow of decedent”; when the neighbour Abijah Wiggins swore his deposition at Abbeville in November 1870 she is “Mrs Cyntha Ward the widow of deceased.” In 1880 she was still at Rowville, sixty-six, widowed, keeping house, entered as MOTHER in the household of her youngest son Isaiah. She does not appear in the 1900 census of Alabama, so she died in those twenty years — before the state began registering deaths, which is why there is no certificate for her.

Her dower was eighty acres, measured off by five freeholders on 23 November 1869 and chosen, the writ said, so that none of them was connected to any of the parties by blood or by marriage. She signed everything with a mark, and the clerks spelled her Cynthia, Cyntha and Syntha on the same file.

In October 1844 the Henry County clerk issued a licence to William H. Ward and “Syntha Armstrong,” and a justice of the peace, Wm. R. Kelly, married them on 18 December 1844 — the marriage her husband's estate papers later placed in that county in that year. She was about thirty, and Armstrong may be a first husband's name rather than her own: a Wade Armstrong had married a Cynthia Bright in the same county in 1837. If she married William Ward only in December 1844, she was not the mother of his older children — Emily Caroline, born in 1836, among them — but their stepmother; who Caroline's mother was is now an open question.

Four documents in her husband's estate name her, and every one of them calls her only Mrs Cynthia Ward, widow of the deceased. Her maiden name has not survived in anything this project has read.

192.s:
Gershom Tuttle was born on 11 June 1769 at Bristol, Connecticut. He is the third Gershom Tuttle in a row in this family, and he is almost certainly the son of the second — the Revolutionary teamster — though that particular link is stated by the family genealogy of 1883 and by the DAR rather than by any record that says so in words, and this project has not been able to close it.

He married Pamelia Strong Clark at Farmington on 8 July 1788, when he was nineteen. In 1791 he and Joseph Tuttle, of Wardsborough, Vermont, bought a fifty-acre lot at Wilmington in that state; by the mid-nineties they had moved west to Paris, in Oneida County, New York, where the 1800 enumeration carries “Gershom Tuttle” and “Gershom Tuttle jun” on one sheet. About 1800 he went north again to the new Black River country and opened a farm of 275 acres some five miles from the site of Watertown, in the town of Rutland.

He was there from the beginning. When Rutland held its first town meeting in March 1803, in David Coffeen's house, he was one of the three men chosen highway commissioner — the same meeting that set a ten-dollar bounty on wolves. In 1806, with Seth Bailey, he built a grist mill on the Black River, the first of its kind there. He was a charter member of the Masonic lodge warranted at Watertown on 17 June 1806, where the roll enters him as “Gershom Tuttle, Jr.” — which is why, seventeen years later and eight hundred miles away, a lodge in Indiana buried him. From 1808 he was one of the county's commissioners for loaning the moneys of the state. In 1810 he took five shares at ten dollars in the Black River Navigation Company. He traded, made potash, and kept a tavern on the great highway to the lake country.

The tavern is what his neighbours remembered. About 1803 a hundred men of two townships assembled there, by appointment, to settle a bet about which town could out-wrestle the other, the winners promised all they could eat and drink. The first Congregational church of Watertown, organised in 1803, met in his ball-room when it had nowhere else, and he was an original member. He was fined eight dollars in 1809 for not turning up as a grand juror. The family book calls him “a man of excellent character, genial temper, very fond of a joke, a capital story teller,” and that is the man the records show.

He was commissioned second major of the Jefferson County militia on 5 April 1805, and on 4 April 1808 lieutenant-colonel of the 76th Regiment — the regiment the county histories simply call Tuttle's. In the War of 1812 the Watertown militia belonged to it and were turned out en masse whenever invasion threatened; at the Battle of Sackets Harbor on 29 May 1813 the county history posts the militia “in the edge of the woods, back of the clearing,” under Colonel Gershom Tuttle. (A second and unrelated Colonel Gershom Tuttle, of Massachusetts and of the regular army, died at that same post during the war and lies under the monument there; the militia command is ours.) He resigned in 1814.

In 1816 he took the family to Vigo County, Indiana. A federal land clerk entered him on 22 November 1817 as “Gershom Tuttle, Jeff'n Co N.Y.” and, three weeks later, as “Gershom Tuttle, Fort Harrison.” He became a county commissioner in 1820. The last summer of his life a sheriff was advertising a half-quarter section “the property of Gersham and Chester Tuttle” for sale on execution at the suit of John F. King, and his patent for eighty acres came through under James Monroe's hand on 15 July 1823, seven weeks before he died. On 29 August he made a will leaving everything to Pamelia for life and naming no child at all.

He died on the Friday night of 5 September 1823 in Otter Creek Township, in the fifty-fourth year of his age. Terre Haute's first newspaper reported that “on Sunday last his remains were consigned to the earth, accompanied with Masonic honors by the Terre Haute Lodge of which he was a member.” The estate turned out to be insolvent and was still in court nine years later. His grave has never been located.

Full dates: b. 4 Nov 1770 Farmington, Conn. – d. 22 Apr 1851 Nashville, Ind. (her stone, Southview Cemetery; the 1883 book gives 15 Apr, Find a Grave’s header 15 Nov) [TUTTLE-150 series, 27 Oct 2026]

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HER MAIDEN NAME IS CLARK. “STRONG” IS A MIDDLE NAME [TUTTLE-46, 7 August 2026]. G. F. Tuttle 1883, p. 512, in Col. Gershom’s own sketch: “He m. in Farmington, Conn., July 8, 1788, Pamelia Strong Clark of F., b. Nov. 4, 1770. Her brother was an officer of the U.S.A., and d. while in charge of the U.S. arsenal in Troy, N.Y. Gen. Newman Strong Clark of the Dept. of the Pacific, was her nephew. She d. at Nashville, Ind., April 15, 1851, a. 81.”

⛔⛔ THE STRONG DOOR IS SHUT. Dwight’s Descendants of Elder John Strong (1871) was searched in both volumes — no Pamelia Clark born 1770, no Tuttle marriage, no “Clark of Farmington.” The Elder John Strong descent that this chart has quietly assumed is not established and is now actively unsupported by the standard Strong genealogy. Her mother may still have been a Strong — that is a guess, not a finding.

⚠ Her death date is in conflict: Tuttle 1883 says 15 April 1851; Find a Grave memorial 16018171 says 15 November 1851. She is buried at Southview Cemetery, Nashville, Brown County, Indiana — ninety miles from her husband’s grave, because she outlived him by twenty-eight years and followed a child south.

Buried Southview Cemetery, Nashville, Brown Co., Indiana, with a headstone photograph. Her name is the “Strong Clark” carried down through Clark Strong Tuttle to Dennis Clark and Richard Clark — four generations of it.

⭐ 27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep. ⭐⭐ HER DEATH DATE IS ON HER STONE, AND IT IS NEITHER OF THE TWO DATES THE PROJECT CARRIES. The stone reads 22 APRIL 1851. The 1883 Tuttle genealogy says 15 April; Find a Grave's own header says 15 November; the stone its own contributor photographed says April 22. AND THE AGE LINE CONFIRMS HER BIRTHDAY: 80 years, 5 months and 18 days before 22 April 1851 is 4 NOVEMBER 1770, to the day — an independent contemporary witness to the birth date this chart has only from the 1883 book. This resolves node 193's stated conflict and should change the node's dates field. [TUTTLE-214]

⭐ 27 Oct 2026 — content round 2 (R2_fs_memories). FamilySearch gives d 15 April 1851 at Nashville, Brown, Indiana [TUTTLE-219] ⚠ Death date — FamilySearch: 15 Apr 1851 (agrees with the book, not the stone)
193.s:
Pamelia Strong Clark was born on 4 November 1770 at Farmington, Connecticut. Clark was her surname; Strong was a middle name, and it descended four more generations — Clark Strong Tuttle, Dennis Clark, Richard Clark — long after anyone remembered where it came from. On 8 July 1788, aged seventeen, she married Gershom Tuttle of Bristol.

She spent the next twenty-eight years moving west with him: Wilmington in Vermont, Paris in Oneida County, and about 1800 the new Black River country of Jefferson County, New York, where her husband farmed 275 acres, built a mill and kept the tavern that gave the neighbourhood its ball-room. Her son Chester was born at Sackets Harbor in 1796; Cynthia at Watertown in 1803; Amanda in 1810; Clark Strong in April 1811; Asa in 1813. In 1816 the family went on to Vigo County, Indiana.

Her husband died on 5 September 1823, leaving a will that gave her everything for life, with power to provide “for any of our children for whom she may think necessary to provide.” Three weeks later she gave bond as executrix, with Abraham and Henry Markle as her securities, and the inventory of the whole estate came to a little over six hundred dollars. It was insolvent. Her co-executor Nathaniel Huntington was out of the sheriff's reach by 1829 and dead by 1831.

What followed is the hardest stretch of any life on this chart. The probate court cited her in January 1829, again in November 1829, and summoned her again on 2 November 1830 to show cause “why she has not made a final settlement of the estate of Gursham Tuttle deceased, of which she is the executrix.” In March 1831 she petitioned to be let out of it, through a solicitor, in words that are still painful to read: the estate's business was “long since closed,” but “the papers of said Estate were left in the possession of Nathaniel Huntington Esq. who is dead, and they are now in so confused and mutilated a situation that no accurate statement of the condition of the Estate could be made from them.” On 29 December 1831 the court issued a writ of attachment for her body for contempt. The sheriff executed it on 2 February 1832 and charged eighty-three and a half cents in fees. Bail was set at ten dollars.

She outlived her husband by twenty-eight years and followed one of her children ninety miles south into the hills of Brown County. She died on 22 April 1851, and her stone at Southview Cemetery, Nashville, reads: In Memory of PAMELIA TUTTLE DIED April 22 1851 Aged 80 Y's, 5 M's, 18 D's. Count the age back and it lands, to the day, on 4 November 1770 — her own stone confirming the birthday the family book recorded.

According to the Tuttle family genealogy of 1883, her brother was an officer of the United States Army who died while in charge of the federal arsenal at Troy, New York.

240.x:
Full dates: 22 Nov 1785 – 21 Jan 1861, Meigs Co., Ohio

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ NEW NODE, 7 August 2026 [ROUSH-54]. This is the rung that opens two Revolutionary patriots.

Son of George Roush and Catharine Zerkel. Married 18 May 1808 — “Francis Watkins, Justice of the Peace, pronounced the words that made them one” — his own cousin Regina Roush. A baptismal register printed in the 1928 genealogy records “John, Nov. 22, 1785. Bap. Wit. John Roush, wife Susannah, Jan. 5, 1786.”

He and Regina settled in the Nease Settlement, Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio — ⭐ the same few square miles where their great-great-grandson John G. Roush was born in 1877, and where the Roush and Nease families that later intermarried were founding neighbours. They lie in a family plot beside Regina’s father Jonas, with no stone marking their graves.

The move is dated by their children. Benjamin was born at Graham Station, Mason County, Virginia in August 1816; his sister Hannah was born in the Nease Settlement in May 1820. So John and Regina crossed from Virginia into Ohio between those two dates — which is exactly why Benjamin’s birthplace is Virginian and his siblings’ are not.

⚠⚠ GRADED PROBABLE ON PURPOSE. Everything above this couple is DAR-verified; everything below Benjamin is ours from records. The one link still resting on a single source is Benjamin as their son — the 1928 genealogy, p. 464: “5. BENJAMIN ROUSH, fifth child of John and Regina Roush, was born August 30, 1816.”

Outstanding — and this is the single most valuable document left on the Roush line: the Meigs County, Ohio probate death record for Benjamin Roush, 1897, or John Roush’s 1861 Meigs County estate file naming son Benjamin. Either one converts this node to Documented and the whole patriot descent with it. ⛔ Benjamin is not in the West Virginia death index — searched Mason Co. 1897 and Benjamin Roush statewide, all years. He died in Ohio.

⭐ 27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep. JOHN AND REGINA ROUSH'S GRAVES ARE MARKED, AND THE CEMETERY HAS A NAME. The 1928 book says 'There is no stone marking their graves'; a modern granite marker now stands over them at GILMORE CEMETERY, MINERSVILLE, MEIGS COUNTY, OHIO - which is therefore the 'Nease Settlement' burial ground the book describes. Jonas Roush (d. 14 Dec 1850), whose grave the book says John and Regina's lie beside, is placed by Find a Grave in the same cemetery. [ROUSH-91] A PERIOD RECORD OF THE 1808 MARRIAGE EXISTS AND HAS BEEN PHOTOGRAPHED. [ROUSH-54]/[ROUSH-55] carry the 18 May 1808 marriage of John and Regina from the 1928 book alone. A photograph of the original register page is posted to John's Find a Grave memorial: a manuscript volume whose leaf carries the pencilled archival note 'Marriage Rec. / No 1 / 1806-1850' and whose first spread lists the marriages in order, Francis Watkins officiating at most of them. [ROUSH-92]
240.s:
John Roush was born on 22 November 1785 in Shenandoah County, Virginia, a son of George Roush and Catharine Zerkel, and was baptised into the Lutheran faith on 5 January 1786, with another John Roush and his wife Susannah standing as witnesses.

On 18 May 1808 he married his own cousin, Regina Roush, the daughter of Jonas Roush. The county's oldest marriage book records it on its first page, in the family's older spelling: “John Rausch to Regenna Rausch, May 18, 1808,” by Francis Watkins, Justice of the Peace. Eleven children followed, and the New Haven Lutheran church register is said to have carried the birth and baptism of every one of them.

Benjamin, the fifth, was born at Graham Station on the Virginia side in August 1816; Hannah was born in the Nease Settlement, in Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio, in May 1820. Between those two births John and Regina crossed the river for good, into the few square miles where the Roush and Nease families who later intermarried were founding neighbours - the same ground where their great-great-grandson John G. Roush would be born more than fifty years on. He was known in the family as “Blackbird John.”

He could not write. Every deed he made he signed “John his + mark Roush.” In the twenty months between July 1848 and March 1850 he settled land on four Roush men - Abel, James, John Junior and Benjamin. On 9 August 1849 he cut the east strip of Section 25, Town 3, Range 12 in two on a single day before a single justice and two witnesses: seventy acres running north from the south-east corner to John Roush Junior, and sixty-nine acres and twenty poles running south from the north-east corner to Benjamin, each for five hundred dollars. Not one of those deeds says father, or son, or heir. No wife joined in any of them to release her dower, and there was no Regina in his house when the census taker came in 1850.

He was sixty-six then, living four doors from Benjamin in Sutton Township. He died on 21 January 1861. Regina's father Jonas had spent his last years in her home and lies in the same ground. For most of a century John and Regina's graves were unmarked - the 1928 family history says the two graves just north of Jonas's were pointed out to the compilers by people who knew, “altho we have had them definitely pointed out to us.” Today a granite stone at Gilmore Cemetery in Minersville carries the name ROUSH, and underneath, JOHN 1785 - 1861 and REGINA 1788 - 18. Whoever ordered it still could not supply her death year, and the cutter left the last two figures off.

Full dates: 30 Nov 1788 – death not established

⭐⭐⭐⭐ NEW NODE, 7 August 2026 [ROUSH-54]. Daughter of the patriot Jonas Roush and Barbara Fox; married her cousin John Roush on 18 May 1808. A Roush married a Roush — both of them grandchildren of the same Shenandoah Valley family, which is a pedigree collapse waiting to be drawn once the generation above is proved.

⭐⭐ The DAR has approved this exact person twice — on Jonas Roush’s ancestor record the approved lineages include “child REGINA — spouse JOHN ROUSH” (National Nos. 569934 and 1076887).

⭐ Her father spent his last years in her house. The 1928 genealogy says Jonas Roush “spent his last years in her home in the Nease Settlement” — and Jonas’s own Revolutionary pension file, independently, records that he removed to Meigs County, Ohio to live with a daughter. Two sources that never met, agreeing.

⭐ 27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep. Regina has a grave marker, and it leaves her death year uncut. Find a Grave memorial 72226047 places her at Gilmore Cemetery, Minersville, Meigs County, Ohio, sharing the modern ROUSH stone with John; the inscription reads 'REGINA 1788 — 18' and stops. [ROUSH-93]
241.s:
Regina Roush was born on 30 November 1788, the second child of Jonas Roush - a private of the Virginia line who was at the siege of Yorktown and saw Cornwallis surrender - and his wife Barbara Fox.

On 18 May 1808, at nineteen, she married her cousin John Roush before Francis Watkins, a justice of the peace, who entered the couple on the first page of the county's oldest marriage book as “John Rausch to Regenna Rausch.” A Roush had married a Roush: both of them grandchildren of the same Shenandoah Valley family. Eleven children were born to them. Benjamin, the fifth, arrived at Graham Station in August 1816; Hannah, in May 1820, was born after the move across the Ohio into the Nease Settlement.

Her father came to live with her. The 1928 family history says Jonas “spent his last years in her home in the Nease Settlement near where he lies buried,” and his own Revolutionary pension file, written down from his sworn statement and quite independent of the book, records that he removed to Meigs County, Ohio in June 1837 to live with a daughter. He died there on 14 December 1850. The Daughters of the American Revolution have twice approved lineages that run through “child REGINA - spouse JOHN ROUSH.”

When she died is not known and was not known in 1928, when the compilers of the family book wrote plainly that it “has not been ascertained.” There are indications. She was not in her husband's household in 1850, and in none of the five deeds he made in 1848-50 did a wife join to release her dower, which Ohio law of the day would normally have required of a married man - so she had very probably died before the summer of 1848.

She lies at Gilmore Cemetery in Minersville, beside her husband and near her father. The granite over the two of them reads JOHN 1785 - 1861 and REGINA 1788 - 18, and there the inscription stops.

242.s:
David Altman was born about 1788 in Pennsylvania and farmed in Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio - the Roushes' own township, and the Duckworths' county. He was already there in 1840, when the census taker wrote the name down as “Attman.”

In 1850 he was sixty-two, with a thousand dollars of land, keeping house with Margaret, fifty-six, also Pennsylvania-born, and four Ohio-born children: Jacob, twenty-three, and Solomon, nineteen, both farming with him, Mary, fourteen, and Samuel, twelve. A John Altman, about thirty-one and born in Ohio, headed a second Altman household in the same township with a wife and four sons.

244.s:
George Duckworth was a hatter in the Bury district of Lancashire. He is known from one line of one page: on 21 January 1839, when his son James married Ann Collins at the parish church of St Mary, Bury, the curate entered the groom's father as “George Duckworth” and his rank or profession, in the column kept for it, as “Hatter.”

Hatting was Bury's trade beside cotton and coal, and it was a skilled one; his son went down the pit instead, was entered in the same register as a collier, and signed the book with a mark. A Richard Duckworth stood as witness that day and signed with a mark too - very likely George's brother or his other son. Whether George lived to see his son and daughter-in-law take their children across the Atlantic about 1850 is not known. Nothing else of his life has been traced.

246.s:
Adam Collins lived at Freetown, in Bury, Lancashire. His daughter Ann was under twenty-one when she married James Duckworth, a collier, at St Mary's church on 21 January 1839, and because she was a minor her father's consent was required - which is the only reason his name is in the register at all. His own occupation was written in the last column of the page; the word is too far gone to read with confidence, and it has been left blank rather than guessed at.

Eight years later and an ocean away from Bury, his daughter and her husband named a son Adam. He was born on 14 March 1847 - the only Adam among the Duckworths, and still an Adam Duckworth when he died a miner in Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio, in 1919.

321.s:
Mary Thorn died in Greene County, Alabama, shortly before 23 January 1844. She was the widow of James Thorn, who had made his will on 12 June 1837 and whose estate was proved there in October 1839; his will names his own children but no wife at all, which is one reason she is probably his second wife and not the mother of his family.

Her own next of kin were Stephenses. The court that opened her estate on 23 January 1844 cited Moore, James, Lewis and William Stephens, Esther Hitt, Lucinda Ball and Elizabeth Bevers as her nearest relations; James Stephens was appointed administrator; and when the estate was finally divided on 12 October 1846 it went in ten equal shares to that same set of brothers and married sisters, with the share of Esther Hitt — by then dead — going to her “Representatives,” which is how a court treats a predeceased child. The most economical explanation is that Stephens was her first married name and Thorn her second, making those ten her children. No document has ever used the word, so this is a strong reconstruction and not a settled fact; she may equally have been their sister or aunt.

Her inventory, taken on 27 April 1844, catalogues her entire world down to an eighteen-cent umbrella and a woman’s saddle — and then one line worth more than all the rest together: “1 Negro woman Jane — 475.00.” Jane had been hired out for seventeen months and was sold at the estate sale on 29 April 1844 to the administrator, James Stephens, for $700. The whole sale raised $1,075.86, so Jane was sixty-five per cent of everything Mary Thorn owned, and roughly $70 of Moore Stephens’s $107 share was her price. The clerk summarised the packet on its outside wrapper in two lines, and the first line is her name.

Mary had also been lending money to the men around her: her papers include promissory notes on Charles Stephens for $15.13 and $32.40 and on Lewis Stephens for $100. Her land was sold at the ordinary sale to Andrew Norwood for $127.09.

384.s:
Gershom Tuttle was born on 22 August 1738 at Farmington, Connecticut — in the parish of New Cambridge, which later became the town of Bristol. His father was Ensign Gershom Tuttle and his mother was Lois Allis.

On 22 December 1757, at Deerfield in Massachusetts, he married Tabitha Mitchell. The Deerfield clerk styled him “of New Cambridge” and gave the bride no parish, which is what a clerk does for a local bride — and she was local in more than one sense: her mother Mary Allis and his mother Lois Allis were sisters. He married his own first cousin.

His father died in 1777, leaving a will made that May which gave the widow Lois a third for life and divided the rest among “my Three Sons Gershom, Oliver and Samuel Tuttle,” and appointed “my Son Gershom Tuttle whole and sole Executor.” The executor's account of “Gershom Tuttel Executor” was allowed in January 1779.

He is a patriot of the Revolution, and the service is logistics rather than battle — which in Connecticut in 1780 mattered as much. He was a conductor of teams, which meant he ran wagon trains of provisions out of Connecticut into New York State: some three thousand barrels, about five hundred tons, averaging a hundred and fifteen miles a haul. On 23 May 1780 the Connecticut General Assembly paid him £285.13.8 in wages and £60.13.11 for forage in advance, and still owed him £200.2.8. He is listed first of the nine conductors. The Daughters of the American Revolution recognise him as ancestor A131791, rank teamster, “Conductor of teams transporting supplies for the army.”

After the war he moved north. At Claremont, New Hampshire — where his father had died — he signed a town recommendation of Ambrose Cossitt as justice of the peace on 17 December 1789, with his brother Oliver and his son Solomon, and in 1790 he headed the only Gershom Tuttle household in the census of the whole country. About 1790 he went on to Clinton in Oneida County, New York, and afterwards joined the settlement at Watertown in Jefferson County. He was alive to see his son become a colonel of militia there.

He died on 5 January 1818, in his eightieth year. Where, and where he lies, is not documented by any record; the family genealogy gives no place and the DAR's “Watertown” carries no source. No Gershom Tuttle appears in Jefferson County in the 1820 census, four county histories record no death, and neither Rutland's nor Watertown's cemetery transcriptions hold him.

The Tuttle family genealogy of 1883 makes him the first deacon of Watertown’s first church, organised in 1803. The church’s own historian, who read its minutes, dates the Tuttle deaconship to 1808 and gives it to his son the colonel, so the honour may belong to the son.

385.s:
Tabitha Mitchell was born on 9 February 1736/7, the daughter of Joseph Mitchell and Mary Allis. The family was at Sunderland, in the Connecticut valley of Massachusetts, where her brother Joseph had been born in 1726/7, and afterwards at Deerfield.

On 22 December 1757, at Deerfield, she married Gershom Tuttle of New Cambridge in Connecticut — and the match was not the mystery it looked like for years. Her mother Mary Allis and the groom's mother Lois Allis were sisters: Lois had married the elder Gershom Tuttle in 1737, and twenty years later Lois's son married Mary's daughter. Tabitha and her husband were first cousins, and the Deerfield venue needs no explaining — the bride was at home.

She went with him through Connecticut, the Revolution, New Hampshire and on into New York. Her father's will, made on 14 April 1792 and proved in November 1794, gives “to my Daughter Tabitha Wife of Gersham Tuttle Twelve Pounds,” beside her sisters Mary Belding and Hannah Bigelow and the children of “my late Son Joseph.” That one clause does three things: it documents her parentage from a record, it documents her marriage, and it shows her alive in the spring of 1792 — which refutes the unsourced “1737–1782” that followed her around.

On the Daughters of the American Revolution's own file for her husband she is recorded as “X Mitchel” — surname and nothing else. This family knows her first name, her birthday, her parents and her grandfather, all from records, and the national society that honours her husband does not.

386.s:
Pamelia Clark's father was a Farmington, Connecticut, man of the Revolutionary generation. His daughter was born there on 4 November 1770 — a date her own gravestone in Indiana confirms eighty years later, to the day, through its age line — and she married Gershom Tuttle at Farmington on 8 July 1788. His name has not been recovered.

He is visible only through his children. One of his sons was an officer of the United States Army who died while in charge of the arsenal at Troy, New York; a grandson was General Newman S. Clarke, born in Connecticut, commissioned an ensign in 1812, brevetted brigadier-general in 1847, and commanding the Department of the Pacific when he died at San Francisco in 1860. The official register of army officers confirms the family's account of the general in every checkable particular.

His daughter carried “Strong” as a middle name, and it descended through four more generations — Clark Strong Tuttle, Dennis Clark, Richard Clark. Whether it came from her mother's family or from somewhere else is not established; the standard genealogy of the Strong family of New England contains no Pamelia Clark born in 1770 and no Clark of Farmington, so the Strong descent this chart once quietly assumed is unsupported.

480.s:
George Roush was born in July 1761 in Frederick County, Virginia — the part of it that became Shenandoah County eleven years later — one of the younger sons of the German immigrant John Adam Roush and his wife Susannah. He grew up on Mill Creek in a house where the Bible was printed in German, and he was eighteen when the Revolution reached him.

He enlisted in the autumn of 1779 and served two months under his own brother, Captain John Roush, “both of Shenandoah County Virginia.” He was drafted again in the spring of 1780 under Captain Joseph Pugh, and a third time in 1781 for three months — that tour, his brother Jonas later swore, as a substitute for another brother, Jacob. Family tradition, collected while his grandchildren were still alive, held that he was at Yorktown and saw Cornwallis hand over his sword; his brother Jonas certainly was. He applied for his pension in 1832 from Ohio and it was allowed as claim S18579. The Daughters of the American Revolution recognise him as Patriot Ancestor A098975.

About 1781, in Shenandoah County, he married Catharine Zerkel, the eldest daughter of Michael and Catharine Zerckel of Forestville. Their children, born over more than twenty years, included Michael, Magdalena, John — who in 1808 married his cousin Regina, Jonas Roush’s daughter — Daniel, Lewis, Catherine, Samuel, Susannah, Jacob, Mary and a second Jonas.

He went down the Ohio ahead of his family about 1798, taking up land in Mason County with his brother Captain John, in whose name the purchase was made; his son Jacob was still born and baptised back in Shenandoah County in 1799. In 1807 he crossed to Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio, buying a level tract from Edward W. Tupper west of the hamlet of Dorcas, near Racine, and he lived on it for the rest of his life. He was a mechanic by trade — a good one, the family said — and a farmer, and when Meigs County organised itself in 1819 his name is among its first jurors. He had been a citizen of three counties at the moment each was created.

Catharine died in Virginia, after a journey home she had pined for; her burial place was never found. On 13 August 1815 George married a widow, Catherine “Kitty” Wolfe, at Gallipolis, and they had one daughter, Hannah. In his last illness, the family remembered, he talked about charging the British and told his comrades to get ready, they were coming over the hill.

Gwathmey's Historical Register of Virginians in the Revolution lists him at page 679 as 'Rousk, George, 73, Meigs Co., O., mpl.' — the age and the county put the entry on our man, applying from Ohio in his seventies.

The portrait of him printed in the family's 1928 history is not the original likeness. The book explains that a schoolmaster boarding in the Roush house — the compiler believed he was one of the Henkels, the Lutheran printing family of New Market — asked one Sunday morning to sketch him, told him to put on the coat of his uniform, and after "considerable reluctance" was allowed to make a small sketch from life. That sketch was still in the family at Racine, Ohio in 1928 and had been shown at Meigs County pioneer meetings; the plate in the book was drawn again from it, "with great difficulty." The 1928 compilers only recovered the sketch through his descendants at Racine: it had been kept by Elizabeth Wilcoxin, then by James L. Wilcoxin, and it was Mrs. Anna Eliza (Salser) Hoops who helped get it back in time for the book.

He died on 31 May 1845 and lies in Weldon Cemetery on the third terrace above the Ohio at Racine, Meigs County. His small marble stone is still legible: “GEORGE ROUSH … DIED May 31, 1845 AGED 84 years.” On 19 August 1933, before about a thousand descendants, the Sons of the American Revolution dedicated a grave marker there; a flat marker lettered “GEORGE ROUSH / CONTINENTAL LINE / REVOLUTIONARY WAR / JUL 1761 – MAY 1845” lies at the foot of the headstone today. His German Bible, said to have come from his father out of Germany, was still in the family in 1928, in the hands of a great-granddaughter at Racine; and of the nine brothers who went to that war he is the only one whose face is known.

481.s:
Catharine Zerkel was George Roush’s first wife and the mother of his children. Two sources that did not consult each other — the family’s own 1928 history and the Daughters of the American Revolution’s record for her husband — agree on her name, and the DAR’s approved applications through their son John are all marked to her rather than to George’s second wife.

The family history makes her the eldest child of Michael and Catharine Zerckel of Forestville in Shenandoah County, born 14 August 1763, with Henry Brock and his wife Magdalene standing as her baptismal sponsors. She married George in Shenandoah County about 1781, and by October 1780 — if the reconstruction of her age holds — she was already a married woman sponsoring a baptism herself. Her first child was born in January 1783. Over the next twenty years there were a dozen more, among them John, born 22 November 1785, who married his cousin Regina Roush.

She went west with her husband — to Mason County about 1798, then across the Ohio into Meigs County in 1807 — and the one story the family kept about her is a homesick one. In declining health she pined for the Virginia home, and at last George set out with her, more than three hundred miles over the mountains on horseback and on foot. They came up the Shenandoah and stood the horses in the door yard of the old plantation. “The joy was too great, she was overwhelmed and wept as a child.” She did not live long after, and was buried in Virginia; where, nobody has recorded. A later Zirkle family historian guessed the old Nease–Zirkle graveyard on Holman’s Creek, where her father and mother lie, but he was guessing. Her husband married again in 1815, so she was dead by then; the year itself has never been documented.

482.s:
Jonas Roush was born in September 1763 at Holman’s Fort in Frederick County, Virginia — soon Shenandoah County — the youngest of the sons of John Adam and Susannah Roush. He was seventeen when his turn came in the Revolution, and the account of it is his own, sworn before a court in Mason County, Virginia on 6 November 1832.

He “entered the service as a substitute for his Brother Henry Roush who was drafted for a tour of three months in the summer of 1781,” served under Captain All in Colonel Bird’s regiment at Falmouth near Fredericksburg, and went out again on a second three-month tour. That second tour took him to the siege of Yorktown, and he was there on 19 October 1781 when Cornwallis’s army surrendered. He fell ill near Fredericksburg while escorting prisoners. The pension was allowed at twenty dollars a year from 4 March 1831 as claim S4785; the Daughters of the American Revolution list him as Patriot Ancestor A098985. His brother Henry’s own Revolutionary record is certified out of the same sheaf of paper.

He married Barbara Fox, of a Shenandoah County family settled near Forestville. Their daughter Regina, born 30 November 1788, married her cousin John Roush in 1808 — the marriage that doubles back through Alec’s tree, so that Jonas and his brother George both stand as ancestors. Other children were Abraham, John, Adam and Philip.

Like his brothers he came down the Ohio. He was living in Mason County, Virginia when he applied for his pension in 1832, and that same year he was named executor of his brother Daniel’s will, which left the residue of the estate “equally divided among the children of my brothers Jonas, George, Henry, Philip and Jacob.” His wife died in the 1830s, and the pension was transferred to Meigs County, Ohio in 1837; the family history says he spent his last years in his daughter Regina’s house in the Nease Settlement, in Sutton Township.

Gwathmey's Historical Register of Virginians in the Revolution lists him at page 679 as 'Rouch, Jonas, Mason Co., 71, mpl.' — Mason County, aged 71, which fits a birth about 1763.

He died on 14 December 1850, aged eighty-seven, and lies in Gilmore Cemetery at Minersville, Meigs County, Ohio — the burying ground of that settlement, which the 1928 historians could only describe as “a family lot.” John and Regina were laid beside him in graves that were never marked. His own stone is still there, worn but standing, and two later Revolutionary War markers have been set by it: an upright government headstone, “JONAS ROUSH / PVT / VA TROOPS / REV WAR / 1763 1850,” and a flat bronze, “JONAS ROUSH / PVT VA REGIMENT / REVOLUTIONARY WAR.”

⭐⭐⭐ NEW NODE, 7 August 2026 [ROUSH-54]. Named as Jonas Roush’s wife by the 1928 Roush genealogy and, independently, by the DAR ancestor record A098985, which lists spouse “BARBARA FOX.”

⭐ Her death is dated by her husband’s pension file, which records that his wife died in February 1837 — the same year he moved to Ohio to live with his daughter. ⚠ The file does not name her; the name comes from the book and the DAR.

⛔ 11 Sep 2026 — DEMOTED documented → probable [BELL-714], adversary-confirmed. Named as Jonas’s wife by the 1928 book and a DAR spouse field; the pension records only that “his wife died in February 1837” without naming her. Outstanding: — Shenandoah County, Virginia, probably in the 1780s. ⚠ The Gilmore stone gives no maiden name and Gilmore holds at least THREE Jonas Roushes (Ohio Gravestone Photo Project index); the attribution rests on a generational argument, not on uniqueness. Confirm by a full reading of the Gilmore Roush lot — which Jonas lies beside which Barbara [ROUSH-107, self-correction #528]. ⚠ The Oct-1836-versus-Feb-1837 conflict between the stone and pension S4785 needs the pension read as IMAGES rather than as an abstract [ROUSH-107].

Also recorded: d. 21 Oct 1836 aged 70 (gravestone, Gilmore Cemetery) — against Feb 1837 (pension S4785); b. about 1766 by the stone’s age.

⭐⭐⭐ 27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep [ROUSH-107]. A STONE THAT NAMES A BARBARA AS JONAS ROUSH’S WIFE. Gilmore Cemetery, Minersville, Meigs Co., Ohio, Find a Grave memorial 59597827, photograph by Paul Rompel 19 Jul 2011, read at the image and legible: “BARBARA / WIFE OF / JONAS ROUSH / DIED / OCT 21 1836 / AGED / 70 YEARS”. Until now this node rested entirely on the 1928 book and a DAR spouse field over a pension file that records only an unnamed wife.

⚠ THE IDENTIFICATION, STATED PROPERLY — and a bad argument withdrawn (self-correction #528). This sweep first wrote “there is one Jonas Roush in this cemetery and he is ours.” That is false: the Ohio Gravestone Photo Project index for Gilmore Cemetery lists JONAS ROUSH THREE TIMES, besides Adam, John and Regina. ⭐ The argument that does work is generational: the stone gives no maiden name — Barbara, not Barbara Fox — but a wife dead in 1836 aged 70 was born about 1766, which is the patriot Jonas’s own generation and no other Jonas’s in that ground: the younger Jonas Roushes of this family were born in the 1800s and had no seventy-year-old wives in 1836. Very probably hers; not certainly.

⚠⚠ BOTH DEATH DATES ARE CARRIED, neither adopted: the stone says 21 October 1836; pension S4785 says “his wife died in February 1837”. Four months apart, and the stone puts her in Ohio where the node’s reading of the pension implies Virginia. Unresolved; a live conflict inside the identification chain, so no grade and no card move.

⭐ [ROUSH-108] A named candidate for her father (node 966), family-posted and unsourced on the same memorial: “Barbara was the daughter of Adam Fuchs …” — dates garbled, county wrong, lead only.
483.s:
Barbara Fox married Jonas Roush, probably in Shenandoah County, Virginia in the 1780s. Her people were a Fox family settled near Forestville; the compiler of the 1928 Roush history admitted he knew nothing more of them than that the first federal census showed them to be a prominent family in the neighbourhood.

She is named as Jonas’s wife both by that family history and, independently, by the Daughters of the American Revolution’s record for him. Her daughter Regina, born 30 November 1788, married her cousin John Roush in 1808 and is Alec’s ancestor twice over. There were other children — Abraham, John, Adam, Philip — and the family moved down the Ohio with the rest of the Roush connection into Mason County.

Her husband’s pension file records only that his wife died in February 1837, without naming her; it was that year he gave up his own household and went to live with Regina across the river in Ohio. A stone in Gilmore Cemetery at Minersville, Meigs County, reads “Barbara, wife of Jonas Roush, died Oct. 21, 1836, aged 70 years.” It is very probably hers, though the stone gives no maiden name — Barbara, not Barbara Fox — and there is more than one Jonas Roush buried in that cemetery. What places this one in her generation is the arithmetic: a wife dead in 1836 at seventy was born about 1766, which is the patriot Jonas’s own generation and nobody else’s; the younger Jonases of the family were not yet born in 1766 and their wives were not seventy in 1836. The stone and the pension are four months apart — 21 October 1836 against February 1837 — and nobody has reconciled them. Either way she was dead before her husband crossed the river, and she lies in the same ground he would be buried in fourteen years later.

768.x:
Full dates: b. 11 Aug 1714 Wallingford – Chippens Hill, New Cambridge – d. 13 Aug 1777, Claremont, N.H.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE RANK CONFLICT IS RESOLVED, AND HIS EXACT NEIGHBOURHOOD IS NAMED — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-39]. Miscellaneous Notes on New England Families, continuing: “On his return from the north, Gershom Tuttle joined THE COLONY OF PEOPLE FROM CHESHIRE AND VICINITY who removed to the town of Farmington and settled on CHIPPEN’S HILL, in what was called New Cambridge and is now the town of Bristol. There he had his home and was prominent in church and town affairs. HE SERVED IN THE FRENCH AND INDIAN WARS AND IS CALLED ENSIGN GERSHOM TUTTLE.” ⭐⭐ THAT SETTLES THE CONFLICT LOGGED IN TUTTLE-33. The gravestone calls him ENSIGN; the 1883 book calls him “Capt. of the train-band”. The Ensign’s commission came from the FRENCH AND INDIAN WARS, not the local militia — so the stone is recording war service, and the two titles are two different things. ⭐ NEW RESEARCH TARGET: the Connecticut French and Indian War rolls, c.1755–1762. ⭐⭐⭐ AND IT EXPLAINS THE 1742 PETITION GROUP. He did not drift to Farmington — he went with a COLONY of Cheshire people, which is why Simon Tuttle and the other names on that petition [TUTTLE-20/23] are the same names as the Cheshire records. They moved as a body, and Chippen’s Hill is where they landed. ⚠⚠⚠ AND A LEAD FLAGGED, NOT WRITTEN AS A FINDING. The manuscript continues: “As is well known there was much dissention there in New Cambridge before and during the Revolutionary War. CHIPPENS HILL WAS A CENTER OF EPISCOPALIAN AND ‘TORY’ FEELING. Many of the families…” — and the transcript breaks off there. ⚠ DO NOT DRAW THE OBVIOUS CONCLUSION. Two facts already on this chart point in opposite directions: his son Gershom II is a DOCUMENTED PATRIOT (DAR A131791, paid by the Connecticut Assembly in 1780), and a Simon Tuttle was one of ten men who in 1747 “publikly declared themselves of the Church of England” at New Cambridge [TUTTLE-20]. Read the next page of the manuscript before a word of this goes in as fact. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ “CARLETON” IS SOLVED, AND IT IS ARLINGTON — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-38]. Miscellaneous Notes on New England Families (FS film #007549089, ark 3:1:3QS7-89DX-THK7) — a manuscript that had already solved this problem and cites its sources: “Gershom Tuttle was the son of Timothy Tuttle and his wife THANKFUL DOOLITTLE, and was born in Wallingford, Aug. 11, 1714 (Wallingford Vitals, vol. 2, p. 799). … As a young man Gershom Tuttle removed from Wallingford to northern Massachusetts, where he took up THE LAND WHICH HIS FATHER TIMOTHY TUTTLE HAD OBTAINED IN THE NEW TOWN OF ARLINGTON, JUST ABOVE NORTHFIELD (which later became WINCHESTER, NEW HAMPSHIRE). During the time he was up there he evidently stayed some time in NORTHFIELD (where HIS UNCLE THE REV. BENJAMIN DOOLITTLE was the Pastor of the church) and Sunderland, somewhat farther south. There, in Sunderland, Mass., Gershom Tuttle married, Oct. 17, 1737, LOIS ALLIS (from Sunderland Town records, as given in the History of Sunderland). She was the daughter of WILLIAM ALLIS of Sunderland…” ⭐ The clerk’s hand read “Carleton” and “Earlenton” — it is ARLINGTON, and the flag on that one word was worth keeping. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THE MOVE WAS KINSHIP, NOT SPECULATION. His father held the proprietor’s right; his MOTHER’S BROTHER was the minister twenty miles down the road at Northfield; he lodged with his uncle and married a girl from Sunderland. That also confirms THANKFUL DOOLITTLE as his mother from a third independent direction — this compiler calls Rev. Benjamin Doolittle his UNCLE. ⭐⭐⭐ AND IT MAKES HIS LIFE A SHAPE: Arlington became WINCHESTER, NEW HAMPSHIRE — so the frontier township he settled at twenty-two was in what is now New Hampshire, and he died in New Hampshire, at Claremont, forty-one years later. He went north twice, and the second time he stayed. ⭐ AND WE NOW HAVE THE CITATION FOR HIS BIRTH ENTRY: WALLINGFORD VITALS, VOL. 2, PAGE 799. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE DEED READ AT THE PAGE — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-37]. FamilySearch ark 3:1:3QS7-89ZD-JW67, image 445 of 849, Hampden/Springfield, Massachusetts Land Records 1735–1737: “Know all Men by these presents that I TIMOTHY TUTTLE of Wallingford in the County of New Haven and Colony of Connecticutt in New England, for divers good causes and considerations and perticularly for LOVE, GOOD WILL AND FATHERLY AFFECTION that I have and [bear] to MY SON GERSHOM TUTTLE of Carleton in the County of Hampshire and province of the Massachusetts Bay in New England, have therefore given, granted and firmly pass over … unto him my said son Gershom Tuttle and to his heirs and assigns forever ALL MY RIGHT OF LAND IN SAID [CARLETON], as well that which is already laid out and all other Divisions that shall be hereafter in said TOWNSHIP on my said RIGHT to be laid out and surveyed … I am the True, Sole and Lawfull owner of the above given and Granted premises … to Warrant, Secure and Defend him the said Gersham Tuttle…” ‘Fatherly affection’ is the standard phrase of a New England gift deed, and it is the plainest statement of parentage the period produces. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND IT REWRITES THE ORDER OF EVENTS. He is already “of … the County of HAMPSHIRE, Massachusetts” in 1736 — a year and more BEFORE he married Lois Allis at Sunderland in October 1737. He did not go north because of the deed; he was already there, and his father signed his own share over to him. Sunderland, Hatfield and Montague — the whole Allis country — are in that same county. So the marriage is not a mystery any more: he was a young man on the Massachusetts frontier who married a local girl. ⚠⚠ WHAT “CARLETON” IS, IS STILL OPEN — and the deed itself narrows it hard. It is a TOWNSHIP in which Timothy held a PROPRIETOR’S RIGHT, with later divisions still to be laid out — that is the signature of one of the NEW MASSACHUSETTS TOWNSHIPS granted in 1735, not an old settled town. The transcript renders the name twice and differently (“Carleton”, “Earlenton”), so the clerk’s hand is ambiguous. Identify it against the 1735 Hampshire County township grants and the proprietors’ records — that will say exactly where he was living at 22. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE LAST UNDOCUMENTED LINK IN THE TUTTLE LINE IS CLOSED — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-36]. A DEED OF GIFT OF 1736 IN WHICH TIMOTHY TUTTLE CALLS GERSHOM HIS SON, TWICE. FamilySearch full-text, Springfield, Hampden, Massachusetts. Land Records 1734-1735, 1735-1737, 1736-1744, YEARS: 1736, nine matched passages — “…presents that I TIMOTHY TUTTLE OF WALLINGFORD in …” · “…and are to my SON GERSHOM TUTTLE of Carleton in …” · “…unto him my said son Gershom Tuttle and to his …” · “…to him the said Gershom [Tuttle] his heirs &c…” · “…to and with the said Gershom Tuttle his heirs and…” · “…I the said Timothy Tuttle do bind my self and …” · “…whereof I the said Timothy Tuttle have hereunto …” · “…date above written Timothy Tuttle the above …” The same instrument appears again in Hampden, Massachusetts. Cemetery Land Deeds 1733-1737 — “…and Bare to my son Gershom Tuttle of…” ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND IT EXPLAINS THE MARRIAGE THAT HAS PUZZLED THIS FILE FOR DAYS. Why would a Cheshire, Connecticut man marry LOIS ALLIS at SUNDERLAND, MASSACHUSETTS in October 1737? Because in 1736 his father deeded him land in the Massachusetts Connecticut Valley. (Springfield’s registry served the whole valley — Hampden was part of HAMPSHIRE County until 1812, so these ARE the Hampshire records.) Father gives land 1736 → son marries a valley girl 1737 → son is buying in Farmington by 1739-40. The sequence finally reads. ⚠ TWO THINGS STILL TO DO ON IT: ① open the deed IMAGE — everything above is FamilySearch’s OCR of the deed book, which is the record’s own words but not yet read at the page; ② “Gershom Tuttle of CARLETON” is unexplained — no Massachusetts or Connecticut town of that name fits 1736. Probably an OCR misreading of the son’s residence. Flagged, not smoothed over. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ SPOFFORD’S TRANSCRIPTION READ AT SOURCE, 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-35] — Grave Stone Records from the Ancient Cemeteries in the Town of Claremont, N.H. (1896), image 78: “Tuttle Gershom, Esq.  Aug. 13, 1777, 63y.” ⚠⚠ SELF-CORRECTION #16: TUTTLE-33 transcribed the photograph as “in ye 63d Year of his Age”. Spofford, standing at the stone in 1896, reads it as an AGE — 63 years — and the arithmetic agrees: b. 11 Aug 1714, d. 13 Aug 1777 is 63 years and two days. Spofford’s reading is the one to carry; mine was made from a photograph at an angle. The day I hedged as ‘5th or 15th’ is the 13th. ⛔⛔ AND A BOUNDED NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS. Spofford transcribed EVERY ancient cemetery in the town, and there are only THREE Tuttles in the whole book: “Tuttle Gershom, Esq. Aug. 13, 1777, 63y. · Tuttle Hannah, wife of Oliver. Sept. 12, 1785, 42y. · Tuttle Daniel, son of Oliver and Hannah. March 2, 1777, 4y.” NO WIFE OF GERSHOM I IS BURIED AT CLAREMONT. Lois Allis is not beside him, and she is not in that town at all. So she died before the family left Connecticut, or she is buried somewhere else entirely — see node 769. ⭐⭐⭐ WHAT IS THERE INSTEAD IS A HARDER STORY. The other two Tuttles are his son OLIVER’S wife and OLIVER’S small son: Daniel, aged four, buried 2 March 1777 — and Gershom I himself five months later, 13 August 1777. This family buried a grandson in the spring and the grandfather in the summer of the same year. And Hannah, Oliver’s wife, died 12 September 1785 aged 42 — which is very likely why Oliver left: the 1883 book has him going from Claremont to New York “about 1790”, five years after burying her. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE GRAVE IS FOUND, AND IT IS NOT WHERE THE BOOK SAID — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-34]. ENS Gershom Tuttle, b. 11 Aug 1714 Wallingford, Connecticut; d. 13 Aug 1777, aged 63, at CLAREMONT, SULLIVAN COUNTY, NEW HAMPSHIRE. Buried UNION CEMETERY, Claremont — Section B, Lot 106. Find a Grave memorial 33451086 (created 2009), citing Charles B. Spofford, Grave Stone Records from the Ancient Cemeteries in the Town of Claremont, N.H., 1896 — a published transcription, not a user guess. The transcription records “Esq. — age 63 years.” ⚠⚠⚠ THE 1883 BOOK IS WRONG ON THE PLACE AS WELL AS THE DATE. Entry 925 says “rem. from Cheshire to Bristol, and d. there, a. 74”. He did not die at Bristol and he was not 74. He died at Claremont, New Hampshire, two days after his sixty-third birthday. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THIS EXPLAINS SOMETHING WE HAD NO EXPLANATION FOR. Entry 9251 says his son the patriot “went FIRST TO NEW HAMPSHIRE, thence about 1790 to Clinton, Oneida Co., N.Y.” The New Hampshire stage was his FATHER’S move. Gershom I took the family from Connecticut to Claremont and died there in the second summer of the Revolution. ⭐⭐⭐ AND THE WHOLE SIBLING GROUP WENT AND LEFT TOGETHER: the same 1883 book, image 713, has “OLIVER Tuttle, from CLAREMONT, N.H., to N.Y. state about 1790; rem. from Paris, Oneida Co., N.Y.…” — and Oliver, b. 1739, is Gershom I’s second son. Two brothers, same town, same year, same destination. Cheshire/Bristol, Conn. → Claremont, N.H. → Paris & Clinton, Oneida Co., N.Y. ⭐⭐ HIS CHILDREN, as the memorial links them: Gershom II 1738–1818 (the patriot), Oliver 1739–1834, Samuel 1747–1805, and LOIS, d. 1769 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐ a daughter named LOIS, which is his wife’s name. The 1883 book prints only “He m. ——.” A daughter called Lois is exactly what a man married to LOIS ALLIS (node 769) names his girl. ——— Earlier note: ✅ THE 1777 HEADSTONE IS THIS MAN — GERSHOM I — confirmed by Alec 6 Aug 2026. Not the patriot (II, d. 5 Jan 1818) and not the Colonel (III, d. 5 Sep 1823). The stone’s own arithmetic is what rules them out: “in ye 63d Year of his Age” in 1777 requires a birth in 1714–15, which is I and only I. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HIS HEADSTONE, 6 Aug 2026 — ALEC FOUND IT ON FIND A GRAVE AND SENT THE PHOTOGRAPH [TUTTLE-33]. A slate stone with a winged soul effigy, reading: “In Memory of En[sig]n GERSHOM TUTTLE Who died Aug[us]t [1]5th AD 1777, in ye 63d Year of his Age. A Man of Sober Life, Who Lived beloved & Lamented died, & may his Rest…” ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE ARITHMETIC IS EXACT AND IT PROVES THE MAN. Born 11 August 1714, he turned 63 on 11 August 1777 — so a death in early August 1777 leaves him 62 years old, i.e. IN HIS 63d YEAR, to the week. A gravestone cut in 1777 and a genealogy printed in 1883 agree to the month, from opposite ends of a century. ⭐ UPGRADED part → ok. He now has: a contemporary monument; a birth date corroborated by it; the 1742 New Cambridge petition signed “Gerfhum Tuttle”; Farmington land purchases from 1739-40; his marriage at Sunderland 17 Oct 1737; and the Farmington birth record of his son naming him as father. ⚠⚠ AND IT REFUTES THE 1883 BOOK — sixth error caught in that volume. The book says “rem. from Cheshire to Bristol, and d. there, a. 74”, which would put his death about 1788. The stone says 1777 and 62. The book is wrong by eleven years and the printed “a. 74” is withdrawn. ⚠ RANK CONFLICT, LOGGED: the stone calls him ENSIGN; the 1883 book calls him “Capt. of the train-band.” Both can be true across one life (ensign, then captain) — but the stone is the contemporary document and it chose Ensign. ⭐⭐ HE DIED IN THE SECOND SUMMER OF THE REVOLUTION, while his son Gershom was conducting provision teams for the Connecticut Assembly. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THE FAMILYSEARCH TREE WAS RIGHT — SAY SO. This node’s own outstanding note read: “The FS tree calls him ‘Ensign Gershom Tuttle, 1714–1777’ — a lead to TEST, not to adopt.” Tested. Both the rank and both years are on the stone. That tree has been wrong six times in this project and it is right here, and it deserves the same plain statement the errors got. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE WALL IS DOWN — 6 Aug 2026, ENTRY 925 OF THE 1883 TUTTLE GENEALOGY, READ IN FULL [TUTTLE-30]: “925. Gershom Tuttle, b. Aug. 11, 1714; rem. from CHESHIRE to BRISTOL, and d. there, a. 74. He appears on the Farmington, Conn., rec. as a buyer of land, first in 1739-40, and frequently afterward as buyer or seller. He was CAPT. OF THE TRAIN-BAND. He m. ——.” A birth date, a death, an origin town and a militia rank, for a man who six hours ago had none of them. ⭐ Every part of it corroborates what we already held from records, which is the only way a published genealogy earns credit: he is buying land in Farmington in 1739-40, two years before he signs the October 1742 New Cambridge petition [TUTTLE-20]; and Bristol IS the New Cambridge parish of Farmington until 1785, so the book and the petition describe one man in one place. ⭐⭐ AND IT IDENTIFIES SIMON. Entry 928 Simon Tuttle “rec. a deed of land … from his father, Timothy Tuttle” — so the second Tuttle on the 1742 petition was Gershom’s own BROTHER. ⚠⚠ THE BOOK LEAVES HIS WIFE A DASH — AND WE HAVE HER NAME AND THE BOOK DID NOT. The standard authority on this family for a hundred and forty years prints “He m. ——”; the Sunderland, Massachusetts town record gives LOIS ALLIS, 17 October 1737 (node 769). It also explains the move: a Cheshire man does not start buying Farmington land in 1739-40 by accident — he had married in October 1737. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HIS FATHER IS NOW KNOWN: DEA. TIMOTHY TUTTLE of Cheshire (node 1536), whose child-list on image 575 runs “IV. Mary, b. Oct. 3, 1712 … V. Gershom, b. Aug. 11, 1714” — entry 924 and entry 925, exactly as the numbering predicted. ——— Earlier notes on this node follow. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ NEW NODE, 6 Aug 2026 — a whole generation added at Alec’s request. Named as the father on the Farmington, Connecticut birth record of Gershom the patriot, 22 Aug 1738 (ark 1:1:F74C-P4J). ⭐ His family is reconstructable from the Farmington births: Gershom 1738, Oliver 1739, Eunice 1743, Hannah 1745, Samuel 1747, Huldah 1749 — a child every two years, then an eleven-year gap before the next set (Solomon 1760, Solomon 1762, Theoderit 1763), which belong to his SON and Tabitha Mitchell [TUTTLE-15].

Outstanding: ⛔ His own birth is NOT in the FamilySearch index at all — searched Gershom Tuttle b.1695×1725 across every collection: zero. So the next generation back cannot be reached by index. Routes: Farmington land records (father-to-son conveyance is the classic proof), Hartford District probate, and — most likely — Hampshire Co., Massachusetts records, since he married there. ⚠ The FS tree calls him “Ensign Gershom Tuttle, 1714–1777” — a lead to TEST, not to adopt. ⭐⭐⭐⭐ FOUND IN A DATED DOCUMENT, 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-20]: he signs the October 1742 petition of the inhabitants of NEW CAMBRIDGE to hire a winter preacher, printed as “Gerfhum Tuttle” (long-s for Gershum). His son was four years old in 1742, so this is the father. It puts him there as a ratepaying householder, not just a name in a birth register — and it confirms from a third direction that Bristol and Farmington are one place: New Cambridge petitioned for winter preaching precisely because it was a remote parish of Farmington. ⭐⭐ A second Tuttle household is there too: SIMON TUTTLE, signer in 1744 and one of ten who in 1747 “publikly declared themselves of the Church of England” — the most promising associated name for Gershom Sr.’s family. ⛔ The Bristol history gives NO origin for any Tuttle. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ [TUTTLE-17]: Hampshire Co., Mass. probate, 1739/40, records the appraisers of Samuel Taylor’s estate as “Nathan TUTHILL, William Allis, Joseph Root” — TUTHILL is a spelling of TUTTLE. So there were Tuttles AT SUNDERLAND in 1739, standing beside William Allis in the same document, two years after Gershom married Lois there. That is what explains how a Tuttle came to be in that town at all. Look for Gershom Sr. among the SUNDERLAND / Hampshire County TUTHILLS, not among the Connecticut Tuttles — and SPELL IT BOTH WAYS. ⭐ The removal to Claremont, N.H. is now bracketed at both ends: the family was at Bristol in January 1769 (the daughter's stone, [TUTTLE-170]) and he was dead at Claremont in August 1777. A Farmington/Bristol land sale between those dates would date the move exactly. ⭐ The Connecticut French and Indian War rolls c.1755–62 remain the open question for the Ensign's commission; the Bristol society records and the 1769 stone establish the title but not the service.

Lead, 12 Sep 2026 [TUTTLE-146 §⑤]: FamilySearch full text indexes the 1777 will of Gershom Tuttle of Farmington (ark 3:1:3QS7-L92K-1NM8, proved 27 Sep 1777) naming “my three Sons Gershom, Oliver and Samuel Tuttle” and appointing “my Son Gershom” executor — the ensign naming the patriot. Image not yet opened (FamilySearch blocked the VM before the lane reached it); read it at the page and this rung is documented by the father’s own will.

⭐⭐⭐ HIS OWN WILL, read at the page, read at the page 13 Sep 2026 [TUTTLE-147 §⑤]: the will of Gershom Tuttle of Farmington, 9 May 1777, proved 27 Sep 1777 (Farmington District Probate Records vol. 1–3, p. 441; the original signed paper survives in estate file No. 2757) gives “my wellbeloved Wife Lois” a third for life and “all the remaining Part of my real & personal Estate unto my Three Sons Gershom, Oliver and Samuel Tuttle,” and appoints “my Son Gershom Tuttle whole and sole Executor.” The executor’s account of “Gershom Tuttel Executor” was allowed 25 Jan 1779. This supersedes the 12 Sep lead that rested on the full-text OCR alone.
