768.s:
Gershom Tuttle was born at Wallingford, Connecticut, on 11 August 1714, the fifth child of Timothy Tuttle — the deacon who had cleared his own farm west of the river — and Thankful Doolittle. He grew up in the Cheshire parish, and as a young man he went north out of Connecticut altogether, to the Massachusetts frontier above Northfield, where his father held a proprietor’s right in one of the new townships. He lodged for a time at Northfield with his mother’s brother, the Reverend Benjamin Doolittle, who was minister there. In 1736, while Gershom was already living in Hampshire County, his father signed the whole of that right over to him in a deed of gift made for “love, good will and fatherly affection.”

A year later, on 17 October 1737, he married Lois Allis in her own family’s town of Sunderland. By 1739–40 he was buying land at Farmington, Connecticut, and in October 1742 he signed the petition of the inhabitants of New Cambridge asking for a winter preacher — the clerk spelled him “Gerfhum Tuttle.” He had gone back with a whole colony of Cheshire people who settled on Chippen’s Hill in that remote parish, the place that is now Bristol, and there he was prominent in church and town affairs. The Farmington register records his children: Gershom in 1738, Oliver in 1739, Eunice 1743, Hannah 1745, Samuel 1747 and Huldah 1749; a daughter Lois was born to them about 1751.

He served in the French and Indian Wars, and the rank he carried out of them stayed with him: the Bristol society records call him “Ens.” in 1761 and again in 1770, and so does the stone his daughter Lois was given when she died on 5 January 1769 in her eighteenth year — “Lois Daugtr of En[s]n Garshum & Mrs Lois Tutle.”

After that he moved the family north a second time, to Claremont, New Hampshire, and this time he stayed. The spring of 1777 took his small grandson Daniel, Oliver’s boy, buried at four years old on 2 March. On 9 May Gershom made his will, leaving his “wellbeloved Wife Lois” the use of a third of his estate, half his household goods to his daughter Eunice, wife of Abner Matthews, and the other half to his “Four motherless Grandchildren Hannah Gurdon Asa and Louisa Johnson,” with everything else divided between his three sons, Gershom, Oliver and Samuel, and his son Gershom named sole executor. He died on 13 August 1777, two days after his sixty-third birthday, in the second summer of the Revolution, while that son was conducting provision teams for the Connecticut Assembly. The will was proved at Farmington on 27 September. He lies in Union Cemetery at Claremont, section B, lot 106, under a slate stone cut with a winged soul effigy: “In Memory of En[sig]n Gershom Tuttle … A Man of Sober Life, Who Lived beloved & Lamented died.”

769.s:
Lois Allis was born at Hatfield, Massachusetts, on 13 January 1707/8, the second daughter of William Allis and his wife Elizabeth. While she was small the family moved up the Connecticut River to Sunderland, and it was there, in her father’s own parish, that she married on 17 October 1737. She was twenty-nine. Her husband, Gershom Tuttle, was a Connecticut man who had come north to take up land his father held in one of the new frontier townships; the town clerk entered them plainly — “Tuttle, Gershom, and Lois Allis, were m. Oct. 17, 1737.”

They went back to Connecticut, to the New Cambridge parish of Farmington on Chippen’s Hill, and the Farmington register fills in the next twelve years: Gershom in 1738, Oliver in 1739, Eunice in 1743, Hannah in 1745, Samuel in 1747, Huldah in 1749. A daughter born about 1751 was given her mother’s name. That younger Lois died on 5 January 1769, in her eighteenth year, and the stone raised over her at Bristol names both her parents — “Lois Daugtr of En[s]n Garshum & Mrs Lois Tutle” — the one contemporary monument that puts husband and wife on the same page.

The Allis connection held across two generations: her elder sister Mary had married Joseph Mitchell of the same valley, and in 1757 Mary’s daughter Tabitha married Lois’s son Gershom, so the cousins married and the same Allis parents stand twice in this pedigree.

She was still living in May 1777, when her husband made his will at Farmington and left “my wellbeloved Wife Lois” the use of a third of his estate for life. Where she died, and when, is not known. She is not buried beside him: the 1896 transcription of every ancient cemetery in Claremont, New Hampshire, found only three Tuttles there and none of them his wife, and the Bristol burying ground that holds her daughter does not hold her either.

770.s:
Joseph Mitchell was born in 1705, the third son of Michael Mitchell and Sarah Catlin, into a household that had come through the Deerfield raid of the year before unharmed while his mother’s family was all but destroyed. He was bred a weaver, not a farmer.

On 2 November 1726 he married Mary Allis, daughter of William Allis of Sunderland; their first child, a son Joseph, was born at Sunderland four months later. Then came daughters — Hannah, who married Zadock King in 1751; Mary, married in 1753; Thankful; Lydia; and, on 9 February 1736/7, Tabitha, who in 1757 married Gershom Tuttle of Farmington and so carried this line forward. There was a son Abner as well. The family moved from Sunderland to Deerfield, and after that to Ashfield, up in the hills to the west.

At Ashfield he seems to have kept the first public house in the town. From about 1763 a Joseph Mitchell — this man or his son of the same name — kept an inn on the east side of Bellows Hill; it was to “the house of Joseph Mitchell, innholder” that the voters were summoned for Ashfield’s first legal town meeting on 6 January 1766, where Joseph Mitchell was chosen constable, and the town went on meeting in his tavern until the meeting house was finished in January 1771. Joseph Mitchell was also one of the handful of men who signed the covenant when the church there was gathered. His daughter Mary’s husband, Samuel Belding, was the town’s first selectman and the man who served the warrant.

Mary died on 8 November 1783. Nine years later, on 14 April 1792, describing himself as of Deerfield, Joseph made his will. He gave twelve pounds each to his daughters Mary, wife of Samuel Belding, Hannah Bigelow, and “my Daughter Tabitha Wife of Gersham Tuttle”; eight shillings each to five grandchildren, the children of “my late Son Joseph”; and the land and the residue to his son Abner. He died on 16 September 1794, at Ashfield, and the will was proved at Northampton on 25 November.

771.s:
Mary Allis was born at Hatfield, Massachusetts, on 18 February 1705, the eldest child of William Allis and Elizabeth his wife, and three years older than her sister Lois. The family moved upriver to Sunderland while the girls were small.

On 2 November 1726 she married Joseph Mitchell, a weaver of the Deerfield Mitchells; their first son was born at Sunderland four months after the wedding. Six more children followed — Hannah, Mary, Thankful, Lydia, Abner, and Tabitha, born 9 February 1736/7 — and the household moved from Sunderland to Deerfield and in the end to Ashfield. She died on 8 November 1783; Sheldon’s Deerfield genealogies, which give the date, call her seventy-seven, though by her own birth entry she was seventy-eight.

Her life joins this family’s tree twice. In 1757 her daughter Tabitha married Gershom Tuttle, the son of her sister Lois — first cousins marrying — so William Allis and Elizabeth Davis stand in two places on the same pedigree, and Mary is an ancestor of this family alongside her own sister.

⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE IMMIGRANT — AND HE IS HIMSELF A RECOGNISED PATRIOT [ROUSH-54, 7 August 2026].

DAR Ancestor # A098982 — Service: VIRGINIA, PATRIOTIC SERVICE: “FURNISHED SUPPLIES.” Source: Library of Virginia, APA 241, Impressed Property Claims Certificates 1780–1783, Shenandoah County, #2453. Born 1711 in the Palatinate; died 19 October 1786, Shenandoah County, Virginia. This is Johann Adam Rausch, the man every American Roush of this family descends from.

⚠⚠ GRADED HYPOTHESIS, AND THE REASON MATTERS. 960.s:
John Adam Roush — Johannes Adam Rausch — was born in 1711 in the Palatinate, and the family has always said Darmstadt. He crossed to Philadelphia in the closing months of 1736 and took the oath of fidelity there; the tradition the family carried into the twentieth century was that he and two companions, forbidden to emigrate, were hidden inside hogsheads by a friendly cooper, loaded aboard, and let out at sea. He landed too poor to pay his passage, hired himself out near Philadelphia, stayed on past his term because he was paid unusually well, and then married and went down the Shenandoah Valley.

He settled on Mill Creek in what was then Frederick County, later Dunmore and then Shenandoah, and farmed it; the family says he also kept a mill and a tannery. His wife was Susannah. In 1773 a grant of four hundred acres on Mill Creek was made “to him and his wife Susannah” — the one period land record that names them both. By then he had been in the valley more than thirty years and had raised a large family: seven sons who can be documented one by one — Philip, John, Jacob, Henry, Daniel, George and Jonas — and the daughters Mary Magdalene, Eleanor and Elizabeth. The family’s own voice says nine sons, and its own table says seven; the seven are the ones the wills and the pension files agree on.

Every one of those sons went into the Revolution, and so, in his sixties, did he: the Library of Virginia holds the Shenandoah County impressed-property claim certificate, number 2453, for supplies he furnished the army between 1780 and 1783. The Daughters of the American Revolution recognise him for it as Patriot Ancestor A098982. One son was a captain with two of his brothers in the ranks; two of them substituted for each other; one of them witnessed another’s pension application fifty years later.

He died on 19 October 1786 near New Market in Shenandoah County and was buried at the Old Pine Church. His gravestone survives — a rough slab cut in German by someone who spelled by ear — and it is now kept upright under glass at St Mary’s Pine Church Cemetery at Mount Jackson, where the old burying ground’s stones were moved in 1868. It reads: ANO 1711 GEBOHREN JOHANNES RAUSCH GESTORBEN DEN 19 OCTOBER 1786. The Adam had already dropped out of his name. Susannah outlived him by ten years and lies beside him in a grave that was never marked. In 1936, on the two hundredth anniversary of his crossing, the Roush and Allied Families Association raised a monument over the two of them that names their children one by one and reckons their descendants, living and dead, at about forty thousand American citizens.

It calls the family tanners and builders of churches.

This is the line that reaches him through his son George, the Revolutionary soldier of Weldon Cemetery — the first of three paths on Alec’s chart that end at this one man. That George was his son is the settled family account, stated in four separate places in the family’s own history, and the brothers’ wills and pension files document the sibling group around him; no surviving document names the father in his own words. His 1786 Shenandoah County probate, if it exists, would do it in a stroke.

1536.s:
Timothy Tuttle was born about 1682, probably at New Haven, the son of Simon Tuttle, a cooper, and his wife Abigail. He was roughly three when the family removed to Wallingford about 1685, after his grandmother’s death. He grew up there, and as a young man he went out west of the river to look for land, chose a spot, and cleared it with his own hands — staying out through the week because it was too far to walk home each night, and finding his way back on Saturdays along a line of trees he had blazed through the woods. The place was about a mile east of what became the centre of Cheshire.

He put up a house there about 1706, the same season he married: on 2 November 1706 he took Thankful Doolittle to wife at Wallingford. Family tradition made it the first frame house in Cheshire, and the town’s own historian thought it was more likely the second; under its roof, he wrote, were born the builder’s children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren. It stood empty until, not many years before 1883, it was burned by an incendiary.

His children by Thankful were Ephraim in 1710, Mary in 1712, Gershom in 1714, Timothy in 1716, Simon in 1721 and Moses in 1723. His father gave him nine and a half acres on 10 July 1711. He turns up all through the west-side records: in 1715 the school district runs “as high as Timothy tuttle & timothy Beach’s,” and he signed that December’s petition of the farmers on the west side of the river. He was moderator of the very first meeting of the New Cheshire society on 16 September 1723, served on the committee to manage the ordination, was “Sergeant Tuttle” on the school-house committee in 1729 and society moderator in 1732, and by 1 December 1741 he is “decon Timothy Tuttle” on the committee to petition for town privileges.

Thankful died in November 1728. He married again in June 1729, to Mary, widow of Stephen Rowe, and for the last time on 28 June 1749, to Sarah (Atwater) Humiston. He had also taken a proprietor’s share in one of the new townships granted up in Hampshire County, Massachusetts, and in 1736 he signed the whole of that right over to his second son — “for divers good causes and considerations and perticularly for love, good will and fatherly affection that I have and [bear] to my son Gershom Tuttle.” It is the deed that sent the next generation north.

He died on 15 April 1756 and lies in Hillside Cemetery at Cheshire, under a brownstone carved with a winged soul effigy: “Here Lies ye Body of Deacon Timothy Tuttle he died April 15th 1756 in ye 75th year of his Age.”

1537.s:
Thankful Doolittle was born at Wallingford, Connecticut, on 5 April 1688, a daughter of John Doolittle and Mary Peck — a granddaughter, on her father’s side, of Abraham Doolittle, one of the men who founded the town. She married young. The Wallingford register, printed in the town history of Cheshire, has the entry plainly: “Timothy Tuttle m. Thankfull Doolittle November 2, 1706.” She was eighteen, and her husband built his house out west of the river that same season.

Her children came across seventeen years: Ephraim in 1710, Mary in 1712, Gershom in 1714, Timothy in 1716, Simon in 1721, Moses in 1723. In March 1725 the new Cheshire church admitted her — the roll records her simply as “wife of Timothy Tuttle” — three years before she died. Her husband was not admitted until January 1738/9, ten years after her death.

She died on 23 November 1728, aged forty, with her youngest child five years old. Where she is buried is not recorded. Her husband married again thirteen months later.

Her brother was the Reverend Benjamin Doolittle, Yale 1716, settled as minister at Northfield on the Massachusetts frontier from 1718. When her son Gershom went north as a young man to take up his father’s land above Northfield, it was his uncle’s house he stayed in — and the compiler who recorded that called Benjamin Doolittle his uncle, which is how her motherhood is attested from outside her own family’s records.

Two things about her still rest on compiled authorities rather than on a record read at the page: her birth of 5 April 1688 and her death of 23 November 1728. Jacobus, the 1883 Tuttle genealogy and Beach’s Cheshire all agree on them, and the dates sit exactly in the gap this family’s own chronology predicted; but the Wallingford entries themselves have not yet been opened.

1538.s:
William Allis was born at Hatfield, Massachusetts, on 19 October 1680, the third child of Samuel Allis, the carpenter and builder of Hatfield street, and his wife Alice. His father died when he was ten; his mother remarried and moved six miles up the road to Deerfield, and on the morning of 29 February 1704 she was killed there in the French and Indian raid, along with his brother Samuel. His sister Mary was carried off toward Canada and came home again. William was twenty-three, and he was not in Deerfield that night.

He had married Elizabeth Davis of Northampton in 1703 or 1704. Their children were Mary, born 18 February 1705, and Lois, born 13 January 1707/8, both at Hatfield; Eliphalet in 1710, also at Hatfield; then Zebediah in 1713 and Elizabeth in 1716, both at Sunderland — so the household moved upriver between the end of 1710 and the autumn of 1713. At Sunderland he appraised a neighbour’s estate in 1739 and deeded land to his son Zebadiah. Later the family moved again, to Montague on the other side of the river, where the town register calls him “Mr. William Allis” — a title of standing — when it recorded his wife’s death on 1 May 1758. The same register shows how hard that place could be: in January 1759 his son Eliphalet and his wife Mary buried four of their children in nine days.

William Allis died at Montague on 20 February 1763, aged eighty-two. He stands in this family’s pedigree twice over. His daughter Lois married Gershom Tuttle in 1737; his daughter Mary married Joseph Mitchell in 1726; and in 1757 Mary’s daughter married Lois’s son, so two of his children’s lines run down to the same descendants.

Elizabeth was of Northampton, Massachusetts, and married William Allis of Hatfield in 1703 or 1704. She is named as the mother on all five of their children’s records — Mary 1705, Lois 1707/8 and Eliphalet 1710 at Hatfield, then Zebediah 1713 and Elizabeth 1716 after the family moved upriver to Sunderland. One of the entries for Lois’s birth gives the place as Northampton rather than Hatfield, which is her own town showing through the clerk’s hand.

With her husband she moved again in later life, across to Montague, and there she died on 1 May 1758. The town register records it in a single line: “Allis. May first 1758, Elizabeth Allis wife to Mr. William Allis, died in Montague.” Her husband outlived her by five years. Two of her daughters, Lois and Mary, married into the Tuttle and Mitchell families, and their children married one another, so she is an ancestor of this family along two lines at once.

Her maiden name of Davis rests on compiled family history rather than on any record of her own youth. A genealogy of 1919 says she was “Elizabeth Davis of Northampton”, and a later manuscript repeats it — but the two may be drawing on one another, and the Montague register that records her death calls her only “Elizabeth Allis wife to Mr. William Allis.” Until a Northampton or Hatfield record names her for herself, the surname is probable rather than proved.

1540.s:
Michael Mitchell is first found at Wallingford, Connecticut, in 1695–6, where he held a proprietor’s standing and cast lots with the other townsmen, and he was there again in 1706. Where he came from before that nobody has been able to say: Sheldon’s Deerfield genealogies begin with him, Jacobus gives him four words, and Savage is silent. He married, about 1694, Sarah, daughter of John Catlin of Deerfield.

He moved his family to Deerfield, the most exposed town on the Massachusetts frontier. On the morning of 29 February 1704, when the French and their allies came over the stockade, his whole family escaped unharmed — a sentence Sheldon only had to write because so many of their neighbours did not. His wife’s father and brother were burned in their own house a few hundred yards away.

His children were William, born 1697; Michael, born 8 March 1700/1, afterwards a soldier in Father Rasle’s war and later of Wethersfield, Connecticut; Joseph, born 1705, the weaver, who is this family’s line; and Samuel, born 7 March 1712, very probably the Samuel Mitchell granted land at Sunderland in 1737 on condition he stayed five years. Sarah died on 30 December 1736.

His Wallingford years matter more than they look. The Tuttles were farming west of the river at Wallingford in exactly those years, and Gershom Tuttle was born there in 1714 — so when Michael’s granddaughter Tabitha married Gershom’s son at Deerfield in 1757, it was not a chance meeting a hundred miles from home. It was two Wallingford families who had both gone north, marrying each other.

1541.s:
Sarah Catlin was a daughter of John Catlin — a Wethersfield man who taught school at Newark in New Jersey, served as that town’s attorney and five years its selectman, and then brought his family to Deerfield about 1683, where he was dignified with the title of “Mr.” — and of his wife Mary Baldwin. About 1694 Sarah married Michael Mitchell, and her eldest child was born in 1697.

That marriage is probably why she lived. On 29 February 1704, when the raid came, she was under her husband’s roof and the Mitchell household came through untouched. Her father’s did not. His buildings were all burned and he and his son Jonathan were consumed with them; another son was killed in the Meadow Fight later the same morning; a son and three daughters were carried off toward Canada. Two of those daughters were her sisters Elizabeth, wife of James Corse, and Mary, wife of Thomas Wells, and both were killed on the march. Sheldon, writing of a town where a hundred and twelve people were marched away in a morning, says of her father that “no family suffered more than his.”

She bore at least four sons — William, Michael, Joseph and Samuel — and died on 30 December 1736, about two months before the birth of her granddaughter Tabitha. She is said to lie in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield, where the grave can no longer be picked out.

3072.s:
Simon Tuttle was baptised at New Haven on 28 March 1647, the ninth child of William Tuttle, the immigrant, and his wife Elizabeth. He was bred a cooper. When Wallingford was laid out in 1670 he put his name on the proprietors’ list and was assigned lot No. 13 with eight acres of out-land, but he did not take the allotment up; he stayed on at New Haven, where he was still drawing his share in the third division in 1680 — the list credits him with “two heads,” which is a clerk’s way of saying a wife and no children yet. He had married Abigail about 1679 or 1680. He was of New Haven through 1683 and “of Wallingford” from 1685, moving, it seems, after his mother died in December 1684.

At Wallingford he did well. He drew lot No. 52 with a hundred and four acres in 1686 and lot No. 14 in 1690, was rated at £79 on the grand list of 1701, and from 1708–9 served the town as gauger and packer, the officer who inspects goods sold by weight and measure. His deeds run across three decades and all of them call his father by name: in 1677–8 he sold a cordwainer land “my father, Mr. William Tuttle, bought of John Punderson”; in 1686 six acres “formerly belonging to my father, Mr. William Tuttle”; in 1705 to his cousin Joshua all his right in the Branford division “set to my father, Mr. William Tuttle.” In 1673 he and five of his brothers had signed a right-of-way agreement whose original paper still survived two centuries later, with his signature on it.

He gave land to his sons in his lifetime, as his son Timothy would in turn: nine and a half acres to Timothy on 10 July 1711, “I bought of Roger Tyler,” and a fourteen-acre house lot to Daniel on 23 June 1715. Simon Tuttle died on 16 April 1719 at Wallingford. His widow Abigail outlived him by three years and died on 11 August 1722.

Abigail married Simon Tuttle, the New Haven cooper, probably in 1679 or 1680 — the date is read off a land record rather than a marriage entry, because in 1680 the New Haven proprietors credited Simon with “two heads” in the third division, meaning a wife but as yet no children. She moved with him to Wallingford about 1685 and raised his family there; her son Timothy, the deacon, was born about 1682.

She outlived her husband. Simon died on 16 April 1719; Abigail died on 11 August 1722.

Her own family is not known. An old tradition made her a daughter of Richard Beach, and the Beach surname does fit the neighbourhood — the Tuttles’ neighbour in the 1715 school-district line was a Timothy Beach. But the 1883 Tuttle genealogy itself prints the doubt: Joseph P. Beach of Cheshire, the family’s own authority, “thinks that she could not have been a Beach. Richard’s dau. Abigail is not mentioned in settlement of her father’s estate. The point remains in uncertainty.” Fifty years later Jacobus wrote her into Families of Ancient New Haven as “Abigail — [not Beach]”. Her identity as Simon’s wife and Timothy’s mother is not in question; her surname is simply lost.

3074.s:
John Doolittle was born at New Haven on 14 June 1655, a son of Abraham Doolittle — who had come to New Haven from Boston in 1644, took the freeman’s oath there, served as the county’s chief executive officer, and was one of the founders of Wallingford — and his wife. John married Mary Peck on 13 February 1682/3, and settled at Wallingford, the town his father had helped lay out.

Their children included Esther, born 24 January 1683, who also married a Tuttle; Samuel in 1685; Thankful, born 5 April 1688, who married Deacon Timothy Tuttle in 1706; and Benjamin, born 1695, who took his degree at Yale in 1716, married Lydia Todd the next year, and was settled as the minister of Northfield, up on the Massachusetts frontier, from 1718 until he died suddenly in January 1748. It was to that uncle’s house that Thankful’s son Gershom went when he first travelled north as a young man — which is how a Wallingford family came to have a foothold a hundred miles up the Connecticut River.

Mary died on 1 September 1710. John married again on 29 January 1717, to Grace Blakeslee, and that is the last record of him alive; he was then sixty-one. The year of his death is not established. A John Doolittle who died at Wallingford in 1746–7, aged thirty-five, was a son of the same name, not this man, and the rank “Sergeant” that is often attached to him belonged to his father Abraham.

Mary Peck was born at New Haven on 4 March 1665/6, a daughter of John Peck and his wife Mary Moss. The Pecks, the Mosses and the Doolittles were the three families who founded Wallingford between 1668 and 1670 and whose children married across all three, and on 13 February 1682/3 Mary married John Doolittle, Abraham Doolittle’s son.

Her children included Esther, born January 1683; Samuel, 1685; Thankful, born 5 April 1688, who married Deacon Timothy Tuttle; and Benjamin, born 1695, afterwards minister at Northfield. Mary died at Wallingford on 1 September 1710, at forty-four. Her husband remarried seven years later.

3076.s:
Samuel Allis was born at Braintree, Massachusetts, on 24 February 1647. The town register enters him under the year 1646, because the year then began in March and February was reckoned the twelfth month: “Samuel, sonne of William Alyes & Mary his wife was Borne the 24th. of ye 12 month.” In the Old Style of the time the date is written 24 February 1646/7. His father, William Allis, was a Braintree freeman of 1640 who removed about 1661 up the Connecticut River to the new town of Hatfield.

Samuel followed him there and took his own home lot as a young man of twenty-two. On 4 February 1669 the town granted him a house lot sixteen rods wide next to Samuel Marsh’s, with land in the Plain above the great meadow and ten acres in the swamp by the Mill river — “provided he build a sufficient dwelling house upon his lot by or before the last of May in the year 1671, otherwise to forfeit his land.” Daniel Belden had the lot on the other side. He built, and he stayed: a carpenter and builder, living on the east side of Hatfield street.

About 1675–6 he married a woman named Alice, whose surname no record has ever given. Seven children followed: Mehitable on 2 July 1677; Samuel on 20 February 1679; William on 19 October 1680, from whom this family descends; Mary on 6 July 1682; Thomas on 12 March 1684; Sarah about 1685; and Rebecca on 29 November 1687.

Samuel Allis died at Hatfield on 9 March 1691, aged forty-four, leaving Alice with seven children all under fifteen. She remarried in 1696 and was killed in the raid on Deerfield of 29 February 1704; their son Samuel was killed in the same attack, and their daughter Mary was carried to Canada and survived to come home.

3077.s:
Alice married Samuel Allis, the Hatfield carpenter, about 1675–6, and bore him seven children between 1677 and 1687 — Mehitable, Samuel, William, Mary, Thomas, Sarah and Rebecca. When he died on 9 March 1691 she was left with all of them under fifteen.

On 20 November 1696 she married again, to Sergeant John Hawks of Deerfield: a soldier of King Philip’s war who had been in the Falls Fight and was wounded going to the relief of Hatfield on 30 May 1676, and who had become a permanent settler at Deerfield in 1683. She had a daughter by him, Elizabeth, born about 1697.

On the morning of 29 February 1704 the French and their allies came over the Deerfield stockade. Alice was killed in the village. Her son Samuel Allis, twenty-five years old, was killed in the meadow. Her little daughter Elizabeth Hawks, six or seven, was taken and died on the march to Canada. Her daughter Mary Allis, twenty-one, was also carried off, survived the march, was redeemed, and came home to marry another survivor of the same raid, Nathaniel Brooks, in 1710. Her husband lived, but as Sheldon wrote of him, all his children and grandchildren of the name were lost that day; he ended his life at Waterbury, Connecticut, with the one daughter he had left. This family’s line runs through her third child, William, who was at Hatfield and not in Deerfield that night.

She lies with the rest of the dead of that morning in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield, under a stone that reads: “The grave of 48 men women and children, victims of the French and Indian raid on Deerfield, February 29, 1704.” Her own family name was never written down. The 1919 Allis genealogy leaves a literal blank where the surname should go; Boltwood and Sheldon, both working from the Hampshire County records, call her only “Alice, widow of Samuel Allis.” She is remembered by her first name alone.

3082.s:
John Catlin was born about 1643, the son of a Catlin of Wethersfield, Connecticut, who died when the boy was an infant. He was of Wethersfield in 1662 — the year he married Mary Baldwin — and of Branford by 1665, and from there he went with the New Haven colony party that founded Newark, New Jersey. He is the first man on this chart to live in New Jersey, and he was not a farmer there. In 1676 he kept Newark's first school, in his own house, as the custom then was; the townsmen's vote engaged him to “do his faithful, honest and true endeavour to teach the children or servants of these as have subscribed … english and also arithmetick as much as they are capable to learn and he capable to teach them.” In 1678 he was the town's attorney — not a lawyer, but an “honest brother” charged to see that all town orders were executed and to punish any breach — and he was a selectman from 1676 to 1681.

About 1683 he moved north again, by way of Hartford, to the frontier town of Deerfield in Massachusetts, where he was one of the early permanent settlers. In 1685 he bought the Frary part of home lot 32, four acres on Deerfield street, and lot 33 from John Parsons in the same year; lot 36 was his as well by 1704. In the town records he is given the title “Mr.”, which in a New England town book is a rank and not a courtesy, and he took a prominent part in the town's affairs.

On the night of 28 February 1704 there were 291 people under Deerfield's roofs. Before the next morning was out, all but a hundred and twenty-six of them were dead or being marched through the snow towards Canada, three hundred miles away. The historian of Deerfield wrote that no family suffered more than John Catlin's. He and his son Jonathan were killed defending their house, which was then taken and burned with all his buildings; another son was killed later that morning in the Meadow Fight; a third son, John, and three of his daughters were carried off. Two of those daughters, Elizabeth, the wife of James Corse, and Mary, died on the march. The 1704 casualty list enters him simply as “John Catlin, (?) 60”.

The house that gave the raid its surviving relic still stood in Deerfield until 1848 and was photographed before it came down: Capt. John Sheldon's, built about 1698, which held out while half the village burned. Its front door, hacked through, is kept in Memorial Hall in the village to this day.

His line survived for one accidental reason: his daughter Sarah had married Michael Mitchell about 1694 and was in a household of her own that night. The captured son came home from Canada, and by about 1715 had built a new house on his father's ashes; he was a housewright, and was always known in Deerfield by tradition as “Master Catlin.” The forty-eight who died in the raid lie together in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield under a brownstone block raised over the common grave.

3083.s:
Mary Baldwin was baptized at Milford, Connecticut, on 23 June 1644 — the same day her mother Hannah joined the Milford church and the first four Baldwin children were all baptized together. Her father was Joseph Baldwin, one of the first settlers of the town. On 23 September 1662 she married John Catlin, and in a tangle that is rare even in a small colony she married the son of her own stepmother: her father's second wife, Isabella, was the widow of the elder John Catlin.

She went with her husband from Branford to Newark in New Jersey, where he kept the town's first school, and about 1683 to Deerfield on the Massachusetts frontier. They had ten children. Her father remembered her in his will of 20 December 1680 — “I doe give to my Daughter Mary Cattlin … fortie shillings” — a line in his own instrument, nearly a quarter of a century after she had left his house.

On the morning of 29 February 1704 her husband and one son were killed defending their house at Deerfield and it was burned; another son was killed in the Meadow Fight; a son and three daughters were carried off towards Canada, and two of the daughters died on the march. Mary was taken with the other prisoners to the Sheldon house, the largest in the town, which the attackers had kept as a holding place for captives. A wounded French officer was brought in and laid on the floor, calling for water, and Mary Catlin fed him with water. Someone asked her how she could do that for her enemy. She answered, “If thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him water to drink.” The Frenchman was carried away, the captives were marched off, and Mrs. Catlin was left behind. Afterwards a little boy who had been hidden in the house came out, and she told him to run and hide. The boy said, “Mrs. Catlin, why don't you go and hide?” She said, “I am a captive; it is not my duty to hide, but you have not been taken, and it is your duty to hide.”

That account came down in the family and was written out a century later by a descendant, Lucy D. Shearer; the historian of Deerfield printed it because he judged it an authentic tradition, and he accepted its explanation in five words of his own — this was the place “where Mrs. Catlin relieved the wounded French lieutenant, and secured her own freedom by her practical Christianity.” The house she stood in outlasted her by a century and a half; the “Old Indian House” stood until 1849, and its scarred and battered door is in Memorial Hall at Deerfield still. She lies in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield.

ph.c: The Old Burying Ground at Deerfield, where Mary Catlin was buried five weeks after the raid; the brownstone block marks the common grave of the forty-eight who were killed on 29 February 1704. — Find a Grave contributor 'Cindy Selensky Foster', photographed Sept 2023

6144.s:
William Tuttle came out of England on the ship Planter, which left the port of London in April 1635 and put into Boston about the first of July. He travelled with his wife Elizabeth, their first three children, and — in the same passage — two brothers and their households. The passenger list calls him a husbandman, a man who farmed his own ground; a petition surviving in Boston shows him among the merchant owners of the ketch Zebulon of Ipswich, asking the General Court for two guns to arm her for a voyage to the Indies. The court refused.

Two of his sons were baptized at Charlestown, Jonathan in 1637 and David in 1639, and by June of that year the family had moved to the new colony at Quinnipiac. On 4 June 1639 the planters met in Mr. Newman's barn and signed the church covenant that founded New Haven; William Tuttle's name is on that list for the first time, standing between Benjamin Ling and Ezekiel Cheever, near the head among the principal men. In the first division of land in 1640 he was rated at £100 of estate and seven persons in the family. In 1641 he held the home lot of Edward Hopkins, afterwards governor of Connecticut, and in 1656 he bought from Joshua Atwater a house, home lot and barn on the green. That became the Tuttle homestead, and the family held it for thirty years. Long after, the first building of Yale College was raised on the same ground.

He had land across the water at East Haven as well, enough of it that a stream there is still called Tuttle's Brook and the rise above it Tuttle's Hill. In 1651 he joined Jasper Crane and about fifty others in the New Haven colony's attempt to plant a settlement on the Delaware; the Dutch governor at Manhattan seized the party, held them prisoner and sent them home, and the petition of protest that followed — “the humble petition of Jasper Crane, William Tuttle and many others” — went to the commissioners of the United Colonies. The venture cost him money he did not recover, and after it he turned to farming and to town business.

The colony records catch him at that business constantly: fence viewer for Mr. Davenport's quarter in 1644, laying out allotments and settling boundaries; a juror again and again, his title of “Mr.” always carefully written, which in a New England town record is a rank and not a courtesy; sworn constable in March 1666-7; one of the commissioners who finally settled the line between Branford and New Haven in 1669 and between New Haven, Milford, Branford and Wallingford in 1672. When the meeting house was seated in 1646-7 — the seats graded by descent, public trust, piety and estate — Mr. Tuttle was voted into the first cross seat at the upper end, nearest the pulpit. They catch him in smaller things too. In 1646 he and Jeremy Watts were fined for falling asleep at the watch house. In 1664 a girl caught pilfering tried to drag his fourteen-year-old daughter Mercy into it; the charge collapsed, and before sentence William Tuttle asked the court, “with great affection,” to deal gently with the girl and place her in a pious family.

The town he helped found was drawn out, house by house, a lifetime after he died. A plan of New Haven 'with all the buildings in 1748', engraved in 1806 from General Wadsworth's survey, names every householder and his trade across the nine squares — and the Tuttle name is still scattered through it: a Widow Tuttle on the north road, a Noah Tuttle to the east, an Enos Tuttle, miller, by the harbour, and an Ab. Tuttle who was the sexton. The long hip-roofed building marked 'Yale Colledge, Built 1717' stands on the block beside the green where the family homestead had been.

He died suddenly in the first days of June 1673, leaving no will; his inventory was entered just after that of his neighbour Benjamin Ling, taken on the sixth. A deed he had agreed to was found unsigned. His widow Elizabeth called herself his lawful administratrix, and his Branford division lands were still being parcelled out to his children on 14 February 1705, thirty-two years after he died — his son Simon's deed of that year conveys “all my right in Branford division set to my father, Mr. William Tuttle, now (Feb. 14, 1705) laid out for his children.” The last remainder of the estate was not divided until 1709 — thirty-six years after his death — when it was split into eleven parts, with a grandson appealing the division to Hartford. He lies somewhere under the Old Green at New Haven; the exact spot is not known. Among his descendants is his great-grandson Jonathan Edwards, who studied and taught on the very ground where William Tuttle's house had stood.

6145.s:
Elizabeth Tuttle was born in England about 1609. She was about twenty-six when she crossed to New England in April 1635 on the ship Planter with her husband William and their first three children — John, Hannah and Thomas — in a party that also held her husband's two brothers and their families and his widowed mother. They landed at Boston about the first of July, and a year later, on 24 July 1636, “Mrs. Elizabeth Tuttell” united with the church in Boston. The same church register records her bringing two sons to be baptized: Jonathan in July 1637 and David in April 1639. Within weeks of that second baptism the family had gone to the new plantation at Quinnipiac, which became New Haven.

She bore twelve children and, in a century when that was rare, every one of them lived to grow up: John, Hannah, Thomas, Jonathan, David, Joseph, Sarah, Elizabeth, Simon — from whom this family descends — Benjamin, Mercy and Nathaniel. Her own standing in the town is legible in the dullest of records. When New Haven seated its meeting house in 1646-7, the seats graded by rank, Mrs. Tuttle was placed in the fifth seat in the middle among the wives of the leading men; in 1655-6 in the fourth long seat; in 1661-2 the clerk simply wrote “Sisters Miles, Peck, Lindon, Tuttle and Gibbard.”

Her husband died suddenly in June 1673, leaving no will. Elizabeth took out the administration herself — at a court in June 1674 she appeared to confirm a sale her husband had made and is entered as “widow and relict and lawful administratrix,” signing with her mark. She stayed on at the homestead on the green, where she had lived since 1656, and kept it for another eleven years; in all she lived there twenty-eight.

The widowhood was hard. In November 1676 her daughter Sarah, married to John Slauson of Stamford, was killed; later writers quoting the New Haven court record say she was struck down by her own younger brother Benjamin after a quarrel, and that Benjamin was hanged at New Haven in June 1677. This project has not seen that court record itself. The family's own 1883 genealogy records only the bare dates — Sarah dead on 17 November 1676, Benjamin unmarried, making over his property to his brother-in-law Richard Edwards on 18 June 1677 — and says nothing of how either of them died.

Elizabeth spent her last years with her youngest son, Nathaniel, and died on the last day of 1684. The will she left was presented to the New Haven court on 28 July 1685 and refused: “the other children objected and the court would not allow it.” Her inventory, taken that February, was thought by a later reader to show “a ladylike refinement in apparel and household appointments.” Her gravestone, cut with the old-style date “Age 76: 31:10:1684 — Elisabeth Tutle” (month ten being December under the old calendar), was carried with the others from the Old Green to Grove Street Cemetery in 1821 and stands today in the row along the north wall. Part of its epitaph has crumbled away, but it was copied before it went: “The blest live as They are: the blest That live at Rest.”

6148.s:
Abraham Doolittle was born in England about 1620 and was in New England by 1640. He was at Boston in 1640 and at New Haven by 1644 — the monument later raised over him says 1642 — and from there he never left the colony's service: corporal, freeman, marshal of New Haven Colony from 1662 until the colony was swallowed by Connecticut, townsman, sergeant of the first train band, deputy to the General Court for New Haven and later for Wallingford, town treasurer. In the earliest records the name is written “Dowlittle.” On 10 November 1669 he sat as a juror at New Haven on the same panel as William Tuttle and Roger Alling — his own brother-in-law — in a court presided over by the deputy governor.

That same year he was chosen to superintend the affairs of the new settlement inland, and he became one of the founders of Wallingford. The town historian puts him and John Peck on the spot two years before the town was incorporated: “Abraham Doolittle and John Peck were on the ground in 1668.” He was one of four trustees who managed the plantation until Wallingford was incorporated in 1670, one of the committee that gathered its first church, and deputy for it in 1668 and 1672. During King Philip's War his house was one of those fortified, and he served on the town's vigilance committee in 1675.

He married twice. His first wife was Joan Alling, by whom he had the children of the 1640s and 1650s, including John, born 14 June 1655, from whom this family descends; she died about 1661 and was buried at New Haven. On 2 July 1663 he married Abigail Moss, daughter of his fellow Wallingford founder John Moss. In all there were thirteen children, and when he died on 11 August 1690, aged seventy, seven sons and three daughters survived him; his will names his wife, the seven sons and the three daughters. He lies in the Center Street Cemetery at Wallingford, where the town replaced his worn original stone in 1918 with a tall granite monument that sets out his whole public career. Which of his children belonged to which wife is a question later genealogists have had to reason out; the identification of John as a child of the first marriage rests on their reading rather than on a surviving record.

6149.s:
Joan Alling was baptized at Kempston in Bedfordshire on 12 October 1617, a daughter of James Alling. Her brother was Roger Alling, who became treasurer of the New Haven Colony and a deacon of its church — so when she crossed the ocean she was coming to a family already planted near the top of the colony's affairs.

She was the first wife of Abraham Doolittle of New Haven, and the mother of the children born in the 1640s and 1650s: Abraham, Elizabeth born 12 April 1652, Mary, John born 14 June 1655 — the son from whom this family descends — and Sarah. She died about 1661, before her husband's second marriage in July 1663, and she was buried at New Haven; where, is not known. The town of Wallingford remembered her all the same. When it raised a new monument over Abraham Doolittle in 1918 it cut a line for her near the top: “First wife Joane Alling is buried in New Haven.”

Her place in the family is reasoned rather than recorded. That the children born before 1663 belonged to a first wife and not to Abigail Moss is settled several ways over — Abigail was only about fourteen when John was born — but the naming of that first wife as this Kempston-baptized Joan rests on one genealogist's work. No marriage record for Abraham and Joan survives anywhere.

6150.s:
John Peck was born about 1638, the son of Deacon William Peck of New Haven, the London merchant who had come over on the Hector. He grew up in the colony his father helped found, and became a freeman there in 1669. On 3 November 1664 he married Mary Moss, daughter of John Moss, in New Haven.

In 1668, two years before Wallingford was incorporated, he and Abraham Doolittle were already on the ground there — the town historian puts them in the same sentence — and John Peck settled in the new inland town and stayed. The first of his ten children were born at New Haven and the last six at Wallingford; the eldest, Mary, born 4 March 1666, married John Doolittle, so that the two men who had broken the ground together became grandfathers to the same children.

John Peck died at Wallingford in 1724, about eighty-six years old; Mary outlived him by a year, dying 16 November 1725 aged seventy-eight. They lie in the Center Street Cemetery, in a plot that is now the ninth stop on the town's walking tour, but no stone for either of them survives — none was found when the burying ground was transcribed in 1934, and the two markers standing in the plot today belong to a later John Peck and his wife.

Mary Moss was baptized at New Haven on 11 April 1647, one of the eleven children of John Moss — the long-lived Wallingford founder who was said to have died at 103 — and his wife, whose name no record preserves. On 3 November 1664, aged seventeen, she married John Peck, son of Deacon William Peck; the ceremony was performed by William Jones, afterwards deputy governor of Connecticut.

Her first children were born at New Haven and the last six at Wallingford, where her husband and her father were both among the founders. There were ten in all. The eldest, Mary, born 4 March 1666, married John Doolittle of Wallingford and is the one through whom this family descends. Mary Moss outlived her husband by a year and died at Wallingford on 16 November 1725, aged seventy-eight. She was buried in the Center Street Cemetery, but no stone for her was found when the yard was transcribed in 1934 and none stands there now.

6152.s:
William Allis was made a freeman of Braintree, Massachusetts, on 13 May 1640, and the Braintree town book then carries him through the 1650s as a selectman, as “Deacon Allis”, and as a commissioner, with Thomas Meekins holding land next to his. Where he came from before that is not established: the family genealogy printed in 1919 says he was born between 1613 and 1616 in Essex or London and came over with Winthrop's fleet in 1630, but no earlier authority says anything of the kind, and the same book has been caught inventing a death for his wife, so the crossing and the origin are left where they belong, as that book's claims alone.

In 1641 he married a woman named Mary, whose surname has not survived. Their children were born at Braintree: John in 1642, Samuel on 24 February 1647 — the son through whom this family descends — two boys named Josiah, two named William, Hannah, and Mary. About 1661 he moved the family west to Hatfield on the Connecticut River.

There his title stops being a courtesy and becomes a record. When King Philip's War set the valley towns to garrisoning themselves, the commands were parcelled out: thirty-nine men under Pynchon at Springfield, twenty-nine at Westfield, twenty-six at Northampton, thirty at Hadley — and thirty-six at Hatfield, under Lieut. Wm. Allis, the largest force in the valley after Springfield's. Six more soldiers were ordered to him to be employed through the winter getting out timber for the fortifications at Hatfield and Deerfield. In the same war, on 19 May 1676, his son William, aged twenty, was killed in the Falls Fight at Turners Falls.

His wife Mary died on 10 August 1677. On 25 June 1678 he married Mary, daughter of John Bronson and widow of John Graves of Haddam — and died ten weeks later, in September 1678. A Deerfield land redistribution of 1680 notes the fact in brackets, as a thing everyone knew: “[Lieut. Wm. Allis had died September, 1678.]”

Mary married William Allis in 1641 and spent the next twenty years at Braintree, Massachusetts, bearing a family of eight. The town register records the births without ever giving her a surname: “Mary Allis the dauter of wilom Allis and mary his wife was born the (25)(8)(53)”; “William Allis the sonne of William Allis and Mary his wife was borne the (10)(11)1655”; and, on the same page, the death of a baby — “Josia Allis the sone of William Allis and Mary his wife dyed the (15)(8)1651”. She buried two sons named Josiah and a first son named William in infancy before the William who lived — and that William was killed in the Falls Fight at Turners Falls on 19 May 1676, a year before she died.

Her son Samuel, born 24 February 1647, is the child through whom this family descends. About 1661 the household moved west to Hatfield, and she died there on 10 August 1677, cause unknown. Her husband remarried the following June and was dead himself ten weeks after that.

Her surname is gone, and that is now a settled finding rather than an open question: five independent sources were searched for it — the 1919 Allis genealogy, which prints a literal blank, “In 1641 William Allis married Mary ____ and their eight children were born in Braintree”; Boltwood; Sheldon; Judd; and the primary Braintree register itself, which names her three times only as “Mary his wife” and carries no marriage entry at all. An old family story that she was killed in the Hatfield raid of September 1677 is false — she had died five and a half weeks before it — and the violent death it was reaching for belongs to her daughter-in-law Alice, killed at Deerfield in 1704.

12300.s:
William Peck was born in 1601 and was a merchant in London. In 1637 he sailed for New England on the Hector with his wife Elizabeth and their young son Jeremiah, in the company of Theophilus Eaton, Edward Hopkins and the Reverend John Davenport; the ship reached Boston on 26 June. He went with that company to Quinnipiac, and in June 1639 he signed the Fundamental Agreement that founded New Haven. He was made a freeman there on 29 October 1640.

His home lot was on George Street and his shop fronted on Church Street. He was never a rich man — his estate shows it — but he was a trusted one. He was one of three men who inventoried the estate of Sergeant Thomas Jeffrie in 1661. In December 1662 he stood up at a New Haven town meeting to tell it that the town's elders were not getting enough to eat: there was not wheat and malt enough to go round. With Roger Alling he was appointed a trustee of the fund, £918 in all, that paid for the colony's collegiate grammar school. From 1659 until his death — thirty-five years — he was deacon of the First Church of New Haven, and that is the name he kept.

Elizabeth died in December 1683, and about a year later he married Sarah, the widow of William Holt; his will, drawn 9 March 1689, mentions the second wife and his four children, all of them Elizabeth's. He died in October 1694 while staying at the house of his son Joseph at Lyme, more than forty miles from home. His stone was moved with the rest from the Old Green to Grove Street Cemetery in 1821 and still stands against the north wall there. It settles, in its own worn letters, a date that the books had muddled: “Deacon William Peck, aged 93, deceased Octobr 14, 1694.”

3078.s:
Samuel Davis was born about 1645, probably at Roxbury, Massachusetts — Savage calls him “perhaps son of William of the same” — and a Roxbury church record of 1649 lists a Samuel Davis among William Davis’s children. He removed up to Northampton in 1668 and was made a freeman there in 1676.

He kept choosing the exposed edge. Besides his Northampton land he held shares in the valley’s silver and lead mine venture, which he sold to Medad Pomeroy, and he put his name down as a subscriber to Harvard College. In 1682 he was a grantee of Northfield — a town that had already been burned twice — and in 1685 he was among the men who went back to rebuild it. In March 1676 his wife was one of a long list of Northampton women fined for wearing silk “in a flaunting manner.”

He married twice. His first wife is named in Northfield’s town history as Hannah Edwards, married 4 March 1668 and dead on 11 September 1680; his second was Elizabeth, daughter of William Smead, whom he married in 1681. Savage records two sons — Samuel, born 1672, and John, born 1677 — and three daughters whose names he does not give. Samuel Davis died at Northampton on 26 July 1690, in the epidemic that swept the town that summer.

He is on this chart as the father of Elizabeth Davis, who married William Allis of Hatfield in 1703–4. That link is probable rather than proved: he is the only Davis household of his generation in Northampton, which is where the Allis genealogy says Elizabeth came from, but no record yet names her as his daughter.

52.s:
Benjamin Nott — the name is written Knott about as often as Nott, and the 1881 county history prints its own correction, “Benjamin Knott probably should be Benj. Nott, as per 1810 Federal Census of Wash. Co.” — farmed in Adams Township, near Lowell, in Washington County, Ohio. He was born about 1815–17 in Ohio. Nothing yet found names his own parents, though an elder Benjamin Nott “of Adams” died insolvent in 1822, leaving a widow Polly, and if that man was his father he was orphaned as a small boy on a broke farm on Calls Creek.

He married a Margaret; an index entry for a marriage of “Benj. Nott” to Margaret Kirk in Morgan County on 13 March 1836 is the best lead to her surname, but the image has never been read and a rival Benjamin married a Lavina Tewel in Washington County in 1839. The 1860 census shows the household at Lowell — Benjamin forty-three, a farmer; Margaret forty-three; P. J. fifteen; William F. thirteen; and Jos M eleven. That eleven-year-old is believed to be Joseph McGee Knott, whose 1932 death certificate names Benjamin and Margaret as his parents and Lowell as his birthplace; but the census gives no relationships and its implied birth year for Joseph is about two years out from the certificate, so the link is treated as probable rather than proved.

In July 1861, at forty-six, a Benjamin Nott of the county volunteered for Company A of the Thirty-sixth Ohio and was mustered out in 1864 — and it was him: a state register of soldiers’ graves, compiled in Ohio in the twentieth century, sets down the same service on his card, enlisted 29 July 1861, discharged 4 September 1864, private, Company A, 36th Regiment Ohio Infantry. By 1870 the family was in Marietta, where the census lists Benjamin fifty-three, Margaret fifty-two, John W. twenty-three, Sarah twenty, a baby Henry and three boarders. His last years were hard. In December 1890 the probate court recorded “P. J. Nott, guardian of Benjamin Nott, an Insane person” filing an inventory — the guardian was his own child, the P. J. of the 1860 household. He died between that December and the following 6 July, when the final account was settled: the estate was charged with nothing at all, credited with $10.91, and that sum was found due the child who had cared for him. He died at Marietta on 6 May 1891, of la grippe — the influenza that went round the world between 1889 and 1891 — and the register of soldiers’ graves lays him in Oak Grove Cemetery at Marietta, lot 90, block 19, under an upright stone.

54.s:
Erwin R. Lamb — Irvin on his own gravestone, Irwin in his obituary; the three spellings are one man — was born on 19 March 1840 in Wayne County, Indiana, the second of the ten children of Elias Lamb, carpenter and farmer, and Susannah (Bish) Lamb, who had married at her father’s house in Clay Township on 23 March 1837. His grandparents were Joseph and Lydia (Adamson) Lamb, Quakers who had brought the family from Randolph County, North Carolina, to Wayne County in April 1829, eleven years before he was born. He was reared on his father’s farm in Clay Township and stayed in the county until he was a grown man.

On 14 March 1860 he took out a licence in Wayne County to marry Melissa J. Bailey, the daughter of a neighbouring farming family; the minister’s return on the same leaf of the register is dated the 15th. It was a double season: his elder brother Azel had married Sarah Ann Bailey three months before, in the next township. The census that summer found the newlyweds still under his father’s roof in Clay Township, on a farm the enumerator valued at eleven thousand dollars. Four children came — Alma S., Martha E., Frank A. and May Belle — and then, on the evening of Monday 29 November 1875, after a few days’ illness, Melissa died at Newport in Vermillion County, aged thirty-one. The family had moved there in 1870 with his parents.

On 18 May 1879 he married Mrs. Mary Elizabeth (Jackson) Hall, the widow of a soldier of the 125th Illinois Infantry and the daughter of Arthur Jackson, an early Vermillion County settler who had given three sons to the Union and lost all three. She brought five Hall children with her. The census of 1880 shows the two families together on Main Street in Vermillion — Erwin forty, “Mary E.” forty-one, his own Mattie, Frank and Bell, and her Effie. By 1888 he was living at Newport, and the county’s biographical volume gave him a sketch that spent most of its length on his second wife’s people.

He did not stay in Indiana. He ended his life at Jonesboro, in Craighead County, Arkansas, where he had lived “a number of years,” a member of the First Methodist church and a regular attender until his health failed. He died at St. Bernard’s Hospital at half past midnight on 27 February 1919, aged seventy-eight, after an operation for blood poisoning. The local paper called him “a splendid man” and named as his survivors his wife and two step-children, Mrs. Bertha Conger and A. W. Hall, both of Jonesboro — the Bertha and Allen W. Hall of 1888. His own children, his daughter Martha among them, are not mentioned. He was buried at Jonesboro, under a plain marble block cut IRVIN R LAMB.

He kept the books for other men to the end of his working life: for many years he was clerk at the Old American Hotel in Jonesboro, and he had been retired some time before he died. He and his wife were settled at Jonesboro, in a house on Krewson Avenue, by 1911 at the latest. The last ten days of his life are in the Jonesboro papers almost day by day. He had been ill at home for ten days in October 1918 and in poor health for eight months; on Monday 17 February 1919 an infected foot was amputated at St. Bernard's Hospital, and the paper noted that at his age the operation was a shock to his nervous system; he was reported resting nicely, then improving; the surgeons went back and took the leg off below the knee for gangrene; and he died at half past twelve on the morning of 27 February. Both Jonesboro papers carried him. The Sun called him "an old resident of the city… highly respected by everyone, making a friend of every acquaintance," and named four step-children — A. W. Hall and Mrs. C. C. Conger of Jonesboro, Mrs. Josephine Schweizer of Danville, Illinois, and Mrs. Effie Townsend of Richmond, Illinois. His widow Mary outlived him by two years. She died at the same hospital on 20 February 1921 after a long illness, having lived since his death with her daughter Mrs. Bertha Conger, and was buried from the First Methodist Church.

In May 1890 he was very probably the Erwin Lamb of Plainfield, Indiana, who came down to Terre Haute to stay with two of his children — his daughter, by then Mrs. Mattie Ford, and his son Frank — who were keeping house together on north Third Street.

That he was Martha Ellen Lamb’s father rests on three converging records — her 1945 death certificate names “Erwin Lamb”; the 1880 census puts her in his house as “Mattie E., daughter”; the 1888 sketch lists “Martha E.” among his four children by his first wife — but a two- to three-year disagreement about her birth year runs through them, so the identification is carried as probable.

55.s:
Melissa J. Bailey was born on 24 July 1844 in Wayne County, Indiana. Nothing yet found names her parents; the Baileys and the Lambs farmed adjoining ground in Clay Township, and the county history of 1872 puts “Ithamar Lamb, Milo Bailey, and Lewis Strickler” together on one tract of school land.

On 14 March 1860, aged fifteen, she took out a licence with Irvin R. Lamb of the neighbouring farm; the minister returned the certificate the next day. Three months before, Irvin’s elder brother Azel had married another Bailey, Sarah Ann — two brothers and two Bailey brides in one winter. The census that summer found Melissa living with her husband in his father’s house in Clay Township. Four children followed: Alma S., Martha E. (born at Richmond in August 1865), Frank A. and May Belle. About 1870 the whole Lamb connection moved west to Vermillion County.

She died at Newport at about eight o’clock on the evening of Monday 29 November 1875, after a few days’ illness, aged thirty-one. Her funeral was preached at two the following afternoon in the Methodist Episcopal church by the Rev. Milton B. Wood, and she was buried at Newport. The local paper, which knew her, called her “a United Brethren in belief” and “a kind mother, an affectionate wife, a noble woman and highly esteemed by every person in Newport.” Her daughter Martha was ten. That Martha was her child rests on the 1888 sketch of Irvin’s life, which names the four children of his first marriage, and on dates that fit exactly — strong, but not yet a record that says so outright.

124.s:
George Nease was born on 10 December 1819 - or on 21 November 1820, which is what his own death register says - in Virginia, into one of the Nease families of Mason County who had come down from the Shenandoah Valley with the Roushes and settled both banks of the Ohio.

On 15 December 1848, if the family genealogy is right, he married Nancy Roush. The record side agrees with everything around the claim: in 1850 the census of Mason County, Virginia, shows George, thirty-one, Nancy, eighteen, and an infant daughter, Susan M.; in 1860 the enumerator spelled the surname “Neoce” and the household contained a six-year-old Lewis J. No document outside the book actually states the marriage, and the Mason County marriage index of 1834-1945 has no George Nease in it at all.

He farmed. He and Nancy raised a family in Graham District, and their son Lewis married Martha Love in 1877 and gave the county his own daughter in marriage to a Roush twenty years later.

George Nease died on 21 November 1899 in Mason County - the date the 1928 Roush book gives him to the day - and his widow Nancy signed as the informant, written into the register as “Nancie Nease, wife.” It is the one year the county's death register asked for the dead person's parents, and the clerk wrote “Samuel and Catherine Nease.” That reading does not sit easily with the only Nease couple of that generation in the 1850 census of the county, Emanuel and Catharine, and the question is still open.

He lies at Broad Run. His marker is a small modern block cut GEORGE NEASE 1818 - 1898 - a year adrift at each end from the register and from the book alike.

125.s:
Nancy Roush was born on 16 February 1832, by the family's own book the eleventh child of Anthony Roush and his first wife Elizabeth Rickard. Hers is one of the rungs in this tree that rests on that book alone.

She married George Nease on 15 December 1848, when she was sixteen. The 1850 census finds her eighteen years old with an infant daughter, Susan M., in a Mason County household headed by George, thirty-one. Her son Lewis was born in November 1854, and in 1860 he is six years old in a household the enumerator wrote down as “Neoce.”

In November 1899 she buried her husband and gave the county the information herself; the clerk entered her as “Nancie Nease, wife.” She lived another fourteen years as a widow.

She died on 21 July 1913. The Mason County register puts her age at eighty-one years, five months and five days - which works back to 16 February 1832 exactly, so somebody in that house still had her birthday written down eighty-one years on. Her death was entered twice in the same book, three lines apart: once by the undertaker on the 21st, and once by Dr. D. A. Sayre, who put it at the 1st of July and gave congestion of the lungs. The archivist's own pencil note on the duplicate reads “Probably duplicate.”

She is buried at Broad Run beside George, under a small modern marker cut NANCY NEASE 1828 - 1911. And there is one thing worth saying plainly about her: in February 1897 her granddaughter Bertha Nease married John G. Roush of Mason County, and in doing so married straight back into Nancy's own birth family.

248.s:
His name is written two ways, and the records do not agree.

When George Nease died in Mason County on 21 November 1899, the clerk filled in the parents' column - one of the few years the county's register asked for it - and wrote “Samuel and Catherine Nease.” But the 1850 census of Mason County, Virginia, has only one Nease couple of that generation in it: EMANUEL NEASE, a farmer born about 1792 in Virginia, and CATHARINE, born about 1797, living in the dwelling immediately after Jacob M. Roush. Their sons George and Levi A. are documented brothers. Emanuel was dead by 1870, when Catharine was keeping her own house in Graham District with a grandson of eighteen who “works on farm.”

A broken stone at Union Cemetery, New Haven, appears to name Catharine as the wife of an Emanuel Nease, but the photograph is too worn to carry that weight. Anthony Roush was born on 23 January 1792 in Shenandoah County, Virginia, near Solomon's Church, and was baptised there on 18 March 1792 with Michael Levermore standing sponsor. He was the seventh child of Henry Roush and his wife Dorothy - a Henry who, at twenty-three, had served eighty-eight days as a private in Captain John Tipton's company and been paid off at Romney in October 1775, and for whom his younger brother Jonas later stood substitute.

The family came down into the Ohio Valley, and Anthony with them. On 11 July 1812, when he was twenty, his father deeded him seventy-five acres for three hundred dollars. He married first Elizabeth Rickard, described in the family record as “a sister to the Rickard brothers,” about 1810, and after her a second wife, Catherine Hoffman. His children were set down in a numbered sequence, and Nancy, born on 16 February 1832, was the eleventh of them; she married George Nease in 1848 and is the ancestor of this line.

He probably fell heir to a share of his father's portion of the six-thousand-acre estate in Graham District, Mason County - land that had been fought over in the courts since a petition of 1806.

He lies, the family book says, in the Rickard cemetery in the White Church community of Mason County, under a small stone with no epitaph. No photograph of it has been found and he has no memorial on Find a Grave.

500.s:
Henry Roush was born in 1752 in Shenandoah County, Virginia, the fourth son in the list of John Adam and Susannah Roush’s children; the family’s own historian introduces him as “one of the oldest of the children of John and Susannah Roush.”

He was twenty-three when the war began, and he was in it from the first season. A Virginia State Library archivist certified the record in 1926 from the rolls of companies paid off at Romney: Henry Rouse (Roush) served as a private in Captain John Tipton’s company for eighty-eight days and was paid £6-12s-0d on a receipt dated 25 October 1775. In the summer of 1781 he was drafted again and his younger brother Jonas went in his place — a fact that survives because Jonas swore to it in his own pension application fifty years later. The Daughters of the American Revolution hold a patriot record, A098977, for a Henry Roush born 1752 in Frederick County and died 26 October 1831 in Meigs County, Ohio, which matches him in birth year, death date and death place.

He married Dorothea, and they raised ten children in Shenandoah County near Solomon’s Church — Michael, Christina, Henry Jr., Elizabeth, Susannah, Anthony, Dorothy, Eva and Balser among them. Anthony, born 23 January 1792, is the son through whom this family descends. In 1793 Henry put his hand to the Solomonburg church deed, signing “HENRICH ROUSH” in German on the same page where his wife made her mark; it is why the association that later marked his grave called him the Church Builder.

He followed the Roush migration down the Ohio to Letart Falls in Meigs County, and he settled his children on land as he went: a deed to Henry Jr. in October 1805, seventy-five acres to Anthony for three hundred dollars in July 1812, and in June 1817 land to his son Balser and to his daughters Susanna Linscott and Catharine “for natural love and affection.”

He died on 26 October 1831, aged seventy-nine, and lies in Plants Cemetery above the river at Plants, Meigs County, Ohio. The little stone the 1928 compilers found — “Henry Roush died October 26, 1831, aged 79 years” — has been joined by a granite block carrying a plaque from his descendants: “HENRY ROUSH 1752–1831, ‘The Church Builder’, One of nine brothers who fought in the Revolutionary War, Erected by His Descendants.” A bronze tablet at its foot reads “HENRY ROUSH / PVT CAPT TIPTON’S CO / VA STATE TRP / REVOLUTIONARY WAR / 1752–1831.” The markers were dedicated by the Sons of the American Revolution at the Roush family’s annual meeting on 19 August 1933, on the same afternoon as his brother George’s, a few miles down the Ohio.

Dorothea — Dorothy in the records her neighbours wrote, Dolly in the family — was the wife of Henry Roush Sr. Her surname has never been recovered. The 1928 family historian wrote it once as “Dorothea Nease (?)”, with his own question mark, and once, a few hundred pages later, as plain “Dorothy (Nease) Roush”; the Daughters of the American Revolution’s record for her husband gives her as Dorothea Nehs. None of it is yet a record of her birth.

She married Henry about 1777 and bore ten children in Shenandoah County — Michael, Christina, Henry, Elizabeth, Susannah, Anthony, Dorothy, Eva, Balser. Anthony, born in January 1792, carries this line. In 1793 she witnessed the Solomonburg church deed: her husband signed his name in German, and she signed “DOROTHY ROUSH (her mark)” on the same page.

She went with the family down the Ohio to Letart Falls, and she is believed to have died about the same time as Henry, in 1831. She lies in Plants Cemetery in Meigs County beside him. 290.s:
He was, if his family's own story is true, a small boy found alive on the North Carolina coast sometime between 1735 and 1745 after a shipwreck. He could tell them only that his name was Billie Pigford and that he had sailed from England with his parents, who were not found. A Dutch family took him in. In March 1740 or 1741 the county court dealt with him formally: Rebecca Perry petitioned to be allowed to keep the boy herself, and the court bound him instead to Benjamin Fussell. He was called Lost Billie for the rest of his life, and his great-granddaughter was still telling the story in 1896.

Whatever he came from, he ended a landowner on both banks of Sill's Creek, in the Penderlea country where New Hanover County runs up against Duplin. In 1790 his was the only Pigford household in the whole state. He married a woman named Sarah, remembered in the family only as “a woman of Dutch descent,” and they raised a large family — William, Jacob, Timothy, Solomon, Edward, Martha and Margaret, and, in one transcription of his will, a daughter who had married into the Aiken or Eakins family.

On 27 March 1801 he had his will written out. It gives Sarah all the household furniture and moveable effects and everything else not otherwise left, “to be by her disposed of amongst her children as she may think proper,” together with the plantation he lived on and all the land east of Sill's Creek for the term of her life. Timothy got the land on the west side of the creek. Solomon got the home place after his mother's death — and in return was bound to help his brother Timothy build “a dwelling house, kitchen, corn crib, smoke house, dairy, and in clearing ten acres of land.” To the rest of the children he left one shilling sterling each. He could not sign it. The paper ends “William X Pigford (his mark),” witnessed by William Jones.

He died before March 1803, when the New Hanover Court of Pleas and Quarter Sessions proved the will — and had to do it the slow way, taking the oath of William Bloodworth that the handwriting of the subscribing witness was genuinely his. Both the Sons and the Daughters of the American Revolution carry him as a patriot for signing a 1779 petition from the inhabitants of New Hanover, Duplin and Bladen counties asking that the county be divided so that militiamen could reach their musters; but nobody in this research has yet seen a Pigford name on that sheet, and in 1779 there were two William Pigfords in the county, father and son. He and Sarah lie somewhere in the Penderlea area in unmarked graves.

291.s:
Sarah was the wife of William “Lost Billie” Pigford of Sill's Creek, and she is one of those women the surviving record touches exactly once.

Her husband's will of 27 March 1801 begins with her: “First; I give and bequeath to Sarah, my dearly beloved wife, all my household furniture, moveable effects and all other of my estate… to be by her disposed of amongst her children as she may think proper; and also the plantation whereon I now live, with all the improvements thereon; and all the land I possess adjoining the east side of Sill's Creek, for the term of her life.” She was named executrix. Her son Solomon was to have the home place only after her death, and until then was under orders to help his brother Timothy put up a house.

They had a large family — William, Jacob, Timothy, Solomon, Edward, Martha, Margaret, and the daughter the family book's version of the will calls Elizabeth Aiken. Family tradition set down about 1896 says only that Lost Billie “married a woman of Dutch descent.”

Her own surname was never written down anywhere that survives. The family's historian searched the marriage records of both New Hanover and Duplin counties looking for it and wrote in 1967 that “her family name continues to be beyond the reach of this recorder.” The “Sarah Fussell” that circulates online is a mistake: Fussell was the man her husband was bound to as a boy, not her father. She is believed to lie in an unmarked grave in the Penderlea area, near the old Pigford burying ground.
