108.s:
Elias Lamb was born on 24 September 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, about sixteen miles north of Asheboro — his own obituary says so, and so does the county biographical volume of 1888 that gave him a sketch in his old age. He was the son of Joseph and Lydia (Adamson) Lamb, Quakers. In April 1829, when he was fourteen, his parents took the family out of North Carolina and settled in Clay Township, Wayne County, Indiana, where they farmed until they died. Nine children had been born to them; seven grew up.

He was reared on his father’s farm and learned the carpenter’s trade, which he worked at alongside farming all his life. On 23 March 1837 he married Susannah Bish at the house of her father, John Bish, in Clay Township. When the wedding was paid for he took stock of what he owned and found “a few carpenter tools and $20. in money”; her dowry was about twenty-five dollars’ worth of goods, including a heifer calf. They spent part of the twenty dollars on simple furniture and began housekeeping on his father’s farm on 7 June 1837. In April 1839 they bought a farm adjoining it; that September they swapped farms and moved three-quarters of a mile south, and there they stayed thirty-one years. In 1841 he and Susannah left the Society of Friends and united by letter with the United Brethren church.

Ten children were born to them, of whom one, an infant son, died in June 1844. In politics he was a Free-Soiler until 1856 — “he believed it wrong for one man to enslave his fellow man,” as the account of his golden wedding put it — and then a Republican from the year Frémont ran.

In November 1870 they sold up and bought the Montgomery farm near Perrysville, in Vermillion County; in March 1873 a farm a mile and a half north-west of Newport; and on 3 March 1887 the house in Newport where they spent their last years. On the night of 12 October 1883 burglars broke into the Newport house and beat Elias badly — one eye closed, a bullet grazing Susannah’s head and splitting her ear — until he reached the yard bell-rope and rang the alarm. He never fully recovered from it.

Their golden wedding fell on 23 March 1887. Fifty-eight relatives and friends came; a neighbour, M. G. Rhoads, read out a history of the two old people; two ministers performed the marriage ceremony over again; a senator made some remarks; and then everyone went in to a sumptuous dinner. The presents were listed in the paper down to a china catsup mug and a silver butter knife. They counted that day nine living children, twenty-nine grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren — forty-eight in all, most of them in the room.

The Wayne County clerk issued their marriage licence on 22 March 1837; Richard Jobes, Justice of the Peace, joined them the next day and filed his return in the clerk's office on 8 April, certifying that he had married "Elias Lamb and Susannah Bish of lawful age".

He took sick one Monday in late August 1890 and died at four o’clock on the Sunday morning, 31 August — the Newport Hoosier State printed a column headed “Death of Elias Lamb” the following Wednesday — within a month of his seventy-sixth birthday. The funeral was preached at the United Brethren church by his pastor, the Rev. R. B. Van Allen, and “his remains were followed to the Thomas cemetery by a large concourse of relatives” — the burying ground at Newport, where his stone still stands, cut ELIAS LAMB DIED AUG. 30 1890 AGED 76 YEARS.

109.s:
Susannah Bish was born on 17 November 1818 in Fairfield County, Ohio, about eighteen miles east of Columbus, a daughter of John and Ann Elizabeth Bish — the county biographical volume of 1888 names her parents, and the newspaper account of her golden wedding the year before gives her birthplace to the mile. She was brought up among Lutherans, had what the newspapers of her old age politely called “a very limited education in the old fashioned ‘deestrict schools’,” and learned, in the phrasing of the same account, “the various mysteries of house keeping.” In 1836, by the same 1888 account, she came with her parents to Wayne County, Indiana.

On 23 March 1837, four months past her eighteenth birthday, she married Elias Lamb at her father’s house in Clay Township. Her dowry to the “joint stock company” was about twenty-five dollars’ worth of goods, including a heifer calf. They kept house first on his father’s farm, then on farms of their own three-quarters of a mile away, for thirty-one years. Ten children were born to her; one, an infant son, died in June 1844. In 1841 she and Elias left the Society of Friends — his people’s church, not hers — and joined the United Brethren by letter.

The family moved to Vermillion County in November 1870, and in 1887 into a house in Newport. Four years before that, on the night of 12 October 1883, burglars broke in on them; Elias was badly beaten and a bullet grazed Susannah’s head and split her ear. Their golden wedding, on 23 March 1887, drew fifty-eight relatives and friends, two ministers to perform the ceremony over again, and a table of presents; they counted forty-eight descendants, most of them present.

She outlived Elias by eighteen years. In her last years she made her home with her son-in-law Levi S. Clendenning near Sugar Grove, Illinois, and she died there at three o’clock on the morning of Wednesday 8 April 1908, at ninety. Eight of her children survived her. The funeral was held in the church at Sugar Grove the next morning, and she was brought back to Indiana and buried beside Elias in the Thomas burying ground at Newport, under a stone that says only SUSANNAH, wife of E. LAMB.

110.s:
Milo Bailey is a candidate, not yet an ancestor. He was the son of John Bailey, a Virginian who came out of Kentucky about 1810 to Richmond, Indiana, moved on to Perry Township and then, in 1859, to Clay Township in Wayne County, where — as the county historian put it in 1872 — “his son Milo resides”; John Bailey died in 1863, aged seventy-two. The same page of that history lists “Ithamar Lamb, Milo Bailey, and Lewis Strickler” living on one tract of school land in Clay Township, which is to say that the Baileys and the Lambs were neighbours on the ground.

That neighbourliness is the reason his name is on this chart. In one winter, two Lamb brothers married two Bailey women out of the same township: Azel E. Lamb and Sarah Ann Bailey in December 1859, and Irvin R. Lamb and Melissa J. Bailey in March 1860. Melissa was born in Wayne County on 24 July 1844, so her father was a Wayne County Bailey of exactly Milo’s generation and place. But no record found so far names Milo Bailey’s daughters, and until one does the connection is a reconstruction rather than a fact. A caution runs with it: an unrelated Milo Lamb, of the other North Carolina Lamb family in the same county, sits in the same records and has been mistaken for him before.

216.s:
Joseph Lamb was born in North Carolina about 1782 — the county historian says he died in 1855 “at the age of 73.” The family was living in Randolph County, about sixteen miles north of Asheboro, in 1814, when his son Elias was born there. He married Lydia Adamson — the 1806 bond is made out for “Lidya Addison,” with her brother Samuel Adamson standing bondsman — and they were members of the Society of Friends. Nine children were born to them, of whom seven grew up: Ezekiel, Esther, Smith, Elias, Mournen, Joseph and Ithamar.

In April 1829 he took the family out of North Carolina for Indiana — the ordinary Quaker departure from the slaveholding South — and settled in Clay Township, Wayne County, on land adjoining Perry Township that a widow, Eve Shoemaker, had first taken up in 1821. He farmed there for the rest of his life, and his sons and his wife’s brother settled around him: when the Clay Township school section was sold in 1832 the buyers included Samuel Adamson, and his son Ithamar was living on it forty years later.

Lydia died first — in 1844 by his son Elias’s account, though other records say 1837. Joseph died on 29 July 1855, aged seventy-three, and lies in Sugar Grove Cemetery in Wayne County under a small marble stone, weathered but still readable: JOSEPH LAMB DIED 29th Day of the July of year 1855.

217.s:
Lydia Adamson married Joseph Lamb in North Carolina in November 1806; the marriage bond was made out for “Lidya Addison,” and her brother Samuel Adamson stood bondsman — he later married Joseph’s sister Naomi, so two Adamsons married two Lambs. They were Quakers. Nine children were born to them, of whom seven lived to grow up, among them Elias, through whom this line descends.

In April 1829 she came north with her husband and children to Wayne County, Indiana, and settled in Clay Township; her brother Samuel was one of the buyers when the township school section was sold in 1832. She did not live to be old in Indiana. Her son Elias’s biographical sketch of 1888 says his mother died in 1844. That 1888 sketch is the only source that names her at all: the earlier county history of 1872, which lists her husband and all seven of their surviving children, never mentions his wife by name. She was the only one of the four Lambs and Bishes of her generation on this chart not to be given a stone, or at least not one that survives.

218.s:
John Bish was of Fairfield County, Ohio — his daughter Susannah was born there in November 1818, “about 18 miles east of Columbus.” He and his wife raised ten children to maturity.

In 1836 he brought the family to Wayne County, Indiana, and settled in Clay Township. The following March his daughter Susannah was married to Elias Lamb at his own house — the newspaper account of the couple’s golden wedding, fifty years later, still gave the address as “the residence of John Bish, the bride’s father, in Clay township.” The Bishes lived in Wayne County many years. Later they removed to Miami County, Indiana, where his wife died; afterwards he came back to Wayne County and died on the old homestead — by his stone, on 20 August 1866. He lies in Sugar Grove Cemetery, Row 9 of the north section, in the same burying ground as Joseph Lamb. The inscription has almost gone: the name is a shadow, but “AUG. 20, 1866” and “AGED” can still be made out.

A John Bish married an Anne Campbell in Rockingham County, Virginia, in November 1810; whether that John Bish is this one has not been established.

This identification still rests on the single 1888 biographical sketch of his son-in-law Elias, now supported by the memorial and the stone.

6156.s:
William Davis was born about 1617 and lived at Roxbury, Massachusetts, where he was made a freeman in 1673. His children appear in the Roxbury church records in a single contemporary entry of 1649, when the congregation brought in the children of a newly admitted member: “John Davis, Samuel Davis, Joseph Davis — Children of William Davis whose wife was admitted & so brought her children to p'take of this blessed ordinance.” Samuel, born 21 February 1645, is the son through whom this family descends; the same church book later records him leaving — “Samuel Davis dismissed to North-Hampton” — when he went west up the Connecticut valley.

He married twice. His first wife was Elizabeth, who died or was buried on 4 May 1658. He married second, that October, Alice Thorp, and the Roxbury clerk recorded her end in one unsparing line: “Alice wife of William Davis who dyed in child birth undelivered.” Savage thought him probably a brother of Tobias Davis of the same town — a household that has to be kept carefully separate from his, since it contained a Samuel too.

He made his will on 6 December 1683 and died three days later, on the 9th, aged about sixty-six. That Samuel of Northampton is the same boy named in the 1649 Roxbury entry is the one join in this family that rests on reasoning rather than on a document; Savage himself hedged it with a “perhaps”, and the node is graded accordingly.

12301.s:
Elizabeth was the wife of William Peck, the London merchant who became deacon of the First Church at New Haven. They were married in London, and in 1637 she crossed to New England with him and their young son Jeremiah on the Hector, in the company that would found New Haven; the ship made Boston on 26 June. Their home lot in the new town was on George Street, and her husband's shop fronted on Church Street.

All four of William Peck's children were hers — Jeremiah, John, Joseph and Elizabeth — and they are the four named in his will. John, born about 1638, is the son in this line. She died on 5 December 1683, away from home: she was visiting her son at Lyme, forty miles down the coast, when she died. Eleven years later her husband died in the same place, at their son Joseph's house.

She lies in New Haven. Her grave was on the Old Green with the rest of the founding generation and was moved to Grove Street Cemetery in 1821, where a small rough stone against the north wall carries nothing but a date and two initials: 1683, and under it E P. Her maiden name was never written down by anyone who knew it.

12302.s:
John Moss was at New Haven by 1639, in the first years of the colony, and is one of the three founding names — with Doolittle and Peck — that between them made Wallingford. He served the older town first: he was one of the commissioners New Haven chose to settle its disputed boundary with Branford, and he appears in the colony's records through the 1640s, 1650s and 1660s as a trainband corporal, representative and deputy. In 1670, when Wallingford was incorporated, he moved inland with the rest, and the town's historian, writing in 1870, called him flatly “the ancestor of all who bear the name in these parts.”

He and his wife had eleven children baptized at New Haven between 1640 and 1655. Among them were Mary, baptized 11 April 1647, who married John Peck in 1664 and is the one in this line; Abigail, who married Abraham Doolittle as his second wife; and a second John, born 1650, whose existence has confused genealogists ever since.

He died in 1707, and both the stone over him and every published account agree on the striking thing about him: he was said to be 103. Savage, who printed the figure in 1860, added “perhaps with slight exagg., yet thought to be the oldest that ever died in Connecticut” — and the figure traces back to a centennial sermon preached in 1770, sixty-three years after the funeral, so it should be carried with the same raised eyebrow. His stone stands in the Center Street Cemetery at Wallingford, a heart cut into its face and inside the heart: “Mr John Moss, born 1604, died 1707, Æ 103.”

1000.s:
John Adam Roush — Johannes Adam Rausch — was born in 1711 in the Palatinate, and the family has always said Darmstadt. He crossed to Philadelphia in the closing months of 1736 and took the oath of fidelity there; the tradition the family carried into the twentieth century was that he and two companions, forbidden to emigrate, were hidden inside hogsheads by a friendly cooper, loaded aboard, and let out at sea. He landed too poor to pay his passage, hired himself out near Philadelphia, stayed on past his term because he was paid unusually well, and then married and went down the Shenandoah Valley.

He settled on Mill Creek in what was then Frederick County, later Dunmore and then Shenandoah, and farmed it; the family says he also kept a mill and a tannery. His wife was Susannah. In 1773 a grant of four hundred acres on Mill Creek was made “to him and his wife Susannah” — the one period land record that names them both. By then he had been in the valley more than thirty years and had raised a large family: seven sons who can be documented one by one — Philip, John, Jacob, Henry, Daniel, George and Jonas — and the daughters Mary Magdalene, Eleanor and Elizabeth. The family’s own voice says nine sons, and its own table says seven; the seven are the ones the wills and the pension files agree on.

Every one of those sons went into the Revolution, and so, in his sixties, did he: the Library of Virginia holds the Shenandoah County impressed-property claim certificate, number 2453, for supplies he furnished the army between 1780 and 1783. The Daughters of the American Revolution recognise him for it as Patriot Ancestor A098982. One son was a captain with two of his brothers in the ranks; two of them substituted for each other; one of them witnessed another’s pension application fifty years later.

He died on 19 October 1786 near New Market in Shenandoah County and was buried at the Old Pine Church. His gravestone survives — a rough slab cut in German by someone who spelled by ear — and it is now kept upright under glass at St Mary’s Pine Church Cemetery at Mount Jackson, where the old burying ground’s stones were moved in 1868. It reads: ANO 1711 GEBOHREN JOHANNES RAUSCH GESTORBEN DEN 19 OCTOBER 1786. The Adam had already dropped out of his name. Susannah outlived him by ten years and lies beside him in a grave that was never marked. In 1936, on the two hundredth anniversary of his crossing, the Roush and Allied Families Association raised a monument over the two of them that names their children one by one and reckons their descendants, living and dead, at about forty thousand American citizens.

This is the third of the paths on Alec’s chart that end at this one man, and it comes through his son Henry Roush Sr., the Church Builder of Plants Cemetery. The family’s history introduces Henry as “one of the oldest of the children of John and Susannah Roush,” and the 1936 monument carves his name among the children; as with George and Jonas, the link is as well attested as a single family tradition can make it, and awaits his father’s 1786 Shenandoah County probate to become a record.

The Rickard patriarch came out of Germany to Maryland, and from Maryland his family moved on to Mason County in what is now West Virginia. Four of his sons — Michael, Jacob, John and Joseph — made that second move together, and the Rickards of that county descend from them. Two daughters, Elizabeth and Susannah, married into the Roush family: Elizabeth to Anthony Roush about 1810, Susannah to Lewis Roush, while Michael Rickard married their sister-in-law Mary Roush in 1816 — three marriages binding the two families in both directions.

His name is lost. The small burying ground at White Church in Mason County, where his son-in-law Anthony Roush lies under a stone with no epitaph, is the likeliest place a name still survives.

102.s:
John Fletcher is known from one document. When his daughter Mary Elizabeth died at East Ellen, Vigo County, Indiana, on 16 April 1934, the certificate named her father as John Fletcher and her mother as Sarah Wallace. Nothing else so far found says the two of them belonged to each other.

Where he was born is in dispute, and the dispute is his daughter's own. In 1880, enumerated as a servant at Clinton, she gave her father's birthplace as Pennsylvania; in 1900, keeping her own house in Terre Haute, she gave it as Indiana. Both answers are hers and twenty years apart, and no Fletcher record has yet been found to decide between them.

962.s:
Michael Zerckel — the name is written Zirkle, Zerkel, Zerchel, Sircle, Circle and Zickel in the records, and twice differently on his own family’s gravestones — came south with the Zirkle brothers from Pennsylvania into the Shenandoah Valley. His parents were Ludwig Zirkle and Eve; a deed of 1776 by which he and his wife Catherine sold land in Dunmore County describes fifty-four acres “patented to my mother, Eve Sircle, now deceased … and descended to Michael as eldest son and heir of Eve.”

He settled near Forestville, on Holman’s Creek, in the country that became Shenandoah County, in a neighbourhood where the Zirkles, the Neases and the Roushes lived within a few miles of each other and married one another for a century. His brother Andrew built the stone mill at Quicksburg that still stands. In 1776 Michael’s own name appears on a list of the Dunmore County militia under Captain Jacob Holman — the same captain under whom Henry Roush had served the year before.

He married Catharine, and they had fourteen children. The eldest, Catharine, married George Roush; another daughter, Mary, born 20 June 1770, married Henry Nease in June 1791, and the marriage papers carry her father’s consent signed “Michel Corckel”; his son Henry followed the Roushes and the Neases down the Ohio to the Graham District of Mason County and founded the Zirkle family there. His children’s marriages are a large part of why the Roush, Nease and Zirkle families are braided together in Alec’s tree in three separate places.

A cracked slab in the Zerchel–Nehs burying ground, on the east bank of Holman’s Creek northeast of Forestville, is very probably his — though it should be said in the same breath that the photographs of it are photographs of older prints rather than of the stone itself, that the memorial which carries them is openly unsure which of two graveyards holds him, and that the woman buried beside him raises a problem nobody has yet settled: her stone says she was born in July 1747, which would make her thirteen to fifteen when Michael’s eldest daughter was born on the reconstruction this project adopted, and sixteen on the 1928 book’s printed date of 14 August 1763 — so either the book’s date is right and she was a very young mother, or the alternative nobody has excluded is true and Cadarina was Michael’s second wife, not the mother of the Catharine who married George Roush. The slab is cut in German, with a Pennsylvania-German compass star at its head, and it reads HIR RUET MICHAEL ZICKEL IST GEBOREN DEN 29 JANER 1735 UND GESTORBEN DEN 2 OCTOBER 1811 UND SEIN ALTER WAR 76 JAR 8 MO 3 DA — born 29 January 1735, died 2 October 1811, aged seventy-six years, eight months and three days. What identifies it as his is the name, the Zirkle family’s own graveyard in his own neighbourhood, and the matching stone beside it. The ground has long been unfenced. “The old graveyard used to have a good many tombstones in it,” a Forestville man wrote shortly before his own death, “but for many years it has been unfenced. Now cattle graze over the bodies of our forefathers, most of the tombstones have disappeared.”

That third marriage closed a circle. Her son John Catlin had married Mary Baldwin, Joseph's daughter, in 1662; so her son's wife became her stepdaughter, and Mary Baldwin found herself married to the son of her own stepmother. The two families interlock twice in a single generation.

She came to Deerfield's country as a widow with her boy — the compilers describe her arriving “with her son John as Widow Catlin” — and she was probably the sister of Lawrence Ward of New Haven, Branford and Newark, which is likely how the family came to be in Newark at all. 6166.s:
Joseph Baldwin was among the first settlers of Milford, Connecticut, in 1639, one of three brothers who came over together and were given home lots there after a first stop at New Haven. He married Hannah, who joined the Milford church on 23 June 1644, when their first four children were all baptized at once; Mary, who married John Catlin, was one of the four. Hannah died in 1661, and about 1663 Joseph moved north to Hadley in Massachusetts, where he was made a freeman in 1666. He married twice more: Isabella, the widow of the elder John Catlin and afterwards of James Northam, who died in 1676; and Elizabeth, the widow of Luke Hitchcock and then of William Warriner.

On 20 December 1680 he made his will, and its first words say exactly where he was and how he felt: “In the Name of God Amen the twentieth day of december, One thousand Six hundred and eighty, I Joseph Baldwin Senr of Hadley in the Countie of Hampshire within the Colony of the Massachusetts: being together with old age and of life now Sick and weake of body but of good and perfect Memory, thanks and praise be to Almighty God for it.” He left his wife the use of his house and land at Hadley for her life, excepting the half of his lands he had already made over to his son Joseph; the other half, with the houses and the moveables, went to that son. Then he went through the daughters one by one — five pounds to his “Loveing Daughter Hanah Hull” and five pounds to her daughter Mary Hull when she should reach eighteen; forty shillings to “my Daughter Mary Cattlin”; a legacy to Elizabeth Warriner; something to the children of his daughter Sarah Bartlett, already dead; five pounds each to Martha Hawks and Hannah Hawks — and confirmed to his three sons Benjamin, Jonathan and David the gifts he had made them out of his Milford lands. He signed it before two witnesses, Chiliab Smith, who made his mark, and Samuel Partrigg.

Nearly four years later, on 30 October 1684, he had the will read over to him again and ratified it with some further provisos, appointing his grandson Joseph Baldwin junior his sole executor in place of the son, who had died. He lived only a few days more. The probate clerk headed the inventory “An Inventory of the Estate of Joseph Baldwin Senr who deceased November 3d, 1684, taken this Novembr 8th 1684 by Lt Smith, Chilliab Smith and S. Partrigg” — a day later than the 2 November that the printed genealogies give him. It came to £165 8s 7d, of which his house, barn and home lot at Hadley were valued at £50 and ten acres of land at £45, with debts of £10 14s 3d, leaving a net estate of £154 14s 4d. In the town he had helped to found at the other end of the colony, Milford set a granite boulder by the Wepawaug bridge among its founders' memorials: JOSEPH BALDWIN, OBIT 1690, HANNAH HIS WIFE. The date on it is wrong by six years, and his own probate file says so.

6167.s:
Hannah was the first wife of Joseph Baldwin, one of the first settlers of Milford, Connecticut. She joined the Milford church on 23 June 1644, and on that same day their first four children were baptized together — among them Mary, whose baptism is dated to that day and who grew up to marry John Catlin. Four sons and five daughters are credited to the marriage in all.

She died in 1661 at Milford, and her husband left the next year for Hadley in Massachusetts and married twice more. Nothing of her own origins is established: her Christian name comes from a single line in a compiled genealogy, and the surname Whitlock, and a wedding at High Wycombe in Buckinghamshire in November 1636, are claims made on her behalf by later family writers without a citation. Milford remembers her the way the colony usually did. On the founders' boulder by the Wepawaug bridge her husband's name is cut in full, and under it: HANNAH HIS WIFE.

William Payne, if the reconstruction holds, was born about 1791 in Virginia and was living in Lauderdale County, Mississippi by the 1840s. The 1850 census shows him there at fifty-nine, heading a household of eleven: his wife Mary, thirty, born in North Carolina; four boys born in North Carolina who carried the Eakens surname and were orphans in his care — John W., sixteen, James O., fourteen, Lewis T., twelve, and George W., ten; four younger children born in Mississippi, the eldest of them Sarah H., aged eight; and an eighteen-year-old named Martha Moore.

He was, in short, a Virginian in Mississippi raising another family's orphaned sons alongside his own young children — and in May 1861 a daughter of that house married Joel W. Eakins, of the very family whose boys he had raised.

Whether Sarah Hudson Payne was his daughter or his stepdaughter is exactly what is not settled, and it is why he sits on this chart as a candidate rather than a certainty. The enumerator's ditto marks can be read two ways: as a man with a second family of his own, or as the stepfather of all eight children by a first husband of Mary's named Eakens. 162.s:
Daniel Jones was born about 1806 in North Carolina and was almost certainly the father of Sarah Ann Jones, who married Henry H. Stephens. He belonged to a North Carolina Jones sibling set — an undated power of attorney names “Daniel Jones, Elijah Jones, Sarah… and Absalom Price” acting over the estate of “our dec’d Brother Joel Jones” of Sumter County, Alabama. Joel had gone out to Alabama ahead of them and died there about 1843; Daniel went too.

He was in Sumter County and of full age by 1839, when he stood surety on a $2,200 Orphans’ Court guardianship bond. The 1850 census finds him at dwelling 1186 — Daniel Jones, forty-four, born North Carolina; Susan, thirty-five, born North Carolina; and Elizabeth 13, James 12, Margaret 10 and Mary 6, all born in Alabama. The Alabama births of the younger children put the family’s arrival in the state in the middle 1830s. Two doors up the road lived Henry Stephens with Daniel’s eldest daughter as his wife, and six houses beyond that Henry’s father Moore.

Moore Stephens was more than a neighbour. In March and April 1853 the two men, with Jesse Thomas, were jointly bound for $1,200 and then $2,800 on the administration of Thomas Fowler’s estate, and in January 1854 for $5,000 on the guardianship of Willis Thomas’s two small children. In October 1854, after Sarah’s death, Henry Stephens married Daniel’s second daughter Elizabeth.

He was dead by the last day of 1869, when the Sumter County probate court appointed Henry Stephens guardian of three Stephens boys, each described as “a minor heir of Daniel Jones deceased.” Grandsons can only inherit that way through a parent who has already died, and the dead parent is Sarah. The identification of Daniel as her father rests on that convergence rather than on any document that calls her his daughter, and it is recorded here as probable, not proved.

78.s:
Ben Simmons — B. A. Simmons on his gravestone, Benjamin Asbury Simmons in his family's own reckoning — was born on 26 October 1818 in Georgia — the censuses round it to about 1819 — and came as a young man with his people into Sumter County, Alabama. He married Adeline on 11 May 1847, when he was twenty-eight and she was seventeen.

Their children's birthplaces trace a family moving back and forth along the state line: Alabama in the late 1840s, Mississippi in the early 1850s, Alabama again by the end of that decade. The 1870 census finds him at Cuba as “Benj A Simons,” with Adline and six children in the house. He was still living at Cuba in 1880, and the census of that year — the first that stated outright how the people in a household were related — lists him as father of the household, Adline as mother, and among the daughters “Dellon, 16.” That one page is what gives Alec's line its Simmons parentage, and because it is a single page the link is held as probable rather than proven. Whichever of his daughters the descent runs through — two Simmons sisters married the same Swain man, twenty-two months apart — the parents are the same couple.

A will recorded in the same county very probably names him: Robert Simmons of Sumter County, Alabama, signed his will on 6 March 1845, and when it was probated on 15 November 1855 its fifth item read, 'I hereby appoint my Son Benjamin Asbury Simmons my executor to this my last will and testament.' Our Ben's own stone calls him B. A. Simmons. The same will shows the household's care for its daughters: their share was granted 'to them and the heirs of their bodies; and not to be subject to the debts of their husbands.'

He registered to vote at Cuba on 3 July 1875, entry 64 of the Sumter County book, and unlike most of the page he wrote his own name in a strong, practised hand. The registrar's remarks column gives his living in three words: “Mill & Farm.”

He ended his life just across the line at Kewanee, in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, and died there on 6 April 1894, aged seventy-five. His marble headstone in the churchyard at Salem Baptist, carved with two clasped hands, reads B. A. SIMMONS, HUSBAND OF ADALINE SIMMONS, BORN OCT. 26, 1818, DIED APRIL 6, 1894.

79.s:
Adeline was born on 7 October 1829. The censuses disagree about where — Florida in 1870, Alabama in 1880. She married Ben Simmons on 11 May 1847, at seventeen, and bore nine or ten children over the next twenty years, the last about 1867 when she was thirty-seven. At least two did not live out infancy.

She kept house at Cuba, in Sumter County, through the war and after it, with a few years in Mississippi in the early 1850s that show up only in where her middle children were born. The 1870 census lists her as Adline, forty-one, with six children at home. The 1880 census — the first to state relationships outright — names her as mother of the household, with a sixteen-year-old daughter written “Dellon” among the children. That single page is what connects her to Alec's line, so the link is recorded as probable rather than proven.

Her husband died in April 1894. She outlived him by six years and died at Kewanee, in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, at seventy. Her tall marble headstone at Salem Baptist, beside his, was cut with a weeping-willow panel and reads IN MEMORY OF ADELINE, WIFE OF B. A. SIMMONS, BORN OCT. 7, 1829, DIED SEPT. 25, 1900, AGED 70 YRS. 11 MOS. 16 DAYS.

A sepia photograph of a seated woman in a dark dress with a lace collar and a tasselled ribbon at her throat, posted by a descendant and captioned as Adeline Peavy Simmons about 1875, is the only likeness of her known. The same descendant gives her maiden name as Peavy and her father as Levi Daniel Peavy; no record read here confirms it.

58.s:
Mathew Chalmers was a Scot who settled in Essex County, New Jersey. He is known from the parents’ columns of his daughter’s own marriage record: when Katharine Chalmers, thirty years old, a schoolteacher, born at Orange, New Jersey, married the Paterson silk manufacturer Harry B. Frost at Detroit on 10 June 1896, she gave the clerk her father as Mathew Chalmers and her mother as Ellen King. That one line of a Michigan register is the whole of his documentary existence in this family.

The rest comes at one remove. Two of his grandchildren were given their grandmothers’ maiden surnames as middle names — Katherine King Frost and Harry Bell Frost — which is how this family marked descent. Two more of his daughters, Mrs. Margaret Jordan and Miss Sarah Chalmers, were living at East Orange in 1932, when their sister died. And every census that records Katharine agrees that both her parents were born in Scotland: this is where the line crosses to the old country.

The 1870 census finds the whole family at Orange, in the second ward: Mathews Chalmers, forty-nine, born in Scotland, a retired dealer in stores with real estate worth $4,600 and $1,500 more in personal property; his wife Ellen, forty-four, also Scottish; and four New Jersey-born daughters — Ellen B., thirteen, Margaret, seven, Catharine, four, and Sarah, one. Katharine is the four-year-old, and Margaret and Sarah are the two sisters who outlived her in 1932. That household is what ties the family in this tree to a pair of graves at Rosedale Cemetery in Montclair, four miles from Orange, where a flat granite stone is cut MATTHEW CHALMERS, 1821–1893, beside his wife Ellen’s. He died in 1893, when Katharine was twenty-seven and teaching school.

Ellen King was born in Scotland and lived in Essex County, New Jersey. She is known from a single line of a Michigan marriage register: when her daughter Katharine married Harry B. Frost at Detroit on 10 June 1896, the bride gave her parents as Mathew Chalmers and Ellen King. Her name survives a second way, in a granddaughter — Katherine King Frost, born at Paterson in September 1898, was given her grandmother’s maiden surname as a middle name, which is how this family remembered its women.

Her daughter Katharine was born at Orange in January 1866 and became a schoolteacher; two other daughters, Mrs. Margaret Jordan and Miss Sarah Chalmers, were living at East Orange as late as 1932. Every census return that records Katharine agrees that both her parents were born in Scotland.

In 1870 she was forty-four, keeping house at Orange with her husband Mathews, a retired dealer in stores, and four daughters: Ellen B., thirteen, Margaret, seven, Catharine, four, and Sarah, a baby of one. She outlived him by eleven years. Her stone at Rosedale Cemetery, Montclair, is cut “Ellen B. King, wife of Matthew Chalmers, 1823–1904”. A Newark paper reported that she died at her home at 262 Centre Street, Orange, after a long illness; she had been a member of the North Orange Baptist Church, had lived in Orange more than half a century, and left four daughters. 34.s:
Henry Bradley lived in Barbour County, Alabama, and was dead before October 1891 — the month a county court appointed a guardian for his daughters Alice, fourteen, and Katie, twelve, recording that the minors had no father living. He is named as their father on both girls’ own death records, thirty-two years apart, one clerk writing him Henery; and that, with the silence in the guardianship, is all this family’s own papers hold of him.

In the summer of 1893 a Eufaula weekly printed, four times over, a notice from the Barbour County probate court that hands him back most of a family. His children’s guardian, a Bradley woman, had herself died, and her administratrix was settling the account of her guardianship of “the following named minor children of Henry Bradley, deceased, to-wit: Ida Parker, wife of Lee Parker; Annie Fortner, wife of W. J. Fortner; Henry Bradley, Alice Bradley and Katie Bradley.” Five children, two of them married off already, two of them still the wards the court had taken in two years before — and the phrase that matters, deceased, printed in his own county six years after he died.

He lies at Clayton City Cemetery, a few miles up the road from the farm, inside a rusting iron rail in the old part of the burying ground. His stone is a draped marble tablet carved with swags and a wreath, with the square and compasses of the Freemasons cut into its arch; the inscription reads HENRY BRADLEY, BORN APR. 25, 1836, DIED FEB. 27, 1887, though the figures are worn and those days of the month are the cemetery record’s reading rather than anything that can now be made out with certainty. He was fifty, and he died at Louisville — the Bells’ own village. Beside him, under the same rail, stands a second stone: ELVIRA, WIFE OF HENRY BRADLEY, who outlived him by four years.

He was clerk of the circuit court of Barbour County, Alabama, and he died in office. He was a Confederate soldier, and the wound he took in the war eventually killed him: on Monday 21 February 1887 erysipelas set into the old wound, congestion of the lungs, stomach and bowels followed, and he died at his home in Clayton at one o'clock on the morning of Sunday 27 February 1887. He was buried at Clayton at ten the next morning with Masonic honours. He left his family well provided for by the standards of the place and time - nine thousand dollars of life insurance, two thousand in the Knights of Honor, two thousand in the A.O.U.W. and five thousand in the New York Life. Petitions for a successor were circulating within two days of his funeral, and four men applied for the unexpired term before the governor appointed Capt. John C. McNab to the office in the second week of March.

He married Elvira Loveless on a licence issued at Barbour County on 18 December 1867, the probate judge signing the authorisation the following day. He was thirty-one; she was eighteen. In June 1880 the census found the family at Clayton, Beat 7, Barbour County: Henry Bradley, 44, farmer, born Alabama, both his parents born in South Carolina; Elvira, 31, keeping house, both her parents born in Alabama; and five children -- Ida J. 9, Anna V. 7, Henry R. 5, Alice 3, and Katie, seven months old.

He very probably appears, white and of age, on the Board of Registration's “Return of Qualified Voters” for Precinct No. 9 of Barbour County in July 1867 — line 97, “Bradly Henry”, oath book 5, page 468 — among the first voter rolls taken in Alabama under the Reconstruction acts, on a page where his neighbours are listed White and Colored alternately down the column. A tick in the ‘Check when Voting’ column says he came back and used it. The same precinct return carries a Bell and a Cox: the two families his daughters would marry into were registering at the same table.

So Alice was ten when he died, and the county took charge of her four years later, after her mother had gone too. And the grave argues with the way this family history has described him. A draped marble monument with a Masonic emblem, standing inside its own iron enclosure, is not a poor man’s grave.

35.s:
Her name was Elvira, and that much is cut in marble. She married Henry Bradley in Barbour County, Alabama, by about 1871, when their eldest daughter Ida was born; no marriage return has been found, and she had at least five children who grew up and three who did not. A court notice printed in the Eufaula paper in 1893 names the survivors: Ida, married to Lee Parker; Annie, married to W. J. Fortner; a son Henry; and the two youngest, Alice, born 8 October 1876, and Katie, born in 1879.

She lies at Clayton City Cemetery, beside her husband and inside the same iron rail. Her headstone is a draped marble tablet with a star cut into the arch and a worn verse on the plinth, and it gives her no surname at all — only ELVIRA, WIFE OF HENRY BRADLEY, born in August 1849 and dead in June 1891, the day-figures too worn now to be certain of. That last date answers a question this family could not: she was dead four months before the October 1891 order that made Alice and Katie wards of the Barbour County court. The order speaks only of the father because that is the form of words the clerk used. The girls had lost both parents.

She was forty-one, and she had buried at least three of her children already — one at birth in 1870, a boy of eleven in 1879, and a baby in 1884.

In January 1890, three years a widow, she bought Jake Fortner's house at Mt. Andrew and moved the family there; her daughter Annie was married in that house the following September. She died at Clayton on the afternoon of Sunday 14 June 1891, of cholera morbus, a few hours after dressing her children for Sunday school and sending for the doctor too late. She left five children, the youngest of whom were made wards of the Barbour County court that autumn.

Barbour County, Alabama issued a marriage licence to “Henry Bradly and Elvira Loveless, both of full age” on 18 December 1867, and the Judge of Probate, J. S. The minister never sent the licence back: the printed return underneath — ‘I hereby certify that the above named persons were duly married by me on the ___ day of ___’ — was left blank, so the county book records the authority to marry them and never the wedding itself.

Loveless is how this family has her, and it is not yet proved. It comes from the index entries of her two youngest daughters’ death records, half a lifetime apart — Elveria Loveless on Katie’s in 1924, Elvira Loveless on Alice’s in 1956 — and the screenshot taken of them turned out to be a different document altogether, so neither has been checked against the record itself. Two informants a generation apart agreeing on so unusual a name is worth a good deal. It is not the same as a marriage return, and the marriage return has not been found.

64.s:
John Bell was born on 13 January 1807 in South Carolina. His son’s obituary says his parents brought the family to Alabama from Darlington District about 1830 and settled in the neighbourhood where they stayed for the next century. He is certainly in Alabama by 1836, because in that year he served as a private in Captain White’s company, Regiment of Alabama Volunteers, in the Creek War — a fact nobody in this family knew until 2026, and one that survives only because the government eventually paid him for it in land. He was settled in Barbour County before 1837, and every one of his children was born in Alabama, the eldest, Mary, about 1836 or 1837.

He began buying early. On 19 July 1838 John H. Miller sold him about 189 acres in Township 10, Range 26 for five hundred dollars, Ann Caroline Miller releasing her dower the same afternoon. In January 1841, from Alabama, he sold off a forty-acre Georgia gold-lottery lot in what had just become Forsyth County for thirty dollars, and signed the deed himself — John F Bell — which is worth knowing in a generation where so many men made their mark.

The censuses follow him across half a century. In 1840 there is a boy and a girl under five in the house. In 1850 he is forty-three and farming, with his wife Laney — South Carolina born like him — and Mary 13, William 11, John 9, Kervin 4 and Laney 2. Two of those children matter to this family: William, who would die a Confederate pensioner in 1924, leaving an estate that scattered across his nieces and nephews and so paid out the seven shares that finally proved who Tom Bell’s children were; and John, who would become John T. Bell and father Thomas Jefferson Bell. In 1860 he returns four thousand dollars in land and ten thousand in personal estate, and in the Alabama cotton country of that year a figure like that is largely a statement about people: a John Bell of Barbour County stands in the 1860 slave schedule, and although the name is common the identification is probable. In August 1870 he is sixty-three, with Laney at sixty-four and two grown children still at home, Mary and Archibald — and the very next dwelling on the page is his son John T. Bell, twenty-seven, with a wife and four small children. By June 1880 he is seventy-two and a widower, and he tells the enumerator, in the first census year that asked, that both his own parents were born in South Carolina.

In April 1853 President Franklin Pierce signed his patent: warrant 4615, forty acres and eleven hundredths of an acre, for the Creek War service. He sold that same forty to William Bounds in 1858, and for a generation afterwards his neighbours’ deeds navigated by “the east corner of the Bell forty.” In 1876, at sixty-nine, he gave a crop lien in his own voice — “I John F Bell being indebted to J. C. Jones … thirty five dollars … to make a crop the present year on my plantation in Barbour County Alabama.”

On 1 August 1890, at eighty-three, he divided the home place by deeds of gift — 203⅓ acres each to his son Curvin and his daughter Mary, each to take effect after his death, “I however, holding and retaining the ownership and comfort of said above described lands during my natural life time.” The boundary runs past “the big gate leading to the house” on the public road from Clayton to Louisville. That is why he left no probate file: he had given the farm away and kept the comfort of it. He died on 21 November 1890, and the following November his heirs petitioned to sell 604 acres containing “the John Bell homestead and out houses” for division — in equal thirds to William, to John T., and to the five children of the daughter who had married a Farrior. The boundaries of that tract name the neighbours, and they explain a good deal: the Daniel Norton land to the south, which is why two Bell wives later married a Norton, and the old William Beasley place, in whose little family burying ground he himself lies.

65.s:
She was born in South Carolina about 1806 and came to Alabama as a young wife. In August 1840 she is a tally mark in a column — one woman aged thirty to forty in John Bell’s house in Barbour County, with a baby boy and a little girl. In 1850 she has a name, Laney, and five children. In 1860 she is fifty-three, and the family is prosperous: her husband returns four thousand dollars in land and ten thousand in personal estate. In 1870 she is sixty-four, keeping house, with her grown daughter Mary and her son Archibald still at home, and her son John T. Bell farming the next place along with a wife and four small children.

Three different enumerators in three different hands wrote her name down, and all three wrote Laney. The same 1860 man who wrote her name wrote “S. Carolina” in the birthplace column of the same line, so the capital in her name is his L and not his C.

Then she is gone. By June 1880 her husband is enumerated as a widower, living with a lodger and a girl of fourteen, his children grown and scattered. A transcription of the Beasley family’s little burying ground reads “Bell, Laney (1803 – 6-17-1873)”, which falls inside the window the censuses allow — but no one has photographed the stone, and the plot is a rail-fenced square of a dozen markers standing in second growth on the farm that bounded her husband’s.

Fifty-one years after she died, her eldest son’s death certificate called her Viney. Three census-takers had called her Laney. Nobody now alive knows which she answered to.

So the six were born roughly 1805×1820 — the window in which John Bell was born, 13 January 1807, and the window of Archibald’s marriage to Martha, who released dower in 1809 and 1817.

⭐⭐ And his household held a boy of exactly the right age, twice [BELL-159]. The 1820 Sumter schedule (page 115, indexed “Arel Bell”) tallies one male aged 10 and under 16 — John was thirteen. The 1830 schedule (page 66, indexed “Achable Bell”) tallies one male aged 20 and under 30 — John was twenty-three, and his family left for Alabama “about 1830.” Archibald himself is 45-and-upwards in 1820 and 50–60 in 1830. ⚠ But the bracket is not exclusive: of the seven Bell households on the 1830 Sumter schedule, the elder John Bell’s (p. 93) also holds an anonymous male 20–30 [BELL-166] — the census cannot choose between the two roofs.

⭐ The neighbours run for twenty-six years. Robert Severance is the household directly below him in 1820, sells him land in 1836, and his estate bounds Archibald’s farm in 1846. William Copeland is on the 1830 page and witnesses the will. The Amosons are on both pages, and a daughter married one of them.

⭐⭐ 11 Sep 2026 [BELL-721] — A NEW DEED, A SECOND DOWER RENUNCIATION, AND HIS NAME IN A CLERK’S OWN PEN. Archibald Bell → John B. Divine, 22 Feb 1817, Darlington Deed Book G p. 204: 127 acres “between Bay Branch and Newmans Swamp,” provably the tract he bought from James Hudson in 1810. ⭐ MARTHA BELL renounced dower on it on 24 Feb 1817, by mark, before John Huggins J.P. — a SECOND certified renunciation, eight years after the 1809 one, before the same magistrate. ⭐⭐⭐ And the proof clause calls him “ARCHEY BELL” — image-verified, in the same hand that wrote “Archibald” three times on the same page. That is the Arel/Achable/Archable index-mangling problem caught at its source: his neighbours called him Archey. ⚠ His residence formula oscillates and is quoted rather than smoothed: 1807 “of the same place” (Darlington) · 1810 “of the district of Sumpter” · 1817 “of the State and District aforesaid” (Darlington) — he held land in both. The 127 acres left the family in 1818 (Devine → James Reynolds). Outstanding — and these are the reasons the grade has not moved [BELL-148, BELL-162]: ⛔ No instrument names John Bell as his son, and none places the will’s John Bell in Alabama. ⭐ And the negative is stronger than “not found” — the receipt class most likely never existed. Record Book M, read at the ink [BELL-526]: no return was EVER filed on this estate. Archy Bell’s block (pp. 238–241) ends at Evan Benbow with nothing after it and the Ordinary’s printed qualification line “was duly qualified on the ___ day of ___ 18__” was left blank forever — while the estate on the facing page, in the same clerk’s hand, got a full return filed 20 Jan 1840 with $38.00 coming in from “W. Montgomery OF ALABAMA.” So the one document class that would style a legatee “John Bell of Alabama” moves from unfound toward improbable. ⛔⛔ The cheapest test that could have settled this is now PERMANENTLY closed, not merely unrun [BELL-562]: [BELL-162] named searching the estates of Thomas Bell and John Bell of Sumter as the one action that could materially raise this node — but the Sumter Probate Court’s own General Index to Estates 1784–1960 holds nine Bell entries in total, and there is NO John, Thomas, William Jr., James, Drury, Jesse, Benjamin or Robert Bell estate in Sumter County at any date, ever. The two-roofs problem can never be resolved from probate. ⛔ Two other Sumter Bell households in 1820 — Thomas Bell, on the line immediately above him, and John Bell — also held a boy of John’s age, and if those men are his brothers then the rivals are his nephews, sharing every neighbour and every migration route. ⛔ And the rival persists: in 1830 the elder John Bell’s household (the probable “John Bell Senr” of the 1839 bond) still holds a male 20–30, while Thomas Bell’s household has vanished from the schedule entirely, leaving his boy unlocated [BELL-166]. ⚠ The Darlington-vs-Sumter question has narrowed sharply: beyond the shared “Archy”/“Archibald” usage and the three surnames that cross the creek with him (Huggins, Chaney, Newman), the February 1839 resurvey of his own home plantation — the Sumter estate tract itself — is headed “South Carolina, DARLINGTON DISTRICT” by the deputy surveyor [BELL-170]. His home paperwork crossed the line; a single instrument equating the two men in words is still wanting. ⚠ The 1820 and 1830 tallies also leak by one boy, which is unexplained. ⭐ And the exclusion now runs one way [BELL-172]: no John Bell of the will’s generation is documentable in Sumter or Darlington District in 1840 or 1850 — the one right-age Sumter candidate resolves to James P. Bell by his own will — so the will’s John left the home districts, and ours is the only located right-age John with any documented tie to them. ⭐⭐ 12 Sep 2026 — THE NAMED RIVAL THIS FIELD HAS BEEN MISSING, AND HE IS STILL STANDING: A JOHN BELL OF YORK DISTRICT [BELL-735–BELL-746]. Under the Genealogical Proof Standard a convergent case is not proof while a named competing candidate stands unexcluded, and this one is age-perfect in two consecutive censuses — male 20–29 in York in 1830, male 30–39 in 1840 (roll 516 p. 304, one enslaved person, immediate neighbour John Springs). His father has no name in any record, which is exactly why he cannot be retired. ⭐ What was done about him on 11–12 Sep, so nobody re-runs it: all 324 York documents whose OCR contains “John Bell” were harvested and read — 93 kinship contexts, every one a false positive; not one instrument names his father, mother, sibling or child; the Withers will of 27 Oct 1845 (his last trace) shows him as a subscribing witness and nothing else, signing plain; all thirteen Bells in the 1850 York schedule were read off the manuscript — no John, no Bell widow, three of seven households not York-rooted; the mangled-surname escape is closed in both 1850 and 1860 and in both York and Chester (the one B400 collision, “Ball John 37 NC,” is excluded as North-Carolina-born); and no estate or guardianship was ever opened for any John Bell in York. ⚠ But he did NOT simply vanish: a John Bell was decreed against in York in 1848 and a “John Bell Junr” stands on Dr J. B. Hunter’s books in 1851 — so “absent from the 1850 schedule” is a fact about the schedule, not about the man (self-correction #437). ⛔⛔ A Catawba-leasehold argument that would have excluded him was raised and REFUTED by an adversary the same night [BELL-746]: the Pettus lease table’s “formerly X’s” field contradicts itself on the very tract, an unrelated adult James Davis was already leasing on Steel Creek in 1797, and the series — which names sons-in-law, daughters and heirs constantly — carries not one kin word in the rows at issue. ⭐ FOUR candidates now stand unexcluded: Christopher Bell of York’s seven unnamed heirs · Robert Bell of York’s own son John · a possible Broad-River-side York Bell family · an ordinary unrelated transfer. ⭐ 12 Sep, later — that last strand was TESTED and came back against it [BELL-748]: the 1833 York sale at which a “John Bell Sen” bought is Rev. William Dickson’s of CROWDERS CREEK — western York, the Broad River side — and not one Bell appears among his legatees, witnesses or receipt-signers. ⭐⭐ And an ironmaster’s ledger from that same neighbourhood carries two John Bells, tagging one “John Bell Mountain” while tagging a neighbour “James Moore Indian Land” two lines below in the same clerk’s hand — a clerk who used patronymics (“W’m Felts, James Son”) freely and reached for a place instead. So the Senior/Junior pair sits on the WESTERN side of the district while this rival’s whole documented world is EASTERN, on the Catawba Indian Land: “John Bell Senior of York” now reads as a third man, not as his father. ⭐ Excluded and off the board: the Pickens rival (born North Carolina, stated twice), John Bell Jr of Sumter (held a note in Aug 1821, when our man was fourteen), and the Georgia gold-lottery route (lot 891 was drawn by John F. BALL of Twiggs). ⭐⭐ What would settle it, named and reachable: the original 1830 Catawba lease — SCDAH holds the 128 originals returned in 1840, transfers signed and dated on the dorse, and Robert Bell’s son John signed cleanly three times in 1802–04, so a John Bell who MARKS that lease is a third man; and the Secretary of State, Papers Pertaining to State Grants on Catawba Indian Lands, 1798–1853, whose post-1840 neighbour affidavits recite who held a tract, from whom, and how — a series this project has never opened.

⭐ 22 Aug 2026 [BELL-484]: the Darlington Archibald (wife Martha, 1809–1820) and the Sumter Archy (wife Margaret by 7 Oct 1829) are now one man stated in the record — “Archd Bell of the district of Sumpter” buying the Darlington tract on 4 May 1810, and “Archey Bell … Margaret Bell the wife of the within named Archibald Bell” on one 1829 deed. His Boykin land came “sold to said A. Bell by General Cantey” — a purchase, not a descent from William Rasor Bell. He witnessed for Jonathan Newman of Sumter District in 1805 and beside a John Bell Senr in 1820 — association, never kinship. Still no document ties him to W.R.B.’s son Archibald; the estate bundle (Sumter Box 10 Pkg 3) was opened the same week — nine leaves, no division, no receipts [BELL-485].

⭐ [BELL-485]: his own estate packet is found (Sumter Bundle 113 Pkg 15): the original signed will of 4 Oct 1839 names wife Margaret, five younger children (Benjamin Sumter, Margaret Louisa, Ezekiel Dixon [#238 — not “Nixon”], Hugh McCallum, Columbus Campbell) and six older (John, Celey Amoson, Harriett, Martha, William Wesley, Jane) — and no father or brother; the sale bill shows the family buying its household back; J. W. Stuckey was guardian ad litem for the three youngest in 1846–47. William Rasor Bell’s own bundle is nine leaves with no division or receipts, the Ordinary’s books of 1809–39 were never filmed, and Sumter equity 1795–1870 holds no Bell partition — so the document that would tie 128 to 256 is not online anywhere now searched.

⭐⚠ 24 Aug 2026 [BELL-502–503, #229]: Archy is now documented holding and mortgaging (1815, to Zachariah Cantey) the 345-acre Lynches Creek tract whose 1785 survey was laid out for William Rasor Bell — the first document putting him on node 256’s ground — but a seventh adversary pass [BELL-512] kept the link at hypothesis: W.R.B. never owned the tract (a locative recital, not a title — and the recital’s companion word is now settled as HARRISON at the ink, an inherited 1780s adjoiner call, not a plat call [BELL-517]), Archy was a serial open-market buyer, and land never conveyed keeps its dead owner’s name for decades.

⛔ 25 Aug 2026 — the online case is CLOSED at the structure, not the query [BELL-514, BELL-517, BELL-518, BELL-521, BELL-522]: the Kershaw conveyance indexes 1791–1824 hold no Bell of ours in either direction (and Book A only opens in 1791, so 1786×91 is unanswerable there); no suit in five volumes of Sumter judgments 1804–26 ever touched the estate — proven in a record class where the Ordinary demonstrably sued his own administrators; the administrator Charles Williams (“of Georgetown district,” Durant in-laws, a rule-41 defaulting guardian in 1821) is dense in Sumter’s equity record 1819–27 with zero Bell connection; and the fiduciary volumes that would carry the one settling line — a distributee entry naming Archibald — were never filmed by anybody: they are SCDAH’s unfilmed Returns Books L 43049 (1816–1916) and Journals L 43051, paper in Columbia. The decisive documents are now all offline and named; the grade holds where seven adversaries left it.

⭐⭐ 9 Sep 2026 [BELL-666] — the widow, found whole. Margaret was a DIXON widow when Archy married her: her sons John H. Dixon — the executor Archy trusted with everything — and William B. Dixon were his stepsons, which is why he named a son Ezekiel Dixon Bell (as Hugh McCallum Bell honours the other executor). After Archy died she remarried a SEVERANCE, tripping the will’s widowhood condition and triggering the 1846–47 partition — and the “Margaret Severance” who bought the plantation on 3 May 1847 was the widow buying her own place back. Her 6 Jan 1849 will names four of the five second-family children — Columbus Campbell Bell is absent, presumed died 1839×1849. The estate never touched Equity (both index B-blocks read whole, with the Belvin partition as control): the whole settlement ran in Ordinary, and its citation names no residences.

27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep. Nothing new reached this node. Bounded negative recorded: Find a Grave memorial search firstname=Archibald lastname=Bell, South Carolina, death 1839 ±10 years — no memorial for him or for any Bell of his household. No burial is known for anyone in this generation, and no likeness can exist. The tunnel lanes (Newspapers.com, Ancestry) did not reach the pre-1840 South Carolina material before they were stopped.
128.s:
Archibald Bell — “Archy” to the clerks who wrote down his name, and the spelling is his neighbours’, not an index’s: a Darlington proof clause of 1817 calls him ARCHEY on the same page where the same hand writes ARCHIBALD three times — was born about 1770 to 1775. If the reconstruction holds he was a son of William Rasor Bell, a planter of Salem in Sumter District who died leaving nine sons, two daughters and a widow named Mary. No document says so.

He farmed on both banks of Lynches Creek, the water that divides Sumter District from Darlington, and his own paperwork crossed the line with him: he is “of the same place” in Darlington in 1807, “of the district of Sumpter” in 1810, and “of the State and District aforesaid” in Darlington again in 1817. He bought land in Darlington in 1806 and sold a hundred and twenty-seven acres of it in February 1817, between Bay Branch and Newmans Swamp. His wife Martha released her dower twice, in October 1809 and February 1817, both times before the same justice of the peace, John Huggins, whose family would later marry into his. He was witnessing and swearing to deeds across the creek in Sumter from 1810, and in 1812 James Hutson senior conveyed land to “Archd Bell of the district of Sumpter” — a Darlington deed whose own index, in the same volume, writes the name out as Hudson James to Archd Bell. In 1815 he mortgaged a 345-acre tract on Lynches Creek to Zachariah Cantey — the same ground a surveyor had laid out for William Rasor Bell thirty years before.

Martha died, and he married Margaret, a Dixon widow with grown sons of her own; that is why one of his children is called Ezekiel Dixon Bell and why John H. Dixon, his stepson, was the executor he trusted with everything. They had five more children, with names that read like a roll-call of his neighbours: Benjamin Sumter, Margaret Louisa, Ezekiel Dixon, Hugh McCallum, Columbus Campbell. He was sued in 1830 for a witness fee. He was still buying land from Robert Severance in 1836, at sixty, the man who had been the household directly below his on the 1820 census page.

He made his will on 4 October 1839, weak in body but of sound mind, and it was filed on the 22nd. He left Margaret the 275-acre plantation for her life or her widowhood, then to the five children of the second marriage; the residue he divided among six more — “John Bell, Celey Amoson, Harriet Bell, Martha Bell, William Wesley Bell, and Jane Bell.” He left a set of blacksmith’s tools and thirteen geese. And he directed that the rest of his property be sold to pay his debts, “including my negroe boy Limus” — a boy of about fifteen who had already been pledged to Henry Scarborough nine months earlier. When the appraisers came on 26 October they valued Limus at seven hundred dollars against an estate of eleven hundred and eighteen. Sixty-three per cent of everything Archy Bell owned was one enslaved child. After the sale he disappears from the record.

His widow remarried a Severance, which tripped the will’s widowhood clause and forced the partition of 1846–47 — and the “Margaret Severance” who bought the plantation in May 1847 was the widow buying her own place back.

Whether the John Bell he named first among his older children is the John Bell who went to Alabama about 1830 is the question this family has not yet answered, and seven adversarial reviews have refused to answer it for him.

129.x:
Also recorded: wife of Archibald Bell by October 1809; living February 1817, Darlington District, South Carolina

⭐ “Martha Bell, the wife of the above named Archibald Bell” appeared twice before a Darlington District justice of the peace — 17 October 1809 and 24 February 1817 — and, examined privately and separately from her husband as the law required of a married woman, released her dower in land he was selling. In 1809 she made her mark. ⭐ The 1809 record, found 13 Aug 2026 [BELL-150], moves her eight years earlier than this file had her, and closes the gap between her documented marriage and John Bell’s birth in January 1807 to under three years.

⚠ She is the weaker of these two nodes and must be judged separately from her husband [BELL-148, BELL-162]. For Martha to be John Bell’s mother, three things must all hold: that the Darlington Archibald and the Sumter Archy are one man; that Martha was the first of his wives; and that the earlier family in his will is hers.

Outstanding: ⛔ No source anywhere states that Martha was the mother of anybody. ⛔ Every document naming her is a Darlington instrument, while every document of the will and the estate is Sumter — so she depends entirely on a merge that is still undocumented. ⚠ His 1839 will names a wife Margaret, and “children by his second marriage” establishes at least two marriages, not exactly two; a Martha who was wife number two of three, and stepmother rather than mother to the older children, fits every record equally well. ⚠ The 1830 Sumter schedule shows the woman of that house aged 30–40, who would have been only nine to nineteen in 1809 — so she is probably Margaret, and Martha is probably already dead. Her maiden name and her dates are unknown.

⭐ [BELL-484]: Martha living 20 Sept 1820 (dower, Sumter); Margaret is Archibald’s wife by 7 Oct 1829 (dower, Sumter) — the change falls 1820×1829, not c.1830.

⭐ 9 Sep 2026 [BELL-666]: the second wife is now documented in her own right — a Dixon widow who became Margaret Severance after Archy’s death (her own will, 6 Jan 1849). This sharpens the Martha→Margaret transition (1820×1829 per [BELL-647]) but still says nothing about which wife mothered John.

27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep. Nothing new reached this node on any lane. Bounded negative: no Find a Grave memorial, no burial, no maiden name, no dates beyond the two dower renunciations and the 1820 × 1829 window already held.
129.s:
Martha Bell appears twice, briefly, and both times because the law required a man’s wife to be asked. In October 1809, and again in February 1817, her husband Archibald sold land in Darlington District, South Carolina, and each time she came before a justice of the peace — the same man both times, John Huggins — who examined her privately and separately from her husband, as the statute said, to be sure a wife was not signing away her dower under his eye. She declared she did it freely and voluntarily, without compulsion, dread or fear of any person whomsoever. In 1809 she made her mark.

She was still living in September 1820. By October 1829 Archibald’s wife is Margaret, a Dixon widow, so Martha died somewhere in that decade.

That is all we have of her. No source anywhere says she was the mother of anybody. For her to be John Bell’s mother three separate things must hold — that the Darlington Archibald and the Sumter Archy are one man, that Martha was the first of his wives rather than the second, and that the older family in his 1839 will is hers — and whether she was is a hypothesis resting on her husband’s.

256.x:
Also recorded: planter of Claremont County; earliest record the Isaac Higgs appraisement, Kershaw District, 21 June 1784 (⚠ #279 withdraws #275 — the Stokes deed is 1787, not 1777); later of Salem, Sumter District; will 26 Dec 1803; administration with the will annexed granted 15 Apr 1809 to Charles Williams — his named executor Moses Gordon never served

⭐ The one link on this branch that is ASSERTED in a document: his will of 26 December 1803 — “I give & bequeath unto my beloved sons, John Bell, Archibald Bell, Thomas Bell, William Bell, James Bell, Drury Bell, Jesse Bell, Benjamin Bell, & Robert Bell…” — recorded 15 March 1809, executor Moses Gordon, witnesses Lewis Bell, Mary Stuckey and a Douglas [BELL-152, BELL-181]. ⭐ And the will names TWO DAUGHTERS as well as the nine sons, which the roster usually quoted omits: MARY BELL (a feather bed) and ELIZABETH BELL (a bed, “& One Cow & Calf which is now call’d hers” — the only line in the document about a child’s own particular possession). ⚠ Never used as research handles, and they should be: daughters marry, and married daughters sign receipts under their husbands’ names [BELL-630]. Wife Mary took a life estate; the land was to be sold at her death or remarriage and divided among the nine sons — that sale, not yet found, would name the whole sibling generation in one instrument.

⭐ His documented life: buying Micajah Stokes’s whole personalty in 1784; settling it on Stokes’s children “for love, good will and affection” in 1787 (the language of kinship); land co-surveyed with Frederick Bell — a documented Revolutionary claimant — on the North Branch of Black River in 1787; co-signing a Darlington-proved deed with Frederick, Mary and John Bell in 1794 [BELL-182].

⭐⭐ 11 Sep 2026 [BELL-718] — HE IS NOW DOCUMENTED IN CAMDEN DISTRICT IN 1787, HOLDING LAND ADJOINING FREDERICK BELL. The grant of 1,000 acres to Frederick Bell, 7 March 1787, recites the tract as “Situate in the District of Camden on the No Branch of Black River … N.E. on Land Surveyed for Wm Rasor Bell, Frederick Bell, Jonathan Newman and Lewis Mathews” — read off the printed grant form. ⭐ Frederick is the man who administered John Bell of Camden’s 1786 estate, and Jonathan Newman is Archy’s own neighbour — the man Archy witnessed for in 1805, and who appraised W.R.B.’s estate in 1809. The neighbour set holds across three generations on one line of one grant. ⚠⚠ Association, NOT paternity — and the record-class fallacy applies with full force: these are the documents that happen to survive, not a census of the relationships that existed. ⭐ A 1794 instrument carries four Bells at once — “Witnesses Wm. Rasor Bell / John Bell / John x Ward ‖ Fredk Bell / her Mary x Bell mark” ⚠ (a TYPED TRANSCRIPT volume, not the manuscript — PROBABLE). ⛔ LEAD — one witness in FIVE filmings, not five witnesses: SCDAH’s index carries “KERSHAW, JOSEPH … SURVIVORS OF ELY KERSHAW VS WILLIAM RASOR BELL, JUDGMENT ROLL, 1785.” Outstanding: ⛔ Why this node is `hyp`, stated as its OWN defect and not node 128’s (corrected 6 Sep 2026 after a three-node grade audit + adversary pass): the 256→128 link — that the Archibald Bell named in W.R.B.’s 1803 will is our Archy Bell of Sumter who died in 1839 — rests on ZERO asserting sources. Across every decade 1780s–1850s of Sumter (1,850 records), Kershaw (670) and Darlington (637), not one instrument styles Archibald Bell as anyone’s son, and not one names a distributee or legatee of William Rasor Bell [BELL-484], [BELL-503], [BELL-512], [BELL-557]. Adjudicated and refused SEVEN times, twice under the explicit heading “128↔256”. ⚠ This node would still be `hyp` if node 128 closed tomorrow — the previous wording of this field stated node 128’s defect instead of this one, which made a single problem look like three on the board. ⭐ What would move it to probable: one line naming Archibald Bell as a distributee of William Rasor Bell — SCDAH Returns Books L 43049 vol. 1 / Journals L 43051, unfilmed paper in Columbia, item ② of the request filed 4 Sep 2026 [BELL-602]. ⛔ 2 Oct 2026 [BELL-775]: SCDAH found no William Bell in the Returns Books index (volumes and spellings checked not stated; Archibald’s returns not addressed), and the Journals L 43051 are unindexed, so staff will not search them. This route now needs a paid researcher in Columbia. ⛔ Separately, and NOT what this badge grades: no document yet ties our John F. Bell of Barbour Co. to Archibald — that is node 128’s own `hyp`. ⛔ His own parents are unidentified; the leading frame is the Raccoon Swamp Bell clan of Albemarle Parish, Surry/Sussex Co., Virginia — narrowed hard on 14 Aug 2026: Rev. James Bell’s will (Sussex WB C p.310, proved 15 Oct 1778) was read off the will book and names six children — no William, no Frederick, no Lewis — ELIMINATING the patriarch’s heir-branch [BELL-193]. Hannah Bell’s will (WB B p.153, proved 17 Mar 1768) reveals the two places a father can still hide: an unnamed SON WHO DIED before 1765 (father of grandsons Silvanus & Zadock Bell), and an ABSENT son Benjamin — “provided he comes himself in person” — gone from Virginia by 1765 [BELL-194]. The patriarch’s own 1746 will, read the same day [BELL-196], names FIVE sons — John Jr., Burrell, Benjamin, Balaam, James — no William in the clan’s senior generation; if WRB belongs here it is as an unnamed grandson via BURRELL or BALAAM — the adversary-verified register work [BELL-197, BELL-199] closed John Jr.’s issue at two sons (Sylvanus & John, by PHOEBE STOKES — Micajah’s sister), and found the second dead son: Balaam Bell d. 1755, widow Mary, posthumous daughter Phoebe — his 1745×55 window fits WRB’s birth. Silvanus STOKES Junr witnessed the 1746 will — the Stokes intimacy begins in Virginia, a generation before WRB’s kinship-language settlement on Micajah Stokes’s children. Otherwise the descent runs outside the clan, e.g. Richard Bell of Lawne's Creek, d. 1734, whose sons include a William [BELL-183–185, BELL-191, BELL-196]. ⛔ The “Rasor” name — likely his mother’s or grandmother’s family — has no located source; no Rasor appears in the parish register. ⭐ His own Patriot case is ONE PRINTED INDENT — Book G No. 30, “Issued the 22d. April 1784 To Mr. William Bell for Eleven pounds Eight Shillings and Seven pence Sterling for two Horses impressed for Militia Use in October 1780.” It is the only William Bell indent in South Carolina unattributed to any man, and no DAR or SAR lineage claims it. ⚠ Nothing yet ties its claimant to him rather than to one of at least six other South Carolina William Bells, and the Chester “W:m Bell Sen:r” is not excluded. ⛔ 29 Sep 2026 [BELL-774]: SCDAH read the ORIGINAL stub (reply of 21 Sep) — it says exactly what the print says, with no district, auditor, assignee or attached slip in its margin, and the Treasury’s Schedule of indents cancelled (S126171 Book 1 p. 85) writes nothing off against it. The stub route to seating it is closed; it stays open, unseated and unexcluded. Frederick’s is now PROBABLE: three indents incl. 50 days at the Siege of Charleston in Capt. John Nelson’s company — a company three pensioners place in the Black River / Salem country of old Camden District [BELL-192, BELL-195].

⭐⭐ Where the case stood after the sweep of 19–20 August 2026 [BELL-382–406]. Book G No. 30 survived three separate attempts to take it off the board in four days and remains unseated and unexcluded. What strengthened: the printed text was transcribed from the surviving counterfoil itself — Wates’s asterisk/dagger marks are a survival map, Book G’s stubs go missing only from No. 251, and No. 30 is unmarked, 220 entries inside the intact run [BELL-385]. The evidence type is pre-approved with an exact precedent: DAR ancestor A008802 carries 46 approved lineages on a single stub-entry citation [BELL-392]. The rival Abbeville claimant is now excluded on his own itemised schedule, and the Chester man’s claims fell from three to two — one of them proved to be William Ball — so £11.8.7 no longer sits between his sums but above both [BELL-395]. What was closed off: no second October-1780 impressment claim exists anywhere in the twelve printed volumes [BELL-384, BELL-391]; his neighbours left six indents between them in 12,242, so no cohort argument can be built [BELL-394]; and the numbered Treasury returns were alphabetical work-batches, never geographic [BELL-396]. Book G No. 30 is cited by nobody in either lineage society, checked against the full source citation of every South Carolina Bell in both [BELL-392].

⭐ And his own paper trail was pushed back and sharpened. There is no South Carolina record of him before 1785, tested across seven name-forms — the apparent 1777/1778 hits are index frames carrying the 1785 judgment roll [BELL-400, BELL-406]. He has two 1785 surveys, not one: 150 acres on Bane Branch, 30 April, and 400 acres on Lynches Creek, 15 June — and both grants issued to Samuel Boykin, who paid the treasury fee, which was the local norm [BELL-400]. ⭐ His own plat survives and is cited to the page — Surveyor-General, Land Plats vol. 9Q p. 383 — and the Surveyor-General’s own index dates it 30 April 1784, a year before the grant’s recital. Volume 9Q is one of six Q-volumes never microfilmed; it is the arbiter of whether his South Carolina floor is 1784 or 1785 [BELL-406].
