256.s:
William Rasor Bell appears out of nowhere in 1784, already styled planter, in Claremont County of old Camden District, South Carolina. In June of that year he helped appraise Isaac Higgs’s estate in Kershaw District; in April 1787 he bought Micajah Stokes’s entire personalty — an enslaved woman named Ann, the horses, the beds, nineteen cattle, for £105 15s — and the very next day began giving it all back to Stokes’s children “for love, good will and affection,” which in the language of that century usually means family. Ann was conveyed twice in two days between two households that were probably kin; she is the only person he is documented ever to have held, and he held her for a day. His own 1790 household was ten people and no one in slavery.

He had two surveys in 1785 — a hundred and fifty acres on Bare Branch in April, four hundred on Lynches Creek in June — and the grants on both issued to Samuel Boykin, who had paid the treasury fee, as was the local habit. His land lay on both watersheds at once: a later grant describes eighty acres “on Charleston Road between Black River and Lynches Creek, bounded N.W. by William Rasor Bell and Fred:k Bells Land.” A 1787 grant to Frederick Bell recites its north-east line as “Land Surveyed for Wm Rasor Bell, Frederick Bell, Jonathan Newman and Lewis Mathews” — one line of one document carrying three surnames that stay beside this family for three generations.

There is a single sheet of paper that might make him a Patriot. Book G, stub number 30, in South Carolina’s Revolutionary indents: “Issued the 22d. April 1784 To Mr. William Bell for Eleven pounds Eight Shillings and Seven pence Sterling for two Horses impressed for Militia Use in October 1780.” It is the only William Bell indent in the state that no man has ever been attached to, and no lineage society claims it. Nothing yet ties its claimant to him rather than to one of at least six other South Carolina William Bells, and the original stub, read at Columbia in 2026, carries no district, no auditor and no assignee to help.

On the day after Christmas 1803, “very sick & weak in body,” he made his will. It divides a plain farmer’s world among a wife and eleven children: the plantation and stock to Mary for her life, to be sold at her death or remarriage and divided among nine sons — “John Bell, Archibald Bell, Thomas Bell, William Bell, James Bell, Drury Bell, Jesse Bell, Benjamin Bell, & Robert Bell” — and feather beds to two daughters, Mary and Elizabeth, Elizabeth also getting “One Cow & Calf which is now call’d hers,” the only line in the document about a child’s own particular possession. The witnesses were Lewis Bell, Mary Stuckey and a Douglas.

He was dead by 1809. His executor Moses Gordon never served, and administration with the will annexed went on 15 April 1809 to Charles Williams of Georgetown District. Jonathan Newman — the man Archy Bell had witnessed for in 1805 — appraised the estate. The sale of the land that would have named all nine sons in one instrument has never been found, and the fiduciary volumes that would carry it are unfilmed paper in Columbia.

His own parents are unidentified. The leading frame is the Raccoon Swamp Bell clan of Albemarle Parish in Surry and Sussex counties, Virginia, where the patriarch’s 1746 will names five sons and no William; if he belongs there at all it is as an unnamed grandson. And the name Rasor — almost certainly his mother’s or grandmother’s family — has never been found anywhere.

257.s:
Mary was the wife of William Rasor Bell of Salem, in Sumter District, South Carolina, and she outlived him. His will of 26 December 1803 left her the plantation and the stock for her lifetime “for the benefit of my children, if she remains single” — the land to be sold at her death or her remarriage and the money divided among their nine sons. When the will was proved in March 1809 she was still living and had not married again.

Nothing else of her is certain. A “Mary x Bell” signs by mark on a Darlington-proved family deed of 1794 beside William Rasor, John and Frederick Bell, and that may be her or may be Frederick’s wife. Her maiden name is unproven — the “Mary English” of the online trees is an unverified compiled claim and is not adopted here. The date of her death, which is the event that triggered the sale of the land among her sons, is unknown, and finding it would uncover the one instrument that names that whole generation at once.

She is on this chart at Alec’s direction, and her grade follows her husband’s: the step from William Rasor Bell down to Archy Bell of Sumter rests on no asserting source at all.

512.s:
This man is a candidate, not a proven ancestor, and the whole line above him waits on him.

If the abstract is right, he is the John Bell who sat on Bear Swamp in Duplin County, North Carolina before the Revolution — seated there by 1762, selling his plantation to his eldest son Frederick in 1765 for a hundred pounds and going on living on it, still “Sr” in 1773, and then gone from every North Carolina record. Frederick Bell is documented in Camden District, South Carolina by May 1777, so the son’s crossing is proved; the father’s is not. Somewhere after January 1773 a John Bell came four hundred miles south to the Black River country, and on 18 October 1786 he made a will there.

That will survives only as a printed abstract, and the abstract is careful in a way that matters. It claims three people in his own voice, by rank: my eldest son Frederick Bell, my eldest daughter Penelope Stuckey, wife Mary. Then it hands money to two more men — to John Bell, and … sterling to William Rasor Bell — with nothing attached but a bare to. Which of those two, if either, was his son is precisely what nobody knows, and a 2004 message-board condensation that said “son William Rasor Bell” was putting in a word the abstract does not contain.

What supports the candidacy is circumstantial and good. John Stuckey of Duplin married a Penelope. Lewis Stuckey’s 1792 deed says his property “descended to me from my Grandfather John Bell,” and by 1794 Lewis is “now of the County of Salem, South Carolina.” In 1790 there was exactly one Frederick Bell in the state. And Frederick Bell is the man who administered this estate.

What stands against it is that nobody can read the original. The Camden probate books for 1786 to 1791 burned with the Claremont courthouse in 1801; the printed abstract’s page 5 is copyright-walled on every free lane; and the surviving packet — South Carolina Archives L 49055, Apartment 6, Package 180, thirteen frames on film C9228 — has never been read by anyone on this project. The route through Penelope’s husband is closed for good: John Stuckey left no Duplin estate file because a sheriff had already stripped him, selling his plantation on the west side of Bear Swamp to satisfy a judgment of £1,658 11s 0½d.

And if he is who the Bertie County papers suggest — a son of Robert Bell of Chowan and Bertie, who died intestate in 1738 — then his own father could not write. Robert signed with a big interlocked R B, while John and his brothers all signed their names.

513.s:
She is one clause in one printed abstract. Brent Holcomb’s summary of a will made in Camden District, South Carolina on 18 October 1786 names a wife Mary, alongside “eldest son Frederick Bell,” William Rasor Bell and “eldest daughter Penelope Stuckey.” That is the whole of her.

Her maiden name is unknown. No record of her has ever been read — not a deed, not a dower release, not a census line — and she is not documented anywhere apart from her husband. No Mary Bell appears in Camden District between 1777 and 1790 as grantor, witness, deponent or head of household, on ground where the same corpus turns up Frederick Bell by name seven times; a Mary Bell who witnessed by mark in Salem County in 1788 cannot be told apart from Frederick’s or William’s wives of the same name, and at least three Mary Bells are documented in that district across those decades.

She stands or falls entirely with her husband. If the identification of John Bell of Camden District fails, she is simply a different woman, and nothing written here would survive it.
